Mill explains production, wages, rent, trade and money, but he also insists that while the laws of production are fixed by nature, the distribution of wealth depends on human laws and customs and can be changed.
context: The book discusses cooperatives, the condition of workers, and the possibility of a stationary state in which growth stops and people turn to improving their lives instead, an idea that has found new readers today. Read the shorter [Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en), published the same year, for a very different answer to the same problems.

about: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' With that opening line Rousseau asks what could make political authority legitimate, and answers that it can only rest on an agreement among free and equal citizens, who together form a sovereign people guided by the general will.
context: Published in 1762 and banned at once in Geneva and Paris, The Social Contract became one of the texts of the French Revolution, and its ideas of popular sovereignty still shape modern democracies. It is short but demanding; read it alongside Hobbes's [Leviathan](/book/270?lang=en), which reaches very different conclusions from a similar starting point.

about: Rousseau imagines a boy named Emile raised from birth by a tutor in the countryside, away from the corruptions of society, and describes his education stage by stage: learning through the senses and experience rather than books, a trade for his hands, and religion and morality only when he is old enough to understand them.
context: Published in 1762, Emile was burned in Paris because of its chapter on religion, yet it transformed ideas about childhood and education. Its last book, on the education of Emile's future wife Sophie, provoked a famous reply from Mary Wollstonecraft in [A Vindication of the Rights of Woman](/book/299?lang=en).

about: In this short, personal book of 1637, Descartes tells how he decided to doubt everything he had been taught and rebuild knowledge on certain foundations. He gives four simple rules of method and arrives at the one thing he cannot doubt: 'I think, therefore I am.' From there he goes on to God, the body as a machine and the future of science.
context: Written in French rather than Latin so that ordinary readers could follow it, the Discourse was originally the preface to three scientific essays, including the one that introduced coordinate geometry. Readers have often compared its journey through doubt with the autobiography of [al-Ghazali](/author/ghazali?lang=en) five centuries earlier.

about: Spinoza's Ethics is written like a geometry book, with definitions, axioms and numbered propositions, yet its subject is how to live a free and joyful life. He argues that God and Nature are one and the same, that everything follows from necessity, and that our happiness grows as we understand our emotions instead of being driven by them.
context: Spinoza, a lens grinder expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community, did not dare publish it; it appeared in 1677, the year he died. It is one of the hardest and most rewarding books in philosophy, and many readers start with Part Three, on the emotions, before going back to the beginning.

about: Hume asks where our ideas come from and finds that all of them trace back to experience. His most famous argument is about cause and effect: we never actually see one thing make another happen, we only see one follow the other, and our expectation that the future will resemble the past rests on habit, not reason.
context: Published in 1748 as a clearer, shorter version of the first part of his [Treatise of Human Nature](/book/278?lang=en), the Enquiry also contains a famous chapter on miracles. Kant said Hume woke him from his dogmatic slumber, and the problem of induction he raised is still discussed today.

about: Hume wrote his Treatise in his twenties, in France, hoping to do for the study of the mind what Newton had done for the physical world. In three books on understanding, the passions and morality, he argues that the self is only a bundle of perceptions, that we cannot prove causes exist, and that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.
context: Published in 1739 and 1740, it 'fell dead-born from the press', as Hume put it, and he later rewrote its ideas in shorter books such as [An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding](/book/277?lang=en). Today it is considered one of the most important works of philosophy in English.

about: Young Candide is taught by his tutor Pangloss that this is the best of all possible worlds. Then he is kicked out of the castle for kissing the baron's daughter and sets off on a journey through war, shipwreck, the Lisbon earthquake, the Inquisition, slavery and the golden land of El Dorado, while Pangloss keeps insisting that everything is for the best.
context: Published anonymously in 1759 and banned almost at once, Candide is Voltaire's furious and very funny attack on philosophical optimism. Its final advice, that we must cultivate our garden, is still quoted. It is short, fast and the perfect introduction to the Enlightenment; continue with [Zadig](/book/280?lang=en).

about: Zadig is a wise and good young man in ancient Babylon, and his wisdom brings him nothing but trouble. In one famous chapter he describes the queen's lost dog and the king's runaway horse without having seen them, simply by reading their tracks, and is fined for it. He rises to become the king's minister, falls, becomes a slave and wanders the East, wondering whether justice governs the world.
context: Published in 1747 in the style of the Oriental tales that the Arabian Nights had made fashionable, Zadig is one of Voltaire's most charming stories. Its chapter of deduction from small clues is often cited as an ancestor of the detective story, long before [Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en).

about: Exiled to England in 1726, Voltaire spent more than two years there and came back an admirer. In these letters he describes the Quakers, the Parliament, the freedom of trade and religion, inoculation against smallpox, the science of Newton and the philosophy of Locke, and the strange genius of Shakespeare, always with an eye on what France lacked.
context: When the book appeared in French in 1734 it was condemned and burned in Paris, because every compliment to England was an attack on the French monarchy and church. It is lively, witty and a good place to see how the Enlightenment spread. Read [Candide](/book/279?lang=en) for Voltaire the storyteller.

about: These essays come from Parerga and Paralipomena, the collection of shorter writings that finally made Schopenhauer famous in 1851, after decades of neglect. Written for general readers, they deal with everyday subjects such as reading and books, thinking for oneself, style, noise and the conduct of life, with sharp wit and the pessimism for which he is known.
context: Schopenhauer was one of the best prose writers among philosophers, and these essays are the easiest way into his thought. Some of his opinions, especially about women, are prejudiced even for his own century. His influence on Nietzsche, Tolstoy and Freud was enormous; see [The Birth of Tragedy](/book/93?lang=en).

about: Emerson's first collection of essays, published in 1841, contains 'Self-Reliance', with its call to trust your own thought, its warning that a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds and its claim that whoever would be a man must be a nonconformist. The other essays, on history, friendship, love, heroism, the Over-Soul and circles, share the same bright, aphoristic style.
context: Emerson was the central figure of American Transcendentalism, and these essays influenced Thoreau, Whitman and even Nietzsche, who read them again and again. They are best read slowly, a page at a time, for sentences that stay with you; then go on to [Walden](/book/287?lang=en).

about: In July 1845 Henry David Thoreau moved into a small cabin he had built himself beside Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts, and lived there for two years and two months. Walden tells what he learned, from the exact cost of his boards and nails to the changes of the seasons, the habits of animals and the sounds of the railway across the pond.
context: 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately,' he writes, and the book is an argument for a simpler life with fewer possessions and more attention. Published in 1854, it has inspired environmentalists, minimalists and anyone tired of hurry. Thoreau was a friend of [Emerson](/book/286?lang=en), who owned the land.

about: Walt Whitman published the first Leaves of Grass himself in 1855, with twelve untitled poems and no name on the title page, only his portrait in work clothes. He spent the rest of his life expanding it, edition after edition, until it became a book of hundreds of poems celebrating the body, democracy, America and every kind of ordinary person.
context: Whitman's long, free-verse lines broke with all the rules of poetry and influenced poets around the world. Emerson wrote to him, 'I greet you at the beginning of a great career.' The collection includes 'Song of Myself' and 'O Captain! My Captain!', his elegy for Abraham Lincoln. Read it aloud.

about: Emily Dickinson lived almost all her life in her family's house in Amherst, Massachusetts, and wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems, of which only about ten were published while she was alive. After her death in 1886 her sister found them among her belongings, and the first selections appeared in the 1890s.
context: Her short poems, with their dashes, unexpected rhymes and sudden images, speak of death, nature, faith and the inner life with extraordinary intensity: 'Because I could not stop for Death', 'Hope is the thing with feathers', 'I'm Nobody! Who are you?'. The early editors smoothed some of her punctuation, but her voice is unmistakable.

about: In 1798 two young poets, William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, published a small anonymous book of poems that changed English poetry. It opens with Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner', the sailor who shoots an albatross, and closes with Wordsworth's 'Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey', with simple poems in between about country people, children and feeling.
context: In the preface to the second edition Wordsworth defined poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings and called for the language that people really speak. The book is usually taken as the beginning of the Romantic movement in England. Continue with [Keats](/book/293?lang=en) and [Byron](/book/295?lang=en).

about: John Keats died of tuberculosis in Rome in 1821 at the age of twenty-five, after barely five years of serious writing, and he left some of the most loved poems in English. Readers come for the odes of 1819, to a nightingale, to autumn, on a Grecian urn with its 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty', and for his sonnets and narrative poems full of colour, taste and touch.
context: Keats asked that his grave carry no name, only the words 'Here lies one whose name was writ in water.' His letters, which show a brilliant mind at work, are worth seeking out too. Read [Endymion](/book/294?lang=en) for his first long poem, and [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en) for the poets who came just before him.

about: 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever': so begins Keats's first long poem, published in 1818. In four books, the shepherd-prince Endymion, who has dreamed of the moon goddess Cynthia, searches for her under the earth, beneath the sea and through the air, meeting other lovers on the way, until he learns how earthly and divine love meet.
context: Keats himself called the poem the work of an immature mind, and the hostile reviews that followed were later blamed, wrongly, for his early death. Its rich, rushing verse shows the poet he was becoming. For the mature Keats, turn to his [Poems](/book/293?lang=en).

about: In Byron's comic epic, Don Juan is not the famous seducer but a handsome young man whom women keep falling for. Sent away from Seville after a scandal, he survives a shipwreck, falls in love with Haidée on a Greek island, is sold as a slave in Constantinople, fights at a Russian siege, becomes a favourite of Catherine the Great and finally reaches English high society.
context: Published in cantos between 1819 and 1824 and left unfinished when Byron died in Greece, the poem is full of digressions, jokes and attacks on the politicians and poets of his day. Its quick, conversational stanzas make it one of the most readable long poems in English. Compare the serious young Byron of [Childe Harold's Pilgrimage](/book/296?lang=en).

about: A young English nobleman, tired of pleasure, sets out alone across Europe: Portugal, Spain at war, Albania, Greece under Ottoman rule, and in later cantos the field of Waterloo, the Rhine, the Alps and Italy. The poem mixes travel, history and the melancholy thoughts of a hero who looks very much like Byron himself.
context: When the first two cantos appeared in 1812, Byron said, 'I awoke one morning and found myself famous.' The poem created the Byronic hero, brooding, proud and restless, who appears in so much later literature. Then read [Don Juan](/book/295?lang=en) to see Byron laughing at the image he had created.

about: On a spring evening some thirty pilgrims meet at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, about to set out for the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury, and the innkeeper proposes a contest: each will tell stories on the road. Knights and millers, a nun, a monk, the five-times-married Wife of Bath and a con-man Pardoner tell romances, saints' lives, sermons and very rude jokes.
context: Chaucer was writing the Tales at his death in 1400 and never finished, but the General Prologue alone is a gallery of medieval English society. His Middle English can look difficult at first; reading it aloud helps a great deal. The collection invites comparison with the frame story of the Arabian Nights and with Boccaccio's Decameron.

about: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft answered a French politician who had proposed that girls receive only a limited domestic education. Women, she argues, are not naturally weaker in mind; they seem so because they are denied education and taught that their only purpose is to please men. Give them the same rational education, she says, and they will be better wives and mothers, and better citizens.
context: The book takes particular aim at Rousseau's ideas about women in [Emile](/book/273?lang=en), and it is one of the founding texts of feminism. Wollstonecraft died in 1797 after giving birth to her daughter, Mary Shelley, the author of [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en).

about: Against his father's wishes, young Robinson Crusoe of York goes to sea, is captured by pirates and enslaved in Morocco, escapes and becomes a planter in Brazil, then is shipwrecked on an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco. Alone for years, he salvages tools from the wreck, builds a shelter, grows grain, tames goats and keeps a journal, until one day he finds a single human footprint in the sand.
context: Published in 1719, the book was presented as a true memoir and became one of the most influential novels ever written. Some scholars have wondered whether Defoe knew Ibn Tufail's [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/1966195?lang=en), the Andalusian tale of a man alone on an island, which had been translated into English in 1708.

about: Moll Flanders tells her own story: born in Newgate prison to a mother who was transported for theft, she is raised by the parish, seduced young, and goes through five husbands, one of whom turns out to be her own brother. When her looks fade, she becomes one of the most skilful thieves in London, until she is caught and sent to Virginia, where she finally prospers.
context: Published in 1722, the novel is frank about money, sex and survival in a world where a woman alone had few options, and Moll is vivid, practical and never entirely trustworthy. Defoe presents it as a moral tale of repentance, but readers have always enjoyed the sins more. Compare his [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en).

about: When the poor Durbeyfield family learns that they descend from the ancient d'Urbervilles, they send their eldest daughter Tess to claim kinship with a rich family of that name. The son, Alec, takes advantage of her, and Tess returns home in shame. Years later she finds love with the idealistic Angel Clare, but when she confesses her past on their wedding night, he cannot forgive her.
context: Published in 1891 with the defiant subtitle 'A Pure Woman', Tess outraged many Victorian readers with its defence of a woman condemned by double standards. Its landscapes of rural Wessex are among the most beautiful in English fiction, and its ending is unforgettable. Hardy's next novel, [Jude the Obscure](/book/308?lang=en), went even further.

about: Jude Fawley, a young stonemason in a Wessex village, teaches himself Latin and Greek and dreams of studying at Christminster, a city modelled on Oxford. The colleges ignore him, an early marriage to Arabella traps him, and his deep love for his free-thinking cousin Sue Bridehead puts them both outside respectable society, with tragic consequences.
context: Published in 1895, the novel was attacked so fiercely for its criticism of marriage, class and religion that Hardy gave up writing novels and spent the rest of his life writing poetry. It is his darkest book and one of his most powerful; read [Tess of the d'Urbervilles](/book/306?lang=en) first.

about: White Fang is born in the frozen wild of northern Canada, three-quarters wolf and one-quarter dog. After his mother is captured, he grows up among the dogs of an Indigenous camp, is sold to a cruel man who turns him into a fighting dog, and nearly dies before a mining engineer, Weedon Scott, rescues him and slowly teaches him to trust a human being.
context: Published in 1906, the novel is told largely from the animal's point of view and follows the reverse journey of [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en), from wildness to companionship. Jack London's descriptions of the North and of an animal learning love remain gripping for young and adult readers alike.

about: Humphrey Van Weyden, a gentle literary critic from San Francisco, is thrown into the sea when his ferry sinks and is picked up by a sealing schooner bound for Japan. Its captain, Wolf Larsen, is a brute of extraordinary strength and intelligence who reads philosophy and believes that life is meaningless and only the strong survive, and he makes Humphrey a cabin boy.
context: Published in 1904, The Sea-Wolf is a sea adventure and a battle of ideas between a softened intellectual and a ruthless individualist, later joined by the poet Maud Brewster. Jack London meant it as a critique of the Nietzschean superman. For London's own semi-autobiographical struggle, read [Martin Eden](/book/312?lang=en).

about: Martin Eden, a rough young sailor from the docks of Oakland, saves a young man from a fight and is invited to dinner with his wealthy family, where he falls in love with the delicate Ruth Morse. Determined to become worthy of her, he educates himself in libraries and starts to write, through poverty, hunger and hundreds of rejection letters.
context: Published in 1909 and drawing heavily on Jack London's own life, the novel is a portrait of a self-made writer and a bitter look at success, class and individualism. Many readers find it London's best book. For London at sea, read [The Sea-Wolf](/book/311?lang=en).

about: Sara Crewe arrives at Miss Minchin's boarding school in London as its richest pupil, the beloved daughter of a captain in India, and is treated like a princess. When news comes that her father has died penniless, she is sent to live in a cold attic and work as a servant. Sara decides to behave like a princess anyway, kind and dignified, whatever happens to her.
context: Published in its full form in 1905, A Little Princess is a story about imagination as a way of surviving hardship, and its magical turn in the attic is one of the best moments in children's literature. Frances Hodgson Burnett also wrote [The Secret Garden](/book/315?lang=en).

about: The tortoise who beats the hare, the fox who decides the grapes he cannot reach must be sour, the boy who cried wolf, the ant and the grasshopper, the lion spared by a grateful mouse: these short animal tales, each ending with a lesson, are attributed to Aesop, said to have been a slave in Greece in the sixth century BC.
context: The fables have been retold in every language and age, and their morals have become everyday sayings. In Arabic literature, the same tradition of wise animals lives in [Kalila wa Dimna](/book/1965500?lang=en), and some writers linked Aesop with Luqman the Wise. They are perfect for reading aloud, one fable at a time.

about: Georges Duroy, a handsome former soldier back from Algeria with no money and no talent, meets an old comrade who gets him a job at a Paris newspaper. He cannot write, but he is charming, and he discovers that women can open every door. One affair at a time, he climbs to wealth and power, through journalism, politics and a colonial scheme in Morocco.
context: Published in 1885, Bel-Ami is Maupassant's sharpest novel, a portrait of a cynic and of the newspapers, financiers and politicians of the Third Republic who made him possible. It is fast, witty and still relevant to any age of influence and spin. For Maupassant's shorter fiction, read [Boule de Suif](/book/320?lang=en).

about: In the winter of 1870, with Rouen occupied by the Prussian army, ten travellers squeeze into a coach to escape to Le Havre: wine merchants, a factory owner, a count and countess, two nuns, a democrat and a plump prostitute everyone calls Boule de Suif. When the respectable passengers grow hungry, she shares her basket of food with them. Then a Prussian officer at an inn refuses to let the coach leave unless she spends the night with him.
context: Published in 1880 in a collection of war stories by Zola's circle, this long story made Maupassant famous overnight, and Flaubert called it a masterpiece. It is a merciless portrait of hypocrisy, of good people who use someone and then despise her. For Maupassant's novel of ambition, read [Bel-Ami](/book/319?lang=en).

about: In the provincial town of Saumur, old Félix Grandet, a former cooper who has grown rich through shrewd deals, keeps his wife and daughter in near-poverty, rationing sugar and candles while his gold piles up. When his elegant young nephew Charles arrives from Paris just as his own father has gone bankrupt, Eugénie falls in love for the first time and secretly gives him her savings.
context: Published in 1833, this is one of the most compact and accessible novels of Balzac's vast Human Comedy, and Grandet is one of literature's great misers, alongside Molière's Harpagon. The quiet tragedy of Eugénie, who waits for years in a house without warmth, is the heart of the book.

about: Emma, a farmer's daughter raised on romantic novels, marries Charles Bovary, a kind and dull country doctor in Normandy, and soon finds married life nothing like the books. Seeking passion and luxury, she takes lovers, buys beautiful things on credit from a scheming merchant, and sinks deeper into debt and disappointment.
context: When the novel was serialised in 1856, Flaubert was put on trial for offending public morals and acquitted. He worked for years on every sentence, and his precise, ironic style made Madame Bovary a model for the modern novel. Its portrait of a woman trapped by her dreams and her society remains painfully alive.

about: In 1840 eighteen-year-old Frédéric Moreau, on a river boat to his provincial home, sees Madame Arnoux, the wife of an art dealer, and falls in love for life. Over the next decade in Paris he drifts between her, a courtesan and a wealthy widow, between friends who become revolutionaries and careerists, while the revolution of 1848 rises and fails around him.
context: Published in 1869, Sentimental Education is Flaubert's portrait of his own generation and of a young man who never quite acts, and it draws on his youthful love for an older married woman. Less dramatic than [Madame Bovary](/book/324?lang=en), it is admired by many writers as his greatest novel.

about: After the First Punic War, the city of Carthage cannot pay the mercenaries who fought for it, and they rise in revolt. In the middle of this savage war stands Salammbô, the daughter of the general Hamilcar Barca and a priestess of the goddess Tanit, and Mathô, a Libyan mercenary chief who steals the goddess's sacred veil and becomes obsessed with her.
context: Published in 1862 after Flaubert travelled to Tunisia to see the site of Carthage, the novel is based on the account of the historian Polybius and is full of extravagant colour and violence, a complete contrast to [Madame Bovary](/book/324?lang=en). For North African readers, it is a strange and vivid European vision of their ancient past.

about: Étienne Lantier, an unemployed mechanic, arrives on a freezing night at a coal mine in northern France and takes work underground beside the Maheu family. He sees the hunger, the danger and the long hours of the miners and their children, and when the company cuts wages he leads a strike that grows desperate as the winter goes on.
context: Published in 1885 after Zola went down the mines himself to research it, Germinal is the most powerful novel of his Rougon-Macquart cycle. Its title comes from the spring month of the revolutionary calendar, the season of seeds, and at Zola's funeral in 1902 miners walked behind the coffin chanting it.

about: Nana, the daughter of a Paris laundress, steps onto the stage of the Théâtre des Variétés with no voice and no talent and becomes the sensation of the season. As a courtesan of the Second Empire she ruins one rich admirer after another, bankers, aristocrats and a devout count, who sacrifice their fortunes and families to her.
context: Published in 1880 as part of Zola's Rougon-Macquart cycle, Nana is a fierce portrait of a society rotting from within, and it ends in July 1870 as crowds outside shout for war with Prussia, the war that would bring the Empire down. It is a book for adult readers, written with Zola's unflinching realism; see [Germinal](/book/327?lang=en).

about: Thérèse has been married off to her sickly cousin Camille and lives with him and his mother in a gloomy shop in a Paris arcade. When Camille brings home his robust friend Laurent, Thérèse and Laurent begin an affair, and during a boating trip on the Seine they drown Camille and make it look like an accident. Their freedom turns into a nightmare of guilt, under the silent eyes of Camille's paralysed mother.
context: Published in 1867, it was Zola's first great success and a scandal; in his preface he defended it as a scientific study of temperament. It is short, dark and gripping, a psychological thriller before the term existed. Read [Germinal](/book/327?lang=en) for Zola's mature work.

about: The narrator dips a small cake called a madeleine into a cup of tea, and the taste suddenly brings back the whole world of his childhood summers in the village of Combray: his mother's goodnight kiss, his aunt's room, the church steeple, the two walks his family took. The middle section, 'Swann in Love', goes back in time to tell how the elegant Charles Swann fell into a jealous passion for Odette.
context: Swann's Way, published in 1913 at Proust's own expense after publishers refused it, is the first volume of In Search of Lost Time, one of the longest and most influential novels ever written. This is the classic English translation by C. K. Scott Moncrieff. Proust's long sentences reward patience: read slowly and let them carry you.

about: Pavel Chichikov, a polite and plump gentleman, arrives in a provincial town and begins visiting the local landowners with a strange offer: he wants to buy their dead serfs, peasants who have died but are still listed on the tax registers until the next census. Each landowner he meets, the sentimental Manilov, the suspicious widow Korobochka, the brawler Nozdryov, the bear-like Sobakevich and the miser Plyushkin, is a comic masterpiece.
context: Published in 1842, Dead Souls is Gogol's great comic novel of Russian life, and the idea for it came from Pushkin. Gogol meant it as the first part of a trilogy, but burned much of the second part shortly before he died. Dostoevsky's first novel, [Poor Folk](/book/19?lang=en), grew directly out of Gogol's world.

about: Arkady Kirsanov comes home from university to his father's estate, bringing his friend Bazarov, a medical student who believes in nothing but science and calls himself a nihilist. Bazarov dissects frogs, mocks art and the aristocratic manners of Arkady's uncle Pavel, and ends up fighting a duel with him, until he falls in love with a cool, intelligent widow and discovers feelings his theories cannot explain.
context: Published in 1862, the novel made the word nihilist famous and angered both the older and the younger generation, who each felt caricatured. Bazarov is one of the great characters of Russian fiction, and the quarrel between parents and children it describes never goes out of date.

about: A young landowner goes hunting across the forests and fields of central Russia and records the people he meets: peasants, millers, coachmen, singers, small landowners and their serfs. In 'Bezhin Meadow' he spends a night by a fire listening to village boys tell ghost stories; in 'The Singers' a tavern holds its breath for a song contest.
context: Published as a book in 1852, these sketches showed serfs as thinking, feeling human beings, and they are said to have influenced Tsar Alexander II, who abolished serfdom in 1861. They are also some of the most beautiful nature writing in Russian. Turgenev's major novel is [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en).

about: Nora Helmer seems to be a happy, playful wife whose husband Torvald calls her his little lark and treats her like a child. But years earlier, when he was seriously ill, she secretly borrowed money to save his life by forging her father's signature, and now the man who lent it is threatening to tell everything.
context: First performed in Copenhagen in 1879, A Doll's House ends with one of the most famous moments in theatre, when Nora closes the door behind her. The ending was so shocking that a German production forced Ibsen to write an alternative one, which he called a disgrace. Read [Hedda Gabler](/book/339?lang=en) next.

about: Hedda Gabler, the proud daughter of a general, has just returned from her honeymoon with George Tesman, a decent but dull scholar she married out of boredom. When Eilert Løvborg, a brilliant former admirer who has given up drink and written a remarkable book, reappears in their lives, Hedda sets out to control his fate, with her father's pistols close at hand.
context: First performed in 1891, the play is one of the greatest roles for an actress in modern drama, and Hedda remains a mystery: bored, cruel, trapped and fascinating. It is less about ideas than [A Doll's House](/book/338?lang=en) and more about character, and it still holds audiences.

about: Mrs Alving is about to open an orphanage in memory of her late husband, a respected captain whose dissolute life she hid from everyone, including her son. When Osvald comes home from Paris, ill and despairing, the lies of the past come back like ghosts, and the pious Pastor Manders, who once sent her back to her marriage, has to face what his advice cost.
context: Published in 1881, Ghosts caused a scandal across Europe for openly discussing inherited disease, religious hypocrisy and the duties of marriage, and theatres refused to stage it for years. Its last scene, at sunrise, is one of the most devastating in Ibsen. Read [A Doll's House](/book/338?lang=en) first.

about: Peer Gynt is a Norwegian peasant's son who lies, boasts and dreams his way through life. He runs off with a bride on her wedding day, nearly marries the daughter of the Troll King, abandons the faithful Solveig, makes a fortune in slaving and trade, passes himself off as a prophet among the Bedouins of the desert, and comes home as an old man to face the Button-Moulder, who wants to melt down his soul.
context: Written in 1867 as a verse drama, Peer Gynt is Ibsen's most fantastic work, a satire of self-deception in which Peer peels an onion looking for its core and finds only layers. Edvard Grieg's music for it, including 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' and 'Anitra's Dance', is famous around the world.

about: Jim, a young British officer who dreams of heroism, is chief mate of the Patna, an old steamer carrying eight hundred Muslim pilgrims to Mecca. One night the ship strikes something in the dark, and convinced she is about to sink, Jim jumps into a lifeboat with the other officers, leaving the pilgrims behind. The ship does not sink, and the disgrace follows him across the East.
context: Told largely by Conrad's narrator Marlow, Lord Jim (1900) follows Jim to a remote Malay settlement where he gets a second chance and becomes Tuan Jim, respected lord of the people. It is a profound novel about honour, cowardice and whether one can ever escape a single moment of weakness. See also [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en).

about: In the imaginary South American republic of Costaguana, Charles Gould, born in the country to an English family, runs the San Tomé silver mine, which has become the centre of its politics. When a revolution breaks out, a load of silver must be hidden, and the task falls to Nostromo, the admired and supposedly incorruptible foreman of the port's dockworkers.
context: Published in 1904, Nostromo is Joseph Conrad's most ambitious novel, a story of revolutions, foreign investment and the corrupting power of wealth that feels startlingly modern. Its shifting timeline makes the opening chapters demanding, but they repay patience. Begin with [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en) if you are new to Conrad.

about: Fifteen stories set in Dublin follow life from childhood through youth and adulthood to death: a boy's first crush and a disappointing bazaar in 'Araby', a young woman unable to leave on a boat to a new life in 'Eveline', clerks, singers and politicians, and finally 'The Dead', in which a man discovers at the end of a winter dance party that he never really knew his wife.
context: Joyce struggled for nearly ten years to find a publisher, who feared the stories' frankness, and the book finally appeared in 1914. 'The Dead' is often called one of the finest short stories in English. Read it before [A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man](/book/346?lang=en) and [Ulysses](/book/347?lang=en).

about: Stephen Dedalus grows up in Catholic Ireland: a frightened small boy at boarding school, a Christmas dinner wrecked by a political quarrel, a teenager terrified by a sermon on hell, a student who discovers that his true calling is not the priesthood but art. Joyce's language grows with him, from baby talk in the first pages to complex reflection at the end.
context: Published in 1916, the novel is based on Joyce's own youth and ends with Stephen deciding to leave Ireland and live by 'silence, exile and cunning'. It is the best way into Joyce before [Ulysses](/book/347?lang=en), where Stephen appears again.

about: On a single day in June 1923, Clarissa Dalloway walks through London to buy flowers for the party she is giving that evening. Her thoughts move back and forth between the present and her youth, to the man she did not marry, while in another part of the city a young veteran of the war, Septimus Warren Smith, struggles with visions he cannot share.
context: Published in 1925, Mrs Dalloway follows the inner lives of its characters as they cross each other's paths, marked by the hours struck by Big Ben. It is one of the great modernist novels and one of the most humane, especially in its portrait of war trauma. It came out of copyright in the United States in 2021.

about: Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman, rents a small house on Long Island next to the mansion of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire who throws enormous parties every weekend. Gatsby has built his whole life around one hope: to win back Daisy Buchanan, Nick's cousin, who lives across the bay with her rich and brutal husband, and whose green dock light he watches at night.
context: Published in 1925, The Great Gatsby is a short, perfectly written novel about the American dream, money and the impossibility of repeating the past, and its final line is one of the most quoted in American literature. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2021.

about: Isabel Archer, a young American with a lively mind and great hopes for her freedom, is brought to England by her aunt. She refuses two excellent suitors, an English lord and an American industrialist, and when she unexpectedly inherits a fortune, she sets out to see the world. In Italy she meets the cultivated Gilbert Osmond, and makes the choice of her life.
context: Published in 1881, the novel is Henry James's early masterpiece, a subtle story of independence, manipulation and the consequences of a free choice. Its scenes of quiet thought, especially Isabel's night by the fire, changed what the novel could do. For a shorter James, read [The Turn of the Screw](/book/353?lang=en).

about: Paul Morel grows up in a mining village in Nottinghamshire, between a rough, drinking father who works the pits and a proud, ambitious mother who pours all her love into her sons. As Paul becomes a young man and an artist, he finds that his mother's love makes it impossible for him to give himself fully to the women he loves, gentle Miriam and passionate Clara.
context: Published in 1913 and closely based on D. H. Lawrence's own family, Sons and Lovers is a powerful novel about mothers and sons, working-class life and the struggle to grow up. Its descriptions of the countryside and the mining town are among the finest in English fiction.

about: Kim is an Irish orphan growing up wild on the streets of Lahore, who speaks Hindustani better than English and is known as the Little Friend of all the World. He becomes the disciple of an old Tibetan lama searching for a sacred river, and as they travel the Grand Trunk Road together, Kim is recruited into the secret world of British intelligence, the Great Game.
context: Published in 1901, Kim is full of the colours, crowds and religions of India, and it is Kipling's finest novel, though it reflects the outlook of the empire. The friendship between the boy and the lama gives it a warmth unique in his work. For his animal tales, see [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en).

about: How did the camel get his hump, the leopard his spots, the whale his throat and the elephant his trunk? Kipling answers in stories invented for his daughter, who wanted them told 'just so', in exactly the same words every time. They are full of nonsense words, repetitions and asides to 'O Best Beloved', the child listening.
context: Published in 1902 with Kipling's own illustrations, the Just So Stories are made to be read aloud, and they remain among the most delightful children's books in English. 'The Cat That Walked by Himself' is a favourite. For Kipling's longer animal tales, read [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en).

about: Gitanjali, 'Song Offerings', is a collection of short prose poems that Rabindranath Tagore translated into English himself from his Bengali songs. They are prayers and meditations on God, nature, love, death and the soul's longing, written in simple, luminous language: 'Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high...'.
context: The English Gitanjali appeared in 1912 with an introduction by W. B. Yeats, and the next year Tagore became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. The poems are short, so they are perfect to read one at a time; continue with his lectures in [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: Nikhil, a wealthy and idealistic landowner in Bengal, wants his wife Bimala to be free, and encourages her to leave the women's quarters and join the world. Then his old friend Sandip arrives, a charismatic leader of the movement to boycott British goods, and Bimala is swept away by his passion for the nation and for her.
context: Told in turn by its three main characters, the novel was published in Bengali in 1916 and is a clear-eyed look at nationalism, idealism and violence during the movement against the partition of Bengal. Satyajit Ray filmed it in 1984. For Tagore's poetry, read [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en).

about: Amal, a young boy, is seriously ill and his adoptive uncle has been told to keep him indoors. From his window he talks to everyone who passes: the dairyman, the watchman, the flower girl. When a new post office opens across the road, Amal becomes convinced that one day the king will send him a letter.
context: Tagore's short play, written in 1912, is gentle, mysterious and deeply moving, a meditation on freedom and death through the eyes of a child. In 1942 the doctor and educator Janusz Korczak staged it with the children of his orphanage in the Warsaw ghetto, shortly before they were deported.

about: In a series of lectures given in the United States and England in 1913, Rabindranath Tagore explains the outlook of the ancient Indian Upanishads for Western listeners: the relationship of the individual soul to the universe, the problem of evil, the meaning of self, love, action and the realisation of beauty and the infinite.
context: Sadhana means spiritual practice or striving. Written in Tagore's own English, the lectures are clear and poetic and offer a gentle introduction to Indian philosophy. They fit naturally beside his [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en) and William James's [Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en).

about: Florence Nightingale wrote this short book in 1859 not for professional nurses but for every woman who might have to care for a sick person at home. Her advice is practical and direct: fresh air, light, warmth, quiet, clean rooms and bedding, good food, and above all careful observation of the patient.
context: Written after her work with wounded soldiers during the Crimean War, Notes on Nursing shaped modern nursing and public health. Some of its medicine is outdated, but its attention to the patient's comfort and dignity is not. It is a reminder that care is a skill as well as a kindness.

about: At Christmas 1848, the scientist Michael Faraday gave a series of lectures for young people at the Royal Institution in London, all about a single candle. Why does the flame have its shape? What happens to the wax? Where does the light come from? Following these questions, he leads his audience to combustion, water, the air we breathe and the chemistry of our own bodies.
context: Published in 1861, the lectures are one of the most famous examples of science explained for young people, full of simple experiments that can be repeated at home with care. Faraday's own great discoveries are recorded in his [Experimental Researches in Electricity](/book/375?lang=en).

about: These are Michael Faraday's own reports of the experiments that made the electric age possible: the discovery in 1831 of electromagnetic induction, the principle behind every generator and transformer; the laws of electrolysis; and his investigations of how electricity and magnetism act through space.
context: Faraday was the son of a blacksmith and left school early to work for a bookbinder, yet he became one of the greatest experimental scientists who ever lived, and words such as electrode, anode, cathode and ion were coined in his work. For his gift for explaining science, read [The Chemical History of a Candle](/book/374?lang=en).

about: Charles Babbage, the mathematician who designed the first programmable computing machines, wrote this memoir in 1864, near the end of his life. He tells how his Difference Engine and his Analytical Engine came to be designed, describes his experiments, travels and famous friends, and wages a long, comic war against the street musicians who disturbed his work.
context: The book is a lively, eccentric self-portrait of a Victorian inventor a century ahead of his time. Babbage's engines were never completed in his lifetime, but their design anticipated the modern computer. For his ideas on industry, read [On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures](/book/378?lang=en).

about: In 1832, after touring the workshops and factories of England and Europe while working on his calculating engines, Charles Babbage wrote this study of how machines and factories work: how tools save time, how the division of labour lowers costs, how prices are set and how industry should be organised.
context: The book was a practical guide for manufacturers and an early work of industrial economics; Mill and Marx both drew on it. It shows the same curious, systematic mind as Babbage's memoir, [Passages from the Life of a Philosopher](/book/377?lang=en).

about: Written by a Roman architect and engineer and dedicated to the emperor Augustus, these ten books cover everything a builder of the ancient world needed to know: the education of architects, materials, temples and the classical orders, theatres, houses, water supply, sundials and machines of war. A building, Vitruvius says, must be solid, useful and beautiful.
context: It is the only complete work on architecture to survive from classical antiquity, and when it was rediscovered in the Renaissance it shaped buildings across Europe. Its description of the proportions of the human body inspired Leonardo's famous drawing of the Vitruvian Man; see [The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci](/book/381?lang=en).

about: Leonardo da Vinci filled thousands of pages with notes and drawings, often written backwards in mirror script: instructions for painters on light, shadow and perspective, studies of the human body, the flight of birds, the movement of water, designs for machines, and private thoughts on art and nature.
context: This edition, prepared by the scholar Jean Paul Richter and first published in 1883, arranges the notebooks by subject and translates them into English. It lets us watch one of the most curious minds in history at work. For the classical source of many of his ideas on proportion, read [Vitruvius](/book/379?lang=en).

about: A Square, a respectable resident of a two-dimensional world called Flatland, describes his society, where women are straight lines, soldiers are sharp triangles and priests are nearly circles, and rank depends on the number of one's sides. Then a strange visitor, a Sphere, arrives from the third dimension, and the Square's world is turned upside down.
context: Published in 1884 by a London headmaster, Flatland is both a playful introduction to the idea of dimensions and a satire of Victorian class and the treatment of women. Mathematicians and physicists still recommend it as a way to imagine worlds beyond our own.

about: William James spent twelve years on this textbook, published in 1890, and it is anything but dry. He writes about habit, attention, memory, the self, emotion and will, and coins the phrase 'stream of consciousness' to describe how thought flows rather than moves in separate pieces. His chapter on habit is still quoted by teachers and coaches.
context: The book helped turn psychology into a scientific discipline in America, and its theory that emotions follow bodily changes is still discussed. James writes as a brilliant essayist as much as a scientist. For his work on religion, read [The Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en).

about: In lectures given in Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902, William James studied religion not through doctrines or churches but through the experiences of individuals: conversion, the sense of a divine presence, the 'healthy-minded' and the 'sick soul', saintliness and mysticism. He judges these experiences by their fruits in people's lives.
context: James draws on Christian, Hindu, Buddhist and Muslim sources, and in his lecture on mysticism he quotes at length from the spiritual autobiography of [al-Ghazali](/author/ghazali?lang=en). The book remains a classic of the psychology of religion. James's earlier work is [The Principles of Psychology](/book/383?lang=en).

about: Why do people buy things they do not need? Thorstein Veblen's answer, in 1899, was that the rich display their status through 'conspicuous consumption' and 'conspicuous leisure', and that everyone below them imitates them as far as they can. He studies fashion, sport, manners, pets and even higher education in this light.
context: Written in a dry, ironic style that often hides how funny it is, the book introduced terms still used today, and its analysis of status and spending is perhaps even more relevant in the age of social media. Compare Adam Smith's view of human motives in [The Theory of Moral Sentiments](/book/263?lang=en).

about: A young governess takes a position at a lonely English country house called Bly, caring for two charming orphaned children, Miles and Flora. She begins to see the figures of a man and a woman around the house, and becomes convinced that they are the ghosts of two former servants who want to possess the children.
context: Published in 1898, The Turn of the Screw is one of the most famous ghost stories ever written, and its power lies in its ambiguity: readers have argued for over a century whether the ghosts are real or the governess is imagining them. It is short enough to read in one evening. For Henry James's novels, see [The Portrait of a Lady](/book/352?lang=en).

about: On Christmas Eve, the miser Ebenezer Scrooge, who answers every greeting with 'Bah! Humbug!', is visited by the ghost of his dead partner, Jacob Marley, dragging the chains he forged in life. That night three more spirits take Scrooge to his Christmases past, present and yet to come, including the poor home of his clerk Bob Cratchit and his sick son, Tiny Tim.
context: Dickens wrote the story in six weeks and published it in December 1843, and it sold out in days. It helped shape how the English-speaking world celebrates Christmas, and its message of generosity has been retold in countless films and plays. For Dickens's longer novels, start with [Great Expectations](/book/29?lang=en).

about: A man rides through a gloomy autumn landscape to the house of his childhood friend Roderick Usher, who has written begging for his company. He finds Roderick nervous and ill, living in a decaying mansion with his twin sister Madeline, who is wasting away from a mysterious disease. When Madeline seems to die, the two men place her body in a vault beneath the house.
context: Published in 1839, this is Edgar Allan Poe's most famous tale of terror, in which the house itself seems to share the life of the family. Every detail builds toward its unforgettable final scene. Poe's tales shaped modern horror; read them beside [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en) and [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en).

about: An Englishman staying in Munich sets out by carriage on Walpurgis Night, ignoring his driver's warnings, and wanders alone into an abandoned village. A sudden snowstorm drives him to shelter in a strange marble tomb, and he discovers that something in the darkness is watching over him. This is the title story of a collection of tales of the supernatural.
context: Bram Stoker's widow published the collection in 1914, two years after his death, and explained that the title story had been cut from the original manuscript of [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en). It reads as a chilling prelude to the novel, and the other stories show Stoker's taste for the weird and the macabre.

about: The London lawyer Mr Utterson is troubled by a strange will: his respected friend Dr Henry Jekyll has left everything to a certain Edward Hyde, a small, repellent man who has just trampled a child in the street and paid the family off with a cheque signed by Jekyll. When Hyde beats a distinguished old gentleman to death, Utterson sets out to discover what hold this man has over the doctor, and the answer, revealed in Jekyll's own final statement, is far stranger than blackmail.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson is said to have written the first draft in a few days in 1886, burned it after his wife's criticism and written it again. The short novel gave the language the phrase 'Jekyll and Hyde' for a split personality. For Stevenson's adventure writing, read [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en), or see his [life](/author/stevenson?lang=en).

about: Lucy Honeychurch, a young Englishwoman travelling in Italy with her anxious older cousin Charlotte, is disappointed to find that their rooms at a Florence boarding house look onto a courtyard. Old Mr Emerson and his silent son George offer to swap: they have rooms with a view. From that small kindness grow a murder witnessed in a piazza, a kiss in a field of violets, and back in England an engagement to the wrong man.
context: E. M. Forster (1879–1970) published the novel in 1908, drawing on his own travels in Italy, and it is his lightest and funniest book, a comedy about the courage to follow one's feelings rather than convention. He later wrote [Howards End](/book/3074?lang=en) and A Passage to India. The 1985 film made the story widely loved.

about: In a provincial English town in the years before the Reform Act of 1832, several lives cross. Dorothea Brooke, idealistic and serious, marries an elderly scholar in the hope of sharing great work and finds herself shut in with a dry, jealous man. The ambitious young doctor Lydgate marries the pretty Rosamond and is slowly worn down by debt, while the town's pious banker hides a shameful past.
context: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), who chose a male name so that her work would be taken seriously. Middlemarch, published in parts in 1871 and 1872, is often called the greatest English novel; Virginia Woolf praised it as one of the few written for grown-up people. Start with [Silas Marner](/book/849?lang=en) if you want a shorter Eliot.

about: Valancy Stirling is twenty-nine, unmarried and crushed by a large, petty family in a small Ontario town, where her only escape is a daydream of a blue castle in Spain. Then a doctor's letter tells her she has a heart condition and perhaps a year to live, and Valancy decides to stop being afraid: she speaks her mind at a family dinner, goes to nurse a dying girl the town has shunned, and proposes to the most disreputable man in the district.
context: Published in 1926, The Blue Castle is L. M. Montgomery's only novel for adults set outside Prince Edward Island, and it has a devoted following. Montgomery (1874–1942), the author of [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en), filled it with the lakes and forests of Muskoka and with her own sharp humour about family life.

about: On a rainy February day in London, two women who barely know each other, the shy Lotty Wilkins and the unhappy, devout Rose Arbuthnot, see the same advertisement: a small medieval castle on the Italian coast is for rent for the month of April. Too poor to afford it alone, they take in two other strangers, a beautiful society lady weary of admirers and an elderly widow who lives among memories of famous men.
context: What happens to the four women among the wisteria and the sunshine is the whole delightful story. Elizabeth von Arnim (1866–1941), born in Australia and a cousin of Katherine Mansfield, wrote it in 1922 after her own holiday in Portofino, and it became a bestseller and later a much-loved film. It is pure comfort reading, wise as well as funny.

about: A young mother, recovering from what we would now call postnatal depression, is taken by her physician husband to a rented country house for a 'rest cure': no work, no visitors, no writing. Confined to an upstairs room with barred windows and torn yellow wallpaper, she keeps a secret journal, and as the weeks pass she becomes convinced that a woman is trapped behind the pattern of the paper, creeping and shaking it at night.
context: Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935) had been prescribed the same treatment herself and later wrote that she published the story in 1892 to save other women from it. This short story is now a classic of feminist literature and of psychological horror. Gilman was also a well-known lecturer and the author of Women and Economics and the utopian novel Herland.

about: Cranford is a small English country town 'in possession of the Amazons': its society is made up almost entirely of genteel single ladies and widows living on very little money, who hide their poverty behind rules of 'elegant economy', strict visiting hours and a candle never lit when one can talk in the dark. Through the eyes of a young visitor, Mary Smith, we follow Miss Matty Jenkyns and her friends through small scandals, fears of burglars, a bank failure and a long-lost brother's return.
context: Elizabeth Gaskell (1810–1865) published the episodes in Charles Dickens's magazine Household Words between 1851 and 1853. Gentle, funny and quietly moving, Cranford is a portrait of kindness in a small community. Gaskell also wrote the industrial novel [North and South](/book/4360?lang=en) and a famous biography of her friend [Charlotte Brontë](/author/cbronte?lang=en).

about: A play called The King in Yellow circulates in secret, and anyone who reads its second act is driven to madness or despair. Its fragments, about the lost city of Carcosa, the Yellow Sign and a pale king in tattered robes, haunt the first stories of this collection: a man convinced he is heir to an American empire, a sculptor who discovers a liquid that turns living things to marble, a church organist pursued by a terrible watchman.
context: Robert W. Chambers (1865–1933) had studied art in Paris, and the later stories in the book are romantic tales of artists' life there. He became a popular writer of romances, but this early collection of 1895 is the work that lasted: it influenced H. P. Lovecraft, as in [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en), and modern horror writers and television.

about: One night Squire Allworthy, the most generous man in Somerset, finds a baby boy in his own bed and decides to raise him. Tom Jones grows up warm-hearted, handsome and constantly in trouble, in love with Sophia Western, the daughter of a hard-drinking neighbour, while Allworthy's sly nephew Blifil plots against him. Thrown out of the house, Tom takes to the road, and his adventures in inns and in London lead to an unexpected discovery about his birth.
context: Henry Fielding (1707–1754) was a successful playwright until censorship closed the theatres to him, and then a magistrate who helped found London's first organised police force, the Bow Street Runners. Published in 1749, Tom Jones is one of the founding comic novels in English, and each of its eighteen books opens with a witty essay addressed directly to the reader.

about: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland around 1818 and never knew his birthday or his father. In this short, powerful book he describes the whippings, the hunger and the separation of families that he saw and suffered, how he secretly learned to read after his master forbade it, and the day he fought back against a brutal 'slave-breaker', which he calls the turning point of his life.
context: Published in 1845, seven years after he escaped to the North, the Narrative made Douglass the most famous Black American of his century; he deliberately left out the details of his escape so as not to endanger those still trying. He became a great orator, newspaper editor and adviser to President Lincoln. Read it with [Olaudah Equiano's narrative](/book/13730?lang=en) and [Up from Slavery](/book/2529?lang=en).

about: On Fleet Street in London stands the shop of the barber Sweeney Todd, where customers sit down for a shave and are never seen again, thanks to a chair that tips them into the cellar. Nearby, Mrs Lovett's meat pies are the most popular in the city. When a sailor disappears with a valuable string of pearls he was carrying to a young woman named Johanna, his friends begin to investigate.
context: The story was first published in instalments in 1846 and 1847 in a cheap weekly magazine, the kind of sensational fiction Victorians called penny dreadfuls; its author is believed to be James Malcolm Rymer, though some credit Thomas Peckett Prest. Sweeney Todd became a legend of the London stage and, much later, of Stephen Sondheim's musical. It is a book for readers who enjoy grim, melodramatic thrills.

about: Strange things are happening at the Paris Opera: stagehands see a man in evening dress with a skull for a face, a box is reserved for a ghost who demands his salary, and a great chandelier crashes into the audience. Meanwhile the young singer Christine Daaé is being taught by a mysterious voice she believes to be an angel of music, until her childhood friend Raoul follows her into the cellars and the lake beneath the building.
context: Gaston Leroux (1868–1927) was a court reporter and theatre critic before he turned to fiction, and he made his name with the locked-room mystery The Mystery of the Yellow Room. Published in 1910, The Phantom of the Opera was not a great success at first, but the 1925 silent film and Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical made its masked figure one of the most famous in the world.

about: King Shahryar, betrayed by his wife, has sworn to marry a new bride every night and kill her at dawn, until Shahrazad, the clever daughter of his vizier, volunteers to marry him and begins a story she leaves unfinished at daybreak. This first of ten volumes contains the opening tales: the merchant and the jinni, the fisherman who finds a jinni in a jar, and the porter and the three ladies of Baghdad, with stories nested inside stories.
context: Richard Francis Burton (1821–1890) was an explorer and linguist who travelled to Mecca in disguise in 1853 and searched for the source of the Nile. His complete translation, privately printed for subscribers in 1885, is famous for its archaic style and for its long footnotes, which are frank and often reflect the prejudices of his time; it is meant for adult readers. For a shorter selection for young readers, see [Andrew Lang's version](/book/479?lang=en).

about: In a quiet Dutch valley on the Hudson River, the lanky, superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane courts Katrina Van Tassel, the daughter of a rich farmer, and competes with the local hero Brom Bones for her hand. Riding home alone after a harvest party where the guests have told tales of the Headless Horseman, the ghost of a soldier who lost his head to a cannonball, Ichabod hears hoofbeats behind him on the dark road.
context: The tale appeared in 1820 in The Sketch Book, which also contains 'Rip Van Winkle', and made Washington Irving (1783–1859) the first American writer famous in Europe. Readers of Arabic may enjoy knowing that he later lived in the Alhambra palace in Granada and wrote Tales of the Alhambra, a loving book of Andalusian legends.

about: What gives a government the right to rule? Locke begins with people in a state of nature, free and equal, possessing natural rights to life, liberty and property, and argues that they create governments only to protect those rights. Property, he says, begins when a person mixes his labour with the land; and a government that violates the trust of its people may lawfully be resisted.
context: Published anonymously in 1689, after the Revolution that brought William and Mary to the English throne, the Second Treatise became one of the foundations of modern liberal democracy, and its echo is clearly heard in the American Declaration of Independence. See [John Locke's life](/author/locke?lang=en), and read [Common Sense](/book/491?lang=en) to see how his ideas spread.

about: After the death of her beloved father, the young and sensitive Emily St Aubert is placed in the care of her aunt, who marries the sinister Italian nobleman Montoni. He carries them off to his gloomy castle of Udolpho in the Apennines, where Emily is cut off from the man she loves and surrounded by mysteries: hidden passages, strange music at night and a black veil she lifts once and cannot forget.
context: Ann Radcliffe (1764–1823) was the most popular novelist of the 1790s and the best paid, and her way of building suspense, then explaining her ghosts away, shaped the Gothic novel. Published in 1794, Udolpho is long and full of landscape descriptions and poems, and it is the book Jane Austen gently mocked in [Northanger Abbey](/book/42?lang=en).

about: In the quiet English village of King's Abbot, the wealthy widower Roger Ackroyd is found stabbed in his study, the night after the death of the woman he hoped to marry. The village doctor, James Sheppard, tells the story, and his new neighbour, a small foreigner who has retired to grow vegetable marrows, turns out to be the detective Hercule Poirot.
context: Published in 1926, the novel contains one of the most famous twists in the history of crime fiction, and in 2013 the British Crime Writers' Association voted it the best crime novel ever written; avoid reading anything about it before you finish. Agatha Christie (1890–1976), the best-selling novelist of all time, introduced Poirot in [The Mysterious Affair at Styles](/book/1134?lang=en).

about: After the death of his great-uncle, a professor in Rhode Island, the narrator finds his papers and begins to piece together a terrifying pattern: a clay sculpture shaped in a young artist's nightmare, a strange cult in the swamps of Louisiana, and a Norwegian sailor's account of a city rising from the Pacific, where something vast and ancient lies dreaming, waiting to wake.
context: Published in the magazine Weird Tales in 1928, the story opens with one of the most famous lines in horror, about the mercy of the human mind's inability to connect all it knows. H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937) died poor and almost unknown, but his cosmic horror has influenced countless writers, films and games; his letters, however, reveal ugly prejudices. Continue with [At the Mountains of Madness](/book/64499?lang=en).

about: 'The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line.' In fourteen essays, W. E. B. Du Bois describes the life of Black Americans after the end of slavery: the hopes and failures of Reconstruction, the poverty of the rural South, the place of education, the music of the spirituals, and the 'double consciousness' of always seeing oneself through the eyes of others. One chapter, on the death of his infant son, is unbearably moving.
context: Du Bois (1868–1963) was the first Black American to earn a doctorate from Harvard and a founder of the NAACP. Published in 1903, the book openly challenged the cautious approach of Booker T. Washington, whose [Up from Slavery](/book/2529?lang=en) is also in the library. It remains a classic of American thought and of the literature of human dignity.

about: Eleven short cases for Hercule Poirot, told by his friend Captain Hastings: a missing film star's diamond, a death in a country house, a kidnapped prime minister, a vanished banker, and a series of deaths among the people who opened an ancient Egyptian tomb, inspired by the excitement around the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922.
context: Published in 1924, these stories show Agatha Christie learning to build a puzzle in a few pages, with the little Belgian's vanity and his 'little grey cells' already at full strength. They are a perfect introduction for readers who want a short mystery; for the full-length novels, see [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: Benjamin Franklin began writing this account of his life in 1771 as a letter to his son, and kept adding to it until shortly before his death. He tells how he ran away from his apprenticeship in Boston at seventeen and arrived in Philadelphia with a few coins and three bread rolls under his arm, and how he built a career as a printer, writer, scientist and public servant.
context: The most famous section is his plan for 'moral perfection', a list of thirteen virtues he tracked daily in a small book, honestly admitting his failures. Franklin (1706–1790), inventor of the lightning rod and bifocals and one of the founders of the United States, never finished the autobiography, which first appeared in French in 1791. It is one of the classics of self-improvement.

about: Hercule Poirot receives an urgent letter from a millionaire in northern France who fears for his life, but by the time Poirot and Hastings arrive, Paul Renauld has been found stabbed and lying in a freshly dug grave beside a golf course. A young and arrogant detective from the Paris police treats Poirot as an old has-been, and the two men race to solve a case with echoes of an old murder.
context: Published in 1923, this was Agatha Christie's second Poirot novel, and it is full of false trails, French atmosphere and a romance for Captain Hastings with a mysterious young acrobat he calls Cinderella. Read it after [The Mysterious Affair at Styles](/book/1134?lang=en).

about: Professor Augustus S. F. X. Van Dusen, known as the Thinking Machine for his pure logic, argues that a clever mind can escape from any prison. To prove it, he has himself locked in a cell on death row for one week, with only his clothes, some tooth powder, two banknotes and his shoes polished. Day by day, small things begin to happen that the guards cannot explain.
context: Jacques Futrelle (1875–1912) was an American journalist whose detective stories were hugely popular, and this one, published in 1905, is the most famous of them, a classic puzzle that still delights readers of mysteries. Futrelle died in the sinking of the Titanic, after making sure his wife got into a lifeboat. Readers who enjoy it should try [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en).

about: A French scholar travelling in Andalusia to look for the site of an ancient battle meets a dangerous bandit and, later, a beautiful gypsy woman in Córdoba. Some months later he finds the bandit in prison awaiting execution, and hears his story: Don José, a soldier from the Basque country, fell in love with Carmen, a cigarette worker in Seville, deserted for her, became a smuggler and a killer, and could not bear to let her go.
context: Prosper Mérimée (1803–1870) was a writer and also France's inspector of historic monuments, who saved many medieval buildings from ruin. Published in 1845, his short novel became world famous through Bizet's opera of 1875. It is a sharp, unsentimental tale of jealousy and freedom, told with the cool eye of a traveller.

about: A respectable architect wakes up to find a dead man in his bath, wearing nothing but a pair of gold pince-nez. On the same night a famous financier disappears from his London home. Lord Peter Wimsey, a witty aristocrat who collects rare books and solves crimes for pleasure, takes up both cases with the help of his loyal manservant Bunter and his friend Inspector Parker.
context: Published in 1923, this was the first of Dorothy L. Sayers's Wimsey novels, and beneath the comedy Lord Peter carries the shell shock of the war. Sayers (1893–1957) was among the first women to receive an Oxford degree, worked in advertising, helped found the Detection Club and later translated Dante's [Divine Comedy](/book/170?lang=en). For another great detective, see [Father Brown](/book/523?lang=en).

about: Olaudah Equiano tells how, as an Igbo boy of about eleven, he was kidnapped from his village in what is now Nigeria, carried across the Atlantic in a slave ship and sold. Renamed Gustavus Vassa, he served a British naval officer through the Seven Years' War, was sold again to a merchant in the Caribbean, traded on his own account and bought his freedom in 1766, before travelling as far as the Arctic.
context: Published in 1789, the book became a bestseller and a powerful weapon of the campaign to abolish the slave trade, which Equiano supported with lectures across Britain. Some historians have questioned whether he was born in Africa or in South Carolina, but his account remains one of the founding works of Black literature in English. Read it with [Frederick Douglass's Narrative](/book/403?lang=en).

about: Gabriel Syme, a poet who has joined a secret squad of philosophical policemen, manages to be elected to the central council of a world anarchist movement, whose seven members are named after the days of the week; he becomes Thursday. Their president, a huge and terrifying man called Sunday, seems to know everything. As Syme tries to stop a bombing, he finds that nothing and no one is what it seems.
context: G. K. Chesterton (1874–1936) was a journalist, poet, novelist and Christian thinker famous for his love of paradox. Published in 1908 with the subtitle 'A Nightmare', this is his strangest and most exhilarating book, a spy thriller that turns into a philosophical fantasy. For his detective stories, read [The Innocence of Father Brown](/book/523?lang=en).

about: Father Brown is a short, shabby Catholic priest with a big umbrella and a round, harmless face, and no one expects him to solve anything. Yet in these twelve stories he outwits the master thief Flambeau, explains an impossible murder in a locked garden and sees the truth that clever detectives miss, because, as he says, his work in the confessional has taught him what people are capable of.
context: Published in 1911, this was the first of G. K. Chesterton's five collections of Father Brown stories, which are as much about faith, pride and human nature as about crime. The friendship that grows between the priest and the reformed thief Flambeau is one of their pleasures. See also Chesterton's novel [The Man Who Was Thursday](/book/1901?lang=en).

about: During the First World War, Captain Hastings, home on sick leave, is invited to Styles Court, a country house where the wealthy Emily Inglethorp has just married a much younger man. One night she dies in agony from strychnine poisoning, and Hastings calls in an old acquaintance, a Belgian refugee living in the village: a small, fussy former police detective named Hercule Poirot.
context: Published in 1920, this was Agatha Christie's first novel, written after her sister challenged her to write a detective story; several publishers rejected it. Her work in a hospital pharmacy during the war gave her an expert knowledge of poisons that shows on every page. Poirot's later cases include [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: Ambrosio, the abbot of a Capuchin monastery in Madrid, is admired by the whole city for his eloquence and his strict virtue. But pride has made him blind to his own weakness, and when a young novice reveals that she is a woman named Matilda who has entered the monastery for love of him, his fall begins, leading him step by step into deception, violence and finally a bargain with the powers of hell.
context: Matthew Gregory Lewis (1775–1818) wrote the novel at nineteen while working at the British embassy in The Hague, and its publication in 1796 caused a scandal that earned him the nickname Monk Lewis. One of the most extreme Gothic novels, it is written for adult readers. Compare it with the gentler terrors of [The Mysteries of Udolpho](/book/3390?lang=en).

about: Walking to London late one summer night, the young drawing master Walter Hartright meets a woman dressed all in white who has escaped from an asylum. Soon after, he takes a post teaching two half-sisters in Cumberland, the gentle Laura Fairlie and the brilliant Marian Halcombe, and discovers a strange likeness between Laura and the woman in white, just as Laura is about to marry the charming Sir Percival Glyde.
context: Published in 1859 and 1860 in Charles Dickens's magazine, the novel was a sensation, and its villain Count Fosco, fat, charming and fond of his white mice, is one of the great characters of Victorian fiction. Wilkie Collins (1824–1889), Dickens's friend and collaborator, tells the story through several witnesses, like a trial. His other masterpiece is [The Moonstone](/book/497?lang=en).

about: A doctor performs a small operation on a young woman's brain so that she can see what the ancients called the great god Pan, the reality behind the world. The experiment succeeds, and destroys her mind. Years later, in London, a series of gentlemen take their own lives after meeting a mysterious, beautiful woman named Helen Vaughan, and two friends set out to discover who she really is.
context: Arthur Machen (1863–1947), a Welsh writer who loved the old landscapes and legends of his home, published the story in 1894, and it was attacked as decadent. It is now considered one of the finest horror stories ever written and a major influence on [H. P. Lovecraft](/book/62316?lang=en). Its power lies in what it leaves unsaid.

about: Laura lives with her father in a lonely castle in a forest of Styria. One evening a carriage overturns near the castle, and a mysterious lady leaves her daughter, Carmilla, in their care. The beautiful, languid guest becomes Laura's intimate friend, but she never prays, sleeps all day and seems to know Laura from a dream of childhood, while the young women of the district begin to fall ill and die.
context: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu (1814–1873), an Irish writer of mysteries and ghost stories, published Carmilla in 1872, twenty-five years before [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en), and it influenced Bram Stoker, also a Dubliner. It is one of the first vampire stories in English, short, atmospheric and more unsettling than frightening.

about: In a cathedral town in southern France, an English scholar buys an old scrapbook from the sacristan, who seems strangely eager to sell it. In other stories a mezzotint of a country house changes each time it is looked at, an ash tree harbours a witch's curse, and a professor on holiday finds an old bronze whistle in the ruins of a Templar church and decides to blow it.
context: M. R. James (1862–1936) was a respected scholar of medieval manuscripts and head of King's College, Cambridge, and later of Eton. He wrote these stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas, and published them in 1904. Precise, dry and full of real antiquarian detail, they define the classic English ghost story. Read them on a winter evening.

about: Two travellers fishing in a remote corner of the west of Ireland find a ruined house on the edge of a chasm, and in the ruins a manuscript. It tells how its author, a recluse living there with his sister and his dog, was besieged by pig-like creatures that climbed from the pit, and how he was carried in visions to a plain surrounded by mountains, and then far into the future to watch the death of the Sun.
context: William Hope Hodgson (1877–1918) ran away to sea at thirteen, later became a writer of horror and sea stories, and was killed in the First World War. Published in 1908, The House on the Borderland mixes a siege story with vast cosmic visions, and Lovecraft admired it greatly; see [At the Mountains of Madness](/book/64499?lang=en).

about: On the wedding day of Conrad, the sickly son of Prince Manfred of Otranto, a gigantic helmet falls from the sky into the courtyard and crushes him.
