The young farmer Gilbert Markham falls in love with her, and when the rumours become unbearable Helen gives him her diary, which reveals the truth about her past and her marriage to the charming, dissolute drunkard Arthur Huntingdon.
context: Published in 1848, Anne Brontë's second novel was a bestseller and shocked readers with its frank picture of addiction and of a woman who leaves her husband to protect her child, at a time when English law gave a wife no right to do so. Anne drew partly on her brother Branwell's decline, and the book is now seen as an early feminist novel. Compare [Agnes Grey](/book/1050?lang=en) and [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en).

about: Lucy Snowe, a young Englishwoman with no family, money or prospects, crosses the Channel alone and arrives at night in Villette, capital of the imaginary kingdom of Labassecour, where she finds work at Madame Beck's school for girls. There, watched by the spying headmistress, she falls quietly in love with a handsome English doctor, suffers a loneliness so deep that she breaks down, and slowly comes to know the fiery, irritable teacher Monsieur Paul Emanuel.
context: Charlotte Brontë based the novel on her own years at a school in Brussels, where she fell unhappily in love with her married teacher, Constantin Héger. Published in 1853, it is darker and more inward than [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en), and George Eliot called it 'a still more wonderful book'. Lucy, who hides her feelings even from the reader, is one of the most modern narrators of the Victorian age. See [her life](/author/cbronte?lang=en).

about: Julien Sorel, the clever, ambitious son of a carpenter in a small French town, worships Napoleon, but after the Emperor's fall the only road upwards for a poor young man is the Church. Hired as tutor to the children of the mayor, Monsieur de Rênal, he seduces the mayor's wife, then trains at a seminary and becomes secretary to a great nobleman in Paris, whose proud daughter Mathilde falls in love with him. At every step he calculates, and at every step his true feelings betray his plans.
context: Stendhal, the pen name of Henri Beyle (1783–1842), who had served in Napoleon's armies, published the novel in 1830 and based it on a real criminal case. Its title probably refers to the army and the Church, the two careers open to ambitious young men. With its sharp analysis of motives, it is a founding work of the psychological novel. Compare [Madame Bovary](/book/324?lang=en).

about: Grigory Pechorin is a young Russian officer posted to the Caucasus: brave, intelligent, handsome and bored with everything. We meet him first through an old captain's story of how he carried off Bela, a Circassian chieftain's daughter, then in a brief glimpse by a traveller, and finally through his own journals, in which he coolly describes toying with a young princess at a spa town, provoking a duel and testing fate with a loaded pistol.
context: Mikhail Lermontov (1814–1841), poet and officer, had himself been exiled to the Caucasus for a poem attacking the court after Pushkin's death in a duel. Published in 1840, the book is one of the first great Russian novels, and its five linked stories show Pechorin from ever closer viewpoints. A year later Lermontov too was killed in a duel, aged twenty-six. See also [Pushkin](/author/pushkin?lang=en).

about: In a quiet provincial Russian town, the elderly liberal Stepan Trofimovich Verkhovensky lives on the generosity of his patroness, Varvara Petrovna, and talks grandly about ideas. Then his son Pyotr arrives, planning to build a secret revolutionary cell and spread chaos, and with him returns Varvara's son Nikolai Stavrogin, a handsome, magnetic and empty aristocrat whom everyone around him, believers and nihilists alike, sees as a leader. Gossip, fires, murder and suicide follow.
context: Fyodor Dostoevsky based the plot on a real case of 1869, when the revolutionary Sergei Nechayev and his followers murdered a student in Moscow. Published in 1871 and 1872, and also translated as Demons or The Devils, it is both a dark comedy and a prophetic warning about political fanaticism. Read [Crime and Punishment](/book/12?lang=en) first, and see [his life](/author/dostoevsky?lang=en).

about: In the sleepy Missouri town of Dawson's Landing in 1830, Roxy, an enslaved woman who is one-sixteenth Black and looks white, fears that her baby son will one day be sold 'down the river'. So she switches him in the cradle with her master's baby, born the same day, and the two boys grow up in each other's places: the false heir becomes a spoiled, cruel gambler, the true one a slave. Only David Wilson, a clever lawyer whom the town thinks a fool, holds the means to discover the truth, through his odd hobby of collecting fingerprints.
context: Mark Twain published the novel in 1894. Beneath its comedy lies a bitter satire of slavery and of the very idea of race, since the town can tell the two boys apart only by the labels it has given them. It was also one of the first novels in which fingerprints solve a crime. Read [Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](/book/49?lang=en), and see [Twain's life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: In 1861 young Samuel Clemens set off by stagecoach across the plains with his brother Orion, newly appointed secretary of the Nevada Territory, for what he expected to be a short adventure; he stayed in the West for years. This comic and partly invented account follows him through the silver-mining boom of Nevada, where he dreams of instant riches, to work as a reporter in Virginia City, to the streets of San Francisco and on a voyage to the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii.
context: Published in 1872, the book shows Mark Twain finding his voice as a teller of tall tales, with famous digressions on the coyote, the jackass rabbit and the story of Grandfather's old ram, which is never actually told. It is also a lively picture of the American West in the days of the Pony Express. Read [The Innocents Abroad](/book/52?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: Harvey Cheyne, the spoiled fifteen-year-old son of an American railway millionaire, falls overboard from a liner off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland and is picked up by a small fishing schooner, the We're Here. Its captain, Disko Troop, does not believe a word about his riches and will not turn back for months, so Harvey must work as a ship's boy for a small wage. Among fishermen of many nations, through fog, storms and the cod season, he slowly learns to be a man.
context: Published in 1897, it is Rudyard Kipling's only novel set entirely in America, written while he lived in Vermont; he studied the Gloucester fishing fleet in detail with the help of his friend Dr James Conland. Spencer Tracy won an Oscar for the 1937 film. Compare [Kim](/book/356?lang=en), another story of a boy's education, and see [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: The second collection of Mowgli's stories follows the boy raised by wolves into his teens. In 'How Fear Came' the elephant Hathi tells how the first tiger got his stripes; in 'Letting in the Jungle' Mowgli brings the jungle down on a village that has turned against his human mother; in 'Red Dog' he and the wolves face a deadly invading pack; and in 'The Spring Running' he feels that he must leave the jungle for the world of men. Other tales include 'The Miracle of Purun Bhagat', about an Indian statesman who becomes a holy man.
context: Published in 1895, the book completes the Mowgli cycle begun in [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en), and it is darker and more mature than the first. Rudyard Kipling wrote both while living in Vermont, drawing on the India of his early childhood. See [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: England during the Wars of the Roses, in the fifteenth century. Young Dick Shelton is the ward of the unscrupulous Sir Daniel Brackley, a knight who changes sides whenever it suits him. When a band of outlaws in the forest begins killing Sir Daniel's men with black arrows and pins up a rhyme accusing him of murder, Dick begins to suspect that his guardian killed his own father. Meanwhile he befriends a boy called John Matcham, who is not what he seems, and meets the young Duke of Gloucester, the future Richard III.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson first published the story as a serial for boys in 1883, the year [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en) appeared as a book, and he pretended to think little of it, but it remains a fast, atmospheric adventure. Its outlaws, the Fellowship of the Black Arrow, echo the legends of Robin Hood. See [his life](/author/stevenson?lang=en).

about: In the autumn of 1878, the young Robert Louis Stevenson spent twelve days walking about 120 miles through the Cévennes mountains of southern France, with a small, stubborn donkey named Modestine to carry his gear, including a huge sleeping sack of his own design. He records his struggles to make her move, nights sleeping under the stars, a stay at a Trappist monastery and the history of the Camisards, the Protestant rebels who rose against Louis XIV in these hills.
context: Published in 1879, this is one of the earliest classics of travel on foot for pleasure, and its route is now a marked long-distance path, the GR 70 or Chemin de Stevenson. Stevenson was then in love with Fanny Osbourne, a married American woman he would later marry, and some passages read like a disguised longing for her. See [his life](/author/stevenson?lang=en).

about: When the American diplomat Hiram B. Otis buys Canterville Chase, an old English country house, he is warned that it is haunted by Sir Simon de Canterville, who murdered his wife in 1575. The Otis family is not impressed: they offer the ghost lubricating oil for his rattling chains, scrub away his famous bloodstain with a modern stain remover, and the mischievous twins play tricks on him until the poor ghost is miserable. Only the gentle daughter, Virginia, takes pity on him.
context: Oscar Wilde published this comic story in 1887. It gently mocks both English snobbery and American practicality, has an unexpectedly tender ending, and has been filmed many times. Read Wilde's fairy tales in [The Happy Prince and Other Tales](/book/67?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/wilde?lang=en).

about: 'Yet each man kills the thing he loves.' In 109 six-line stanzas, Oscar Wilde describes the last weeks of a fellow prisoner in Reading Gaol, a young trooper, Charles Thomas Wooldridge, who had murdered his wife and was hanged in July 1896. The poem follows the prisoners as they watch the condemned man walking in the yard, their sleepless night before the execution and the quicklime grave within the prison walls, and becomes a cry against the cruelty of the prison system itself.
context: Wilde wrote it in France after his release from two years' hard labour for 'gross indecency', and it was published in 1898 under the name C.3.3., his cell number. It was the last work he wrote; he died in Paris two years later. Read it with [De Profundis](/book/68?lang=en), his letter from prison, and see [his life](/author/wilde?lang=en).

about: Axel Heyst, a thoughtful, detached Swede who has decided that the only way to avoid pain is to take no part in life, lives alone on a remote island in the Malay Archipelago after the failure of a coal company. On a visit to a hotel in Surabaya he rescues Lena, a young English violinist in a travelling ladies' orchestra, from the hotel's owner, and takes her back to his island. But the jealous hotelkeeper sends after them three sinister adventurers who believe Heyst is hiding a fortune.
context: Published in 1915, Victory was one of Joseph Conrad's greatest popular successes, a tense thriller and a philosophical tragedy about whether a man can live without commitment. Conrad, a Polish-born sailor who wrote in his third language, English, knew these waters from his years at sea. Read [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en) and [Lord Jim](/book/343?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/conrad?lang=en).

about: In the village of Mellstock, the old church musicians, a band of fiddlers and singers led by the Dewy family, play carols from house to house on Christmas Eve, as they have for generations. But the new vicar wants to replace them with a harmonium, played by the pretty new schoolmistress, Fancy Day. Young Dick Dewy falls in love with Fancy, and so do a wealthy farmer and the vicar himself, while the choir fights its losing battle against change.
context: Published in 1872, this was Thomas Hardy's first success and is the gentlest and most cheerful of his novels, a comic picture of village life inspired by his own family in Dorset, where his father and grandfather played in the church band. Read next [Far from the Madding Crowd](/book/307?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: In the wooded village of Little Hintock, Grace Melbury, the daughter of a timber merchant, comes home from an expensive education and finds that she no longer fits in. She has long been promised to Giles Winterborne, a loyal, simple apple-grower and woodsman, but her father, ambitious for her, pushes her into marriage with the handsome and unfaithful young doctor Edred Fitzpiers. Meanwhile Marty South, a poor girl who loves Giles in silence, sells her beautiful hair to the rich Mrs Charmond.
context: Published in 1887, The Woodlanders was, Thomas Hardy said, in some respects his favourite among his novels as a story. Its picture of the woods, the cider-making and the old ways of the countryside is among his most beautiful, and it questions class and the trap of an unhappy marriage. See also [The Mayor of Casterbridge](/book/488?lang=en) and [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: In the village of Hayslope at the end of the eighteenth century, Adam Bede is a strong and honest carpenter who loves Hetty Sorrel, a pretty, vain dairymaid on the Poyser family's farm. Hetty, dazzled by the attentions of the young squire, Captain Arthur Donnithorne, dreams of becoming a lady. Their secret affair has consequences that drive Hetty to a desperate act and a prison cell, where the young Methodist preacher Dinah Morris comes to comfort her.
context: Published in 1859, this was the first full-length novel by George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), and it was an immediate success; readers argued over who the mysterious author could be. Its warm, detailed picture of country life and its sympathy for flawed people prepared the way for [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en). Read also [Silas Marner](/book/849?lang=en).

about: The novel opens in a German casino, where the beautiful, proud Gwendolen Harleth is gambling and feels herself watched by a young Englishman, Daniel Deronda. Soon after, her family loses its money, and Gwendolen marries the rich, cold Henleigh Grandcourt to save them, breaking a promise she made to another woman. Daniel, raised as the ward of an English baronet without knowing who his parents were, saves a young singer, Mirah, from drowning herself, and through her and her visionary brother Mordecai he begins to discover his own origins.
context: Published in 1876, George Eliot's last novel was unusual in its time for its sympathetic picture of Jewish life and culture in Victorian England. Its portrait of Gwendolen's guilt and suffering inside a cruel marriage is one of the finest psychological studies in Victorian fiction. Read first [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en).

about: In Manchester during the hungry 1840s, Mary Barton, the pretty daughter of a mill worker, is torn between Jem Wilson, an honest engineer who loves her, and Harry Carson, the handsome son of a rich mill owner, who flatters her with dreams of becoming a lady. Her father John, embittered by unemployment, hunger and the death of his son, becomes a trade unionist and a Chartist. When Harry Carson is shot dead, suspicion falls on Jem, and Mary must race against time to save him.
context: Elizabeth Gaskell (1810–1865), the wife of a Unitarian minister in Manchester, saw the poverty of the city's workers at first hand. Her first novel, published anonymously in 1848, shocked middle-class readers and angered some factory owners. Compare her later [North and South](/book/4360?lang=en) and the gentle comedy of [Cranford](/book/697?lang=en).

about: Molly Gibson, the only child of a widowed country doctor in the little town of Hollingford, is still a girl when her father remarries, partly to give her a guide as she grows up. Her stepmother, a former governess, is vain, shallow and a little dishonest, but the stepmother's daughter, Cynthia, glamorous and secretive, becomes Molly's dearest friend. Both girls are drawn to the sons of the local squire, and Cynthia's hidden past brings Molly close to scandal.
context: Elizabeth Gaskell was finishing the novel when she died suddenly in 1865, and the last chapter was never written, though the ending is clear. Many readers consider it her masterpiece, a witty and tender study of family life; Roger Hamley, the squire's scientific son, was partly modelled on the young Charles Darwin, to whom Gaskell was distantly related. Read also [Cranford](/book/697?lang=en) and [North and South](/book/4360?lang=en).

about: The Reverend Septimus Harding, a gentle, elderly clergyman who loves church music above everything, is warden of Hiram's Hospital in the cathedral city of Barchester, an almshouse for twelve old men founded by a medieval will. The post pays him a comfortable income, while the old men receive only small sums. When a young reformer, John Bold, who happens to be in love with Harding's daughter Eleanor, challenges the arrangement and the newspapers take up the scandal, Mr Harding must decide what his conscience demands.
context: Published in 1855, this short novel was Anthony Trollope's first success and the first of his six Barsetshire novels, witty, humane portraits of clergymen and country society. Trollope (1815–1882) wrote most of his books while working full time for the Post Office, where he helped introduce the pillar box. Continue with [Barchester Towers](/book/2583?lang=en).

about: When the old Bishop of Barchester dies, the new bishop is the weak Dr Proudie, completely ruled by his formidable wife and by his oily chaplain, the ambitious Mr Obadiah Slope. Their arrival starts a war in the cathedral close against the high-church party led by Archdeacon Grantly. Meanwhile the widowed Eleanor Bold, now rich, is courted by several suitors, among them Mr Slope, and the Stanhope family returns from Italy with the beautiful, crippled Signora Neroni, who enchants every man she meets.
context: Published in 1857, this sequel to [The Warden](/book/916?lang=en) is Anthony Trollope's most popular novel, a sparkling comedy of church politics, ambition and romance, in which the battles over the next dean and the wardenship of Hiram's Hospital continue Mr Harding's story. Mrs Proudie and Mr Slope are among the great comic characters of English fiction.

about: Augustus Melmotte, a mysterious financier with a shady past in Europe, arrives in London and becomes the toast of society. Aristocrats who despise him crowd his parties, hoping to marry his daughter Marie and her fortune, or to grow rich from his scheme for a great American railway that may never be built, and he even stands for Parliament. Around him swarm the debts and intrigues of the Carbury family: the worthless young Sir Felix and his mother, Lady Carbury, a writer ready to flatter any critic.
context: Anthony Trollope wrote this long, angry satire after returning from abroad disgusted by what he called the commercial profligacy of the age, and it was published in 1875. Melmotte's bubble of credit, built on nothing but confidence, has made the novel strikingly relevant after every financial crash. Read the gentler [The Warden](/book/916?lang=en) for contrast.

about: Redmond Barry, a poor young Irishman with a high opinion of himself, tells his own story, convinced that he is a gentleman and a hero. After a duel he flees his village, serves in the Seven Years' War first in the British army and then, against his will, in the Prussian one, deserts, becomes a card-sharper at the courts of Europe, and finally marries a rich, unhappy widow, the Countess of Lyndon, whose name he takes and whose fortune he squanders.
context: William Makepeace Thackeray (1811–1863) published the novel as a serial in 1844 and revised it later as The Memoirs of Barry Lyndon. Its comedy lies in the gap between how Barry sees himself and what the reader sees: a liar, a bully and a cheat. Stanley Kubrick filmed it in 1975. Thackeray's masterpiece is [Vanity Fair](/book/896?lang=en).

about: During the Third Crusade, a Scottish knight, Sir Kenneth of the Couchant Leopard, meets a Saracen emir in single combat in the desert near the Dead Sea; they fight to a draw and become friends. In the crusaders' camp, King Richard the Lionheart lies ill with fever, and a physician sent by Sultan Saladin cures him with a mysterious talisman. But the Christian camp is full of jealousy and intrigue among the European princes, and Sir Kenneth, who loves Richard's kinswoman Edith, is disgraced.
context: Sir Walter Scott published the novel in 1825. Its most memorable figure is Saladin, shown as wise, generous and chivalrous, often wiser than the quarrelling Christian kings, and the book shaped how European readers imagined the great sultan for a century. Read also Scott's [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en).

about: In the reign of Elizabeth I, Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, the queen's favourite, has secretly married the beautiful Amy Robsart and keeps her hidden at Cumnor Place, an old house near Oxford, because the marriage would ruin his hopes of winning the queen herself. Amy's former suitor, Edmund Tressilian, believes she has been seduced and seeks justice, while Leicester's ruthless servant Richard Varney plots to keep the secret at any cost, all leading up to the queen's spectacular visit to Leicester's castle of Kenilworth.
context: Published in 1821, the novel mixes history and invention: Amy Robsart really died mysteriously in 1560, at the foot of a staircase, though the famous festivities at Kenilworth took place fifteen years later. Sir Walter Scott's portrait of Elizabeth, proud and passionate, is one of the book's pleasures. Read also [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en) and [The Talisman](/book/1602?lang=en).

about: In 1468, Quentin Durward, a penniless young Scot, arrives in France to seek his fortune and joins the Scottish Archers, the bodyguard of the cunning King Louis XI. The king, who prefers spies and intrigue to battles, sends him to escort the young Countess Isabelle de Croye, who has fled the Duke of Burgundy, through dangerous country to the protection of the Bishop of Liège, on a journey the king himself has secretly arranged to end in an ambush.
context: Published in 1823, Quentin Durward was Sir Walter Scott's first novel with a setting on the Continent, and it made him even more popular in France than at home. Its portrait of Louis XI, superstitious, miserly and brilliant, is one of his finest. Read also [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en) and [The Talisman](/book/1602?lang=en).

about: In the 1740s, on the shores of Lake Otsego in the forests of New York, young Natty Bumppo, a hunter raised among the Delaware people and known as Deerslayer, joins his friend Chingachgook to rescue Chingachgook's bride, Wah-ta-Wah, from a Huron war party. They become caught up with Tom Hutter, a rough trapper who lives in a 'castle' built on the water, and his two daughters, the proud, beautiful Judith and the simple, gentle Hetty, as Deerslayer kills a man for the first time and earns a new name, Hawkeye.
context: Published in 1841, The Deerslayer was the last of James Fenimore Cooper's five Leatherstocking Tales to be written but the first in the hero's life. It is still read for its descriptions of the lake and the forest, although Mark Twain mocked its style in a famous essay. Read next [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en).

about: This collection gathers Nathaniel Hawthorne's early stories and sketches: 'The Minister's Black Veil', in which a New England clergyman suddenly appears with his face covered by a black veil and never removes it; 'Dr Heidegger's Experiment', in which four elderly friends drink water from the Fountain of Youth; 'The Ambitious Guest'; 'Wakefield', about a man who walks out on his wife and lives in the next street for twenty years; and many others.
context: The title comes from Shakespeare's King John ('Life is as tedious as a twice-told tale'), since most of the pieces had appeared before in magazines. When the book was published in 1837, and in an enlarged edition in 1842, Edgar Allan Poe praised it in a famous review that set out his own theory of the short story. Read Hawthorne's [The Scarlet Letter](/book/411?lang=en) and [The House of the Seven Gables](/book/444?lang=en).

about: Rip Van Winkle, a good-natured, lazy villager in the Catskill Mountains of New York, loves fishing and telling stories but hates work, and escapes his scolding wife by wandering the hills with his dog. One afternoon he meets a strange company of little men in old Dutch clothes playing ninepins, drinks from their keg and falls asleep. When he wakes, his beard is a foot long, his gun has rusted and no one in the village knows him: twenty years have passed, and the American Revolution has come and gone.
context: Washington Irving (1783–1859) published the story in The Sketch Book in 1819, and with [The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](/book/417?lang=en) it became one of the founding legends of American literature. Rip's name is still used for anyone who has slept through great changes. Irving also wrote [The Alhambra](/book/45043?lang=en), about Moorish Granada.

about: In 1829 the American writer Washington Irving lived for several months in the Alhambra itself, the palace of the Nasrid sultans in Granada, then a half-ruined place inhabited by poor families, old soldiers and storytellers. The book mixes his descriptions of the palace, its courts, fountains and towers, and of the people who lived there, with the legends he heard: the Arabian astrologer, the three beautiful princesses, the Moor's legacy, and the last sultan, Boabdil, sighing as he looked back at the city he had lost.
context: Published in 1832 and revised in 1851, the book did much to make the Alhambra famous around the world and to rescue it from neglect. It is written with deep sympathy for the Moorish past of Andalusia, and a plaque in the palace still honours Irving, who later served as the American minister to Spain. Read also [Rip Van Winkle](/book/55419?lang=en).

about: Christopher Newman, a self-made American millionaire who made his fortune in washtubs and leather, arrives in Paris in 1868 determined to find the best wife money can buy. He falls in love with Claire de Cintré, a beautiful young widow from an ancient aristocratic family, the Bellegardes. Her proud mother and elder brother accept his money and pretend to accept him, but they find an American businessman impossible to bear, and Newman discovers that the family hides a dark secret.
context: Published in 1877, this early novel shows Henry James's lifelong theme, the meeting of open, innocent Americans with old, complicated Europe, in its boldest form, and Newman's honesty against the cold pride of the French nobility gives the story its power. Read also [Daisy Miller](/book/525?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: Lambert Strether, a widowed editor in his fifties from Woollett, Massachusetts, is sent to Paris by the rich widow he hopes to marry, Mrs Newsome, to bring home her son Chad, who is believed to be wasting his life with a wicked woman. In Paris Strether finds Chad transformed into a polished gentleman, falls under the spell of the city and of the elegant Madame de Vionnet, and begins to wonder whether he should be urging Chad to stay. 'Live all you can,' he tells a young friend; 'it's a mistake not to.'
context: Henry James considered this novel, published in 1903, the best of all his books. Written in his late, intricate style, it is a subtle comedy of perception in which everything is seen through Strether's slowly changing understanding. Begin with James's shorter [Daisy Miller](/book/525?lang=en) and [Washington Square](/book/3001?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: An American editor obsessed with the dead Romantic poet Jeffrey Aspern learns that Aspern's former lover, Juliana Bordereau, now very old, lives in seclusion in a decaying palace in Venice with her shy, middle-aged niece, and that she still keeps the poet's letters. Under a false name he rents rooms in their house, fills the garden with flowers and courts the niece's friendship, ready to do almost anything to get hold of the papers.
context: Henry James based this novella, published in 1888, on a story he heard in Florence about a man who tried to obtain Shelley's letters from Claire Clairmont, Mary Shelley's stepsister and Lord Byron's former lover, who lived into old age. It is a subtle study of the ethics of biography and of its narrator's self-deceptions. See also [The Turn of the Screw](/book/353?lang=en) and [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: Undine Spragg, beautiful, ruthless and endlessly dissatisfied, comes to New York from the Midwestern town of Apex with her newly rich parents, determined to rise to the top of society. She marries into an old, refined New York family, then sets her sights higher, moving through divorces and marriages in New York and Paris, always wanting whatever she does not yet have, and leaving her husbands and even her small son behind her.
context: Edith Wharton published the novel in 1913 after years of work, and many critics rank it with [The House of Mirth](/book/590?lang=en) and [The Age of Innocence](/book/840?lang=en) as her greatest achievement. Undine, named after a hair-waving product her father once sold, is one of the most memorable anti-heroines in American fiction.

about: Presented as a manuscript discovered seven centuries in the future, this novel tells the story of Ernest Everhard, a powerful socialist leader in the America of the early twentieth century, through the memoir of his wife, Avis. As he challenges the rich in debate after debate, an oligarchy of giant trusts, the Iron Heel, seizes control of the country, crushing unions, farmers and the middle class, and the resistance is driven underground into a long and bloody struggle.
context: Jack London published the book in 1908, and it is often called one of the first modern dystopian novels; George Orwell admired its prediction of how a ruling class might use violence to keep power. It shows a very different side of the author of [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en) and [Martin Eden](/book/312?lang=en). See [his life](/author/london?lang=en).

about: Jo March, now Mrs Bhaer, and her kind German husband run Plumfield, a school in the country where boys are taught with affection rather than the cane, learning through games, gardens, pets and honest talk as well as lessons. The book follows a year in the lives of a dozen children: Nat, a shy street fiddler; Dan, a wild runaway; Nan, a tomboy; Demi and Daisy, the twins of Jo's sister Meg; and others, through small adventures, pillow fights and a few hard lessons.
context: Louisa May Alcott (1832–1888) published this sequel to [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en) in 1871, and it reflects the progressive ideas about education of her father, the teacher Bronson Alcott. The story continues in Jo's Boys. See [her life](/author/alcott?lang=en).

about: At sixteen and a half, Anne Shirley takes up her first job as teacher of the school in Avonlea, the village on Prince Edward Island where she grew up, full of resolutions never to whip a pupil. Meanwhile Marilla takes in a pair of orphaned twins, angelic Dora and mischievous Davy; Anne and her friends found a society to improve the village, with disastrous results when the hall is painted bright blue; and Anne befriends a lonely, romantic woman, Miss Lavendar, in her little stone house.
context: L. M. Montgomery (1874–1942) published this sequel to [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en) in 1909, a year after the first book's huge success. It is gentle, funny and full of the island's beauty, and the story continues in Anne of the Island. Read also Montgomery's novel for adults, [The Blue Castle](/book/62043?lang=en).

about: Cedric Errol is a golden-haired, warm-hearted seven-year-old living modestly in New York with his widowed mother, whom he calls 'Dearest'. One day a lawyer arrives from England with astonishing news: Cedric is now heir to his grandfather, the Earl of Dorincourt, a bitter, gouty old man who had disowned Cedric's father for marrying an American. Sent to England, the boy innocently believes the best of everyone, including the earl, who slowly changes under his influence.
context: Frances Hodgson Burnett published the novel in 1886, and it was a sensation; the pictures of Cedric in a velvet suit with a lace collar led thousands of mothers to dress their sons the same way, to the boys' lasting embarrassment. Read also [The Secret Garden](/book/315?lang=en) and [A Little Princess](/book/316?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/burnett?lang=en).

about: A boy named Tip, who lives with a cruel old witch named Mombi in the Gillikin country of Oz, carves a man with a pumpkin for a head to frighten her. Instead she brings Jack Pumpkinhead to life with a magic powder, and Tip runs away with him. On their way to the Emerald City they find the Scarecrow, now its king, just as the city is captured by General Jinjur and an army of girls armed with knitting needles, and they join the Tin Woodman, a wooden Saw-Horse and the learned Woggle-Bug to set things right.
context: L. Frank Baum published this sequel to [The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](/book/314?lang=en) in 1904, after thousands of children wrote asking for more. Dorothy does not appear, but its surprising ending, which reveals the true ruler of Oz, made it one of the most loved of the fourteen Oz books Baum wrote. See [his life](/author/baum?lang=en).

about: When their father is suddenly taken away one evening by two strange men, Roberta, Peter and Phyllis must leave their comfortable London home and move with their mother to a small cottage in the country beside a railway line, where she writes stories to earn money. The children wave every day to an old gentleman on the 9.15 train, make friends with Perks the porter, save a train from a landslide by waving red flannel petticoats, and slowly, Bobbie the eldest most of all, try to find out what has happened to their father.
context: E. Nesbit (1858–1924), an English writer and a founding member of the socialist Fabian Society, published the novel in 1906. It is one of the best-loved children's books in English, above all for its final scene on the station platform, and the 1970 film made it a classic again. Read also her [Five Children and It](/book/1060?lang=en).

about: Five children, Cyril, Anthea, Robert, Jane and their baby brother, the Lamb, are spending the summer in the Kent countryside when, digging in a gravel pit, they uncover a Psammead, a grumpy, furry sand-fairy with eyes on long horns like a snail's, who can grant one wish a day. Each wish lasts until sunset, and each goes wrong: they wish to be beautiful and their own servant will not let them in, wish for gold and cannot spend it, wish for wings and end up stranded on a church tower.
context: Published in 1902, E. Nesbit's book was one of the first to bring magic into the everyday world of ordinary modern children, who argue, make mistakes and must get themselves out of trouble, and it influenced writers from C. S. Lewis to J. K. Rowling. The story continues in [The Phoenix and the Carpet](/book/1108?lang=en). Read also [The Railway Children](/book/2073?lang=en).

about: Diamond, the young son of a coachman in London, sleeps in a hayloft above the stables, and one night the North Wind, in the shape of a beautiful woman with long flowing hair, comes in through a hole in the wall and carries him on journeys through the night sky. She can be gentle or terrible, sinking a ship as well as saving people, and at last she takes the sick boy to the mysterious country at her back. In between, Diamond lives a hard, cheerful life in the London streets, helping his family and a crossing-sweeper girl called Nanny.
context: George MacDonald (1824–1905), a Scottish minister and writer, encouraged his friend Lewis Carroll to publish Alice and was a great influence on C. S. Lewis and J. R. R. Tolkien. Published in 1871, this is a strange, tender book about goodness, death and hope. Read also his [The Princess and the Goblin](/book/995?lang=en).

about: Eight-year-old Princess Irene lives in a lonely house on a mountainside, beneath which dwell the goblins, misshapen creatures who were once human and now hate everyone above ground. Exploring the house, Irene finds a hidden staircase and at the top her mysterious great-great-grandmother, who spins an almost invisible thread to guide her. With the help of Curdie, a brave young miner who sings rhymes to drive the goblins away, she uncovers the goblins' plot to kidnap her.
context: Published in 1872, George MacDonald's fairy tale is one of the founding works of modern fantasy; G. K. Chesterton said it made a difference to his whole existence, and Tolkien's goblins owe much to it. The story continues in The Princess and Curdie. Read also [At the Back of the North Wind](/book/538?lang=en).

about: Tom is a little chimney sweep, beaten and overworked by his cruel master Grimes, who has never been taught right from wrong. After he comes down the wrong chimney into a white bedroom in a great house and is chased away as a thief, he runs to a river, falls in, and is turned into a tiny water-baby. Living among the creatures of the river and the sea, he meets the fairies Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid and Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby, who teach him, step by step, to become good.
context: Charles Kingsley (1819–1875), a clergyman, naturalist and reformer, published the story in 1863. Part fairy tale, part satire and part sermon, it joins in the debates of its age, including Darwin's theory of evolution, which Kingsley accepted, and it helped bring about laws against sending boys up chimneys. It also contains prejudices of its time that modern readers find offensive.

about: Tom Brown, the son of a country squire, is sent to Rugby School as a boy, where he finds a world of its own: wild games of football, fights, boyish loyalties and the terror of the bully Flashman, who roasts him in front of a fire. Under the eye of the great headmaster Dr Thomas Arnold, Tom grows from a careless, rough young rebel into a responsible young man, above all after he is asked to look after a gentle, sickly new boy, George Arthur.
context: Thomas Hughes (1822–1896) had been a pupil at Rugby under Arnold, and he published the novel in 1857. It created the school story as a genre and shaped the ideal of the English public school for a century; its villain Flashman was later turned into the roguish hero of George MacDonald Fraser's comic novels. Compare [Little Men](/book/2922?lang=en).

about: Grieving the death of his only son, the old hunter Allan Quatermain sets off on one last adventure with his friends Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good and the mighty Zulu warrior Umslopogaas, who carries a great axe. Travelling deep into unexplored East Africa, they survive an attack on a mission station and a terrifying underground river before reaching Zu-Vendis, a hidden kingdom ruled by two rival sister queens, Nyleptha and Sorais, who both fall in love with Sir Henry.
context: Published in 1887, this sequel to [King Solomon's Mines](/book/2351?lang=en) is H. Rider Haggard's farewell to his famous hero, and Umslopogaas is one of his most memorable characters. Its lost-world adventure influenced many later writers, though, like the earlier book, it reflects the colonial attitudes of its age. See also [She](/book/3281?lang=en).

about: In this short book of parables and prose poems, Kahlil Gibran writes about the greater self that always walks ahead of us, calling us to become what we are not yet: 'You are your own forerunner, and the towers you have builded are but the foundation of your giant-self.' Among its twenty-five pieces are the king who became a hermit, the saint and the brigand, the dying man and the vulture, the scholar and the poet, and the last watchman of the night.
context: Published in New York in 1920, between [The Madman](/book/101?lang=en) and [The Prophet](/book/98?lang=en), the book belongs to the years when Gibran (1883–1931), born in Bsharri in Lebanon, was finding his voice in English, and it carries his own drawings. See [his life](/author/gibran?lang=en).

about: After the death of her silent, eccentric father, seventeen-year-old Maud Ruthyn learns that his will has made her the ward of his brother Silas, a man she has never met, who long ago was suspected of murdering a gambler found dead in a locked room at his house. Her father hoped to clear his brother's name by trusting him. So Maud goes to live at Bartram-Haugh, Silas's decaying mansion, with its sinister servants and his coarse son Dudley, and slowly realises that if she dies before she comes of age, her fortune will pass to Silas.
context: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu (1814–1873), an Irish writer and newspaper owner, published the novel in 1864. A masterpiece of slowly building Gothic suspense, with a terrifying French governess, Madame de la Rougierre, it influenced later writers of mystery and horror. Read also Le Fanu's vampire novella [Carmilla](/book/9338?lang=en).

about: Two friends, the narrator and a tough, practical Swede, are canoeing down the flooded Danube beyond Vienna and Pressburg, and camp for the night on a small sandy island among endless swamps of willow bushes in the middle of Hungary. As the wind blows and the river rises, small, strange things begin to happen: the willows seem to move, a paddle disappears, holes appear in the canoe, and the two men become convinced that they have strayed into a place where another world touches ours.
context: Algernon Blackwood (1869–1951), an English writer who loved wild places, published the novella in 1907 in The Listener and Other Stories. H. P. Lovecraft considered it the finest weird tale in English literature, and its horror comes from what is never shown. Read also Lovecraft's [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en).

about: A young man touring New England to study its old buildings and his own ancestry takes a cheap bus through Innsmouth, a decaying seaport on the Massachusetts coast that the neighbouring towns avoid. Its people have a strange 'Innsmouth look', with bulging, unblinking eyes and rough skin, and an old drunkard tells him the town's secret: a sea captain's dealings in the South Seas with creatures from the deep, and a pact that has changed the town for generations. Trapped overnight in a crumbling hotel, the narrator must run for his life.
context: H. P. Lovecraft wrote the story in 1931, and it appeared as a small book in 1936, the only one of his books published in his lifetime. One of his most popular tales, it mixes horror with a chase thriller and ends with a twist about the narrator himself. Read also [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en) and [At the Mountains of Madness](/book/64499?lang=en).

about: West of Arkham, in the hills of Massachusetts, a surveyor sent to plan a new reservoir finds a stretch of grey, dead land that the locals call the 'blasted heath'. An old man tells him what happened there in 1882: a meteorite fell on the farm of Nahum Gardner, bringing with it a colour unlike any on Earth. Over the following months the crops grow large but taste bitter, the animals change, the trees glow at night, and the family, one by one, fall into madness and decay.
context: H. P. Lovecraft wrote the story in 1927 and considered it his best; it appeared that year in the magazine Amazing Stories. Its horror is not a monster but something truly alien that cannot be understood, and many readers have seen in it a fable about poisoning and radiation. Read also [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en).

about: G. K. Chesterton tells how he set out, as a young man, to invent a new philosophy of his own and discovered that it already existed: it was Christian orthodoxy. In lively chapters full of paradoxes, he argues that the madman is not the man who has lost his reason but the man who has lost everything except his reason, that fairy tales teach truer lessons about the world than modern rationalists, and that tradition is 'the democracy of the dead'.
context: Published in 1908 as a reply to critics of his earlier book Heretics, who said he attacked other people's views without stating his own, Orthodoxy has influenced readers from C. S. Lewis onwards, whether or not they share its faith. Chesterton (1874–1936) also wrote the [Father Brown](/book/523?lang=en) detective stories and [The Man Who Was Thursday](/book/1901?lang=en).

about: The small, round-faced Catholic priest with the shabby umbrella returns in twelve new mysteries, solving crimes not with science or fingerprints but with his deep understanding of human nature and sin. Among them are 'The Absence of Mr Glass', in which he gently deflates a famous criminologist; 'The Paradise of Thieves', set among Italian brigands; and 'The Duel of Dr Hirsch', with his friend Flambeau, the former master thief, at his side.
context: Published in 1914, this is G. K. Chesterton's second collection of Father Brown stories, after [The Innocence of Father Brown](/book/523?lang=en). Chesterton based the priest partly on a real friend, Father John O'Connor, and the stories remain among the most original in detective fiction. See also [Orthodoxy](/book/480?lang=en).

about: In late 1915, Richard Hannay, now a major recovering from wounds received at the Battle of Loos, is called to the Foreign Office and given a desperate mission. Germany is believed to be preparing a religious uprising across the Muslim world, centred on a mysterious prophet known as Greenmantle. With three companions, among them the American John S. Blenkiron and the old Boer hunter Peter Pienaar, Hannay crosses wartime Germany in disguise to reach Constantinople and the besieged Ottoman fortress of Erzurum.
context: John Buchan published this sequel to [The Thirty-Nine Steps](/book/857?lang=en) in 1916, while working for Britain's wartime propaganda and intelligence services, and it drew on real German efforts to rouse the Muslim world against Britain. Its picture of the East reflects the attitudes of a British imperial writer, but as a thriller it is fast and inventive.

about: Philip Carey, orphaned at nine and born with a club foot, is raised by his narrow-minded uncle, a country vicar, and his kind, timid aunt. Painfully shy and ashamed of his foot, he loses his faith at school, studies in Heidelberg, tries to become a painter in Paris and finally trains as a doctor in London. There he falls into an obsessive, humiliating passion for Mildred, a cold and careless waitress who uses him again and again, while he searches for the meaning of a life that seems to have none.
context: W. Somerset Maugham (1874–1965), who was himself orphaned as a boy, had a stammer and trained as a doctor at St Thomas's Hospital in London, published this largely autobiographical novel in 1915. Its title comes from Spinoza's Ethics, where human bondage means our slavery to the passions, and it is often counted among the great novels of the twentieth century. Read also [The Moon and Sixpence](/book/535?lang=en).

about: Charles Strickland is a dull, respectable London stockbroker with a wife and two children, until one day, at about forty, he abandons them without a word and goes to Paris. The narrator, a young writer sent to bring him back, expects to find a love affair, but Strickland has left everything simply to paint. Poor, rude, ruthless and indifferent to everyone, including those who help him, he follows his vision from Paris to Marseille and finally to Tahiti.
context: W. Somerset Maugham published the novel in 1919, loosely inspired by the life of the painter Paul Gauguin. It asks whether genius excuses cruelty, and the narrator's sharp, ironic voice keeps the question open. The title is said to come from a review of Maugham's [Of Human Bondage](/book/654?lang=en), which described its hero as so busy yearning for the moon that he never saw the sixpence at his feet.

about: Constance and Sophia Baines grow up above their parents' draper's shop in Bursley, one of the pottery towns of the English Midlands, in the 1860s. Quiet Constance marries the shop assistant and spends her whole life in the same house and town. Passionate Sophia runs away with a handsome, worthless travelling salesman to Paris, where he abandons her, and she lives through the siege of 1870 and the Commune, building a successful boarding house. The novel follows both sisters from girlhood to old age.
context: Arnold Bennett (1867–1931), who came from the Potteries himself, wrote the novel in 1908 after seeing a fussy old woman in a Paris restaurant and imagining that she too had once been young and beautiful. Its patient, unsentimental picture of time passing through ordinary lives is considered his masterpiece. Compare George Eliot's [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en).

about: In 1888 an English nobleman, John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, and his pregnant wife are put ashore by mutineers on the coast of West Africa. They build a cabin, their son is born, and after both parents die the baby is adopted by Kala, a female ape who has lost her own child. Raised among the apes, Tarzan grows stronger and cleverer than any of them, teaches himself to read from the picture books in his dead father's cabin, and one day meets Jane Porter, the first white woman he has ever seen.
context: Edgar Rice Burroughs (1875–1950), an American who had failed at many jobs before he began writing for the pulp magazines, published the story in 1912, and Tarzan became one of the most famous characters in the world, with more than twenty sequels and countless films. Its picture of Africa and Africans reflects the racial prejudices of its time. Read also his [A Princess of Mars](/book/432?lang=en).

about: John Carter, a Confederate veteran prospecting for gold in Arizona after the Civil War, takes refuge in a cave from attacking Apaches and finds himself mysteriously carried to Mars, which its people call Barsoom. Thanks to the planet's weaker gravity he has enormous strength and can leap great distances. Captured by the fierce, green, four-armed Tharks, he earns their respect, befriends the warrior Tars Tarkas and falls in love with their captive, Dejah Thoris, princess of the red Martian city of Helium.
context: Published as a magazine serial in 1912 and as a book in 1917, this was Edgar Rice Burroughs's first novel and the start of a long series of Barsoom adventures that inspired science-fiction writers, scientists and filmmakers for a century. It is pure pulp adventure, written at great speed. Read also [Tarzan of the Apes](/book/445?lang=en).

about: In 1871, in the remote canyon country of southern Utah, Jane Withersteen, a wealthy young Mormon woman who owns a ranch, a precious spring and many fine horses, refuses to marry Elder Tull, and the church leaders begin to ruin her, driving off her riders and stealing her cattle. She is defended by a young Gentile rider, Bern Venters, and then by the feared gunman Lassiter, dressed in black, who has come to find the grave of his sister and the man who wronged her.
context: Zane Grey (1872–1939), a dentist from Ohio who became the most successful writer of westerns, published the novel in 1912, and it remains his best-known work and one of the most influential westerns ever written. Its hostile picture of the Mormon church leaders caused controversy. Compare the more realistic [The Virginian](/book/1526?lang=en).

about: An Easterner travels to Wyoming in the 1870s and meets the Virginian, a tall, quiet, humorous cowboy whose real name we never learn. Over the following years the Virginian becomes foreman of a large ranch, courts Molly Stark Wood, a spirited schoolteacher from Vermont, faces cattle rustlers, among them his old friend Steve, and finally the villain Trampas, whom he once answered with the famous words: 'When you call me that, smile!'
context: Owen Wister (1860–1938), a Philadelphia lawyer who spent his summers in Wyoming, published the novel in 1902, and it established the western as a popular genre, with its code of honour and its showdown in the street. He dedicated it to his friend Theodore Roosevelt. Compare [Riders of the Purple Sage](/book/1528?lang=en).

about: McTeague is a huge, slow, good-natured dentist without a diploma, practising on Polk Street in San Francisco. His friend Marcus Schouler introduces him to his cousin Trina, and McTeague marries her just after she wins five thousand dollars in a lottery. Jealous of the money, Marcus reports McTeague for practising without a licence, and as the couple sinks into poverty, Trina's love of money becomes a miser's obsession and McTeague's gentleness turns to brutality, leading to violence and a final chase into Death Valley.
context: Frank Norris (1870–1902) published the novel in 1899, and it is one of the major works of American naturalism, showing characters driven by heredity, environment and greed. Erich von Stroheim filmed it in 1924 as Greed, a legendary film that was originally many hours long. Compare [Sister Carrie](/book/546?lang=en).

about: Maggie Johnson grows up in the Bowery, the poorest slum of New York, with a drunken, violent mother, a father who soon dies, and a brother, Jimmie, who becomes a tough truck driver. Despite everything, 'the girl, Maggie, blossomed in a mud puddle'. She works in a collar factory and falls for Jimmie's flashy friend Pete, a bartender, who seems to promise a better world, and when he abandons her, her family and neighbours turn on her.
context: Stephen Crane was only twenty-one when he had this short novel printed at his own expense in 1893, under the pen name Johnston Smith, because publishers thought it too shocking. It sold almost no copies at first, but it is now seen as a pioneering work of American realism. Read Crane's [The Red Badge of Courage](/book/442?lang=en).

about: In a Midwestern town of the late nineteenth century, the Ambersons are the richest and grandest family, with a mansion, a ballroom and a name everyone respects. George Amberson Minafer, the spoiled only grandson, grows up so arrogant that the whole town longs to see him get his 'comeuppance'. As the town turns into a smoky industrial city and the automobile arrives, built by the family's old friend Eugene Morgan, who once loved George's mother, the Ambersons' wealth and importance quietly drain away.
context: Booth Tarkington (1869–1946), from Indianapolis, won the Pulitzer Prize for the novel, published in 1918, and won it again for [Alice Adams](/book/1241?lang=en), one of only a few writers to win the fiction prize twice. Orson Welles filmed it in 1942. It is a moving picture of how progress sweeps away an old world.

about: Thea Kronborg, the daughter of a Swedish Methodist minister in the little desert town of Moonstone, Colorado, has a gift for music that sets her apart. Helped by a doctor, a railway man and a Mexican neighbour who believe in her, she goes to study piano in Chicago, where a teacher discovers that her real gift is her voice. A summer among the ancient cliff dwellings of Arizona awakens her as an artist, and the novel follows her long struggle to become a great opera singer.
context: Willa Cather published the novel in 1915, inspired partly by the Swedish-American soprano Olive Fremstad and partly by her own escape from the prairie to become an artist. The title comes from a painting by Jules Breton of a peasant girl stopping in a field to listen to a lark. Read also [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en) and [O Pioneers!](/book/404?lang=en).

about: In the small town of Winesburg, Ohio, around 1900, young George Willard, a reporter on the local newspaper, listens as one lonely townsperson after another confides in him. Each of these 'grotesques', as an old writer in the opening piece calls them, has seized on a single truth and been twisted by it: a former teacher whose hands frighten him, a doctor who writes thoughts on scraps of paper, a minister who watches a woman through a church window, a woman who runs naked into the rain. In the end George leaves to begin his own life.
context: Sherwood Anderson (1876–1941), who had walked away from a business career to write, published this cycle of linked stories in 1919. Its plain style and its sympathy for inner lives that never find words influenced Hemingway, Faulkner and Steinbeck. Compare the small-town voices of [Spoon River Anthology](/book/1509?lang=en).

about: On a hill above the small Illinois town of Spoon River lie its dead, and in more than two hundred short free-verse poems each of them speaks a kind of epitaph, telling the truth about the life they lived: the respectable banker who cheated, the wife who hated her husband, the town drunkard, the honest judge, the girl who died young, and lovers whose secrets the town never knew. As their voices answer and contradict one another, the hidden history of the whole town emerges.
context: Edgar Lee Masters (1868–1950), a Chicago lawyer who had been a law partner of Clarence Darrow, published the poems in 1915, basing many on people he had known in the Illinois towns of Lewistown and Petersburg. The book was a sensation and one of the best-selling volumes of American poetry. Compare the prose of [Winesburg, Ohio](/book/718?lang=en).

about: Robert Frost's second book is a collection of dramatic poems and dialogues set among the farms of rural New England: two neighbours mending a stone wall in spring, one insisting that 'good fences make good neighbors'; a farmer and his wife talking over the return of an old hired man who has come home to die; a mother who cannot forgive her husband for the calm with which he dug their child's grave; and an apple-picker who, at the end of the harvest, feels sleep coming on.
context: Frost (1874–1963) published the book in London in 1914, while he and his family were living in England, and its plain speech and dramatic power made him famous on both sides of the Atlantic. He later won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry four times. Read also his first book, [A Boy's Will](/book/3147?lang=en).

about: In the rhythm of a drumbeat, this long poem tells the life of Hiawatha, a hero of the Ojibwe by the shores of Gitche Gumee, the 'shining Big-Sea-Water' of Lake Superior: his childhood with his grandmother Nokomis, who teaches him the names of the birds and animals; his fight with his father, the West Wind; his love for Minnehaha, 'Laughing Water', of the Dakota people; the famine that takes her; and his departure as the white men arrive.
context: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882), the most popular American poet of his time, published the poem in 1855, drawing on Native American legends collected by the ethnologist Henry Rowe Schoolcraft and borrowing its metre from the Finnish epic Kalevala. It was an enormous success, though it mixes the traditions of different peoples, and the real Hiawatha was an Iroquois leader. Read also his [Evangeline](/book/2229?lang=en).

about: In twelve linked narrative poems, Alfred Tennyson retells the legend of King Arthur from his coming to his passing: the founding of the Round Table at Camelot, the love of Lancelot and Queen Guinevere, the enchantress Vivien who traps Merlin, the quest for the Holy Grail, the stories of Gareth and Lynette, Geraint and Enid, and Lancelot and Elaine, and the last battle in the west, as the order Arthur built collapses through betrayal.
context: Tennyson (1809–1892), Poet Laureate for more than forty years, published the Idylls between 1859 and 1885, drawing chiefly on Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. Victorian readers saw in Arthur an ideal of duty and in the fall of Camelot a warning about their own society. Compare the medieval [Canterbury Tales](/book/298?lang=en).

about: 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.' In forty-four sonnets, Elizabeth Barrett tells the story of her courtship by the poet Robert Browning: her disbelief that she, an invalid nearing forty who rarely left her room, could be loved; her fear of becoming a burden to him; and her slow, joyful surrender to a love she compares to a new life.
context: The sonnets were written during the courtship, which ended in 1846 with a secret marriage and flight to Italy, away from her tyrannical father. She showed them to her husband only later, and they were published in 1850 under a title meant to disguise them as translations; Browning's pet name for her was 'my little Portuguese'. Read also Robert Browning's [The Pied Piper of Hamelin](/book/16401?lang=en).

about: After telling the Fall of humanity in [Paradise Lost](/book/297?lang=en), John Milton turned to its answer. In four books of blank verse he follows Jesus into the wilderness after his baptism, where Satan tempts him: with bread to end his hunger, with a banquet, with wealth and kingdoms, with the empires of Parthia and Rome, with the learning of Athens, and finally on the pinnacle of the Temple. Jesus refuses each one, and in his calm obedience the poet sees humanity's recovery of paradise.
context: Milton (1608–1674), by then blind, published the poem in 1671 together with his drama Samson Agonistes. Quieter and more philosophical than its great predecessor, it is the work of a poet who had seen the collapse of the revolution he served. See [Milton's life](/author/milton?lang=en).

about: Faustus, a brilliant German scholar who has mastered every branch of learning and found them all empty, turns to magic and conjures the devil Mephistopheles. He signs a contract in his own blood: for twenty-four years of power, knowledge and pleasure, with Mephistopheles as his servant, he will give his soul to Lucifer. Faustus spends his powers on pranks against the Pope, shows for an emperor and a vision of Helen of Troy, 'the face that launched a thousand ships', as the hour of payment draws near.
context: Christopher Marlowe (1564–1593), Shakespeare's great contemporary, who was killed in a tavern brawl at twenty-nine, wrote the play around 1590, and it survives in two versions, of 1604 and 1616; this is the 1604 text. Faustus's final speech, as he waits for midnight, is one of the most powerful in English drama. Compare [Goethe's Faust](/book/165?lang=en).

about: In Venice, the rich and childless Volpone, 'the Fox', pretends to be dying so that greedy men will compete to become his heir by bringing him ever richer gifts. With his clever servant Mosca, 'the Fly', he fools a lawyer named Voltore, an old miser named Corbaccio, who disinherits his own son, and a merchant named Corvino, who is even willing to offer his young wife. But Mosca has plans of his own, and the trickery spirals out of control.
context: Ben Jonson (1572–1637), Shakespeare's friend and rival, wrote the comedy in 1605 or 1606, in five weeks, he boasted. Its characters are named after animals, as in a beast fable: Voltore is the vulture, Corbaccio the raven, Corvino the crow. It remains one of the sharpest satires of greed in English. Compare [The Merchant of Venice](/book/8?lang=en).

about: In fashionable London, Lady Sneerwell and her circle of gossips meet to destroy reputations for fun. Among their targets are two brothers: Joseph Surface, admired by everyone as a man of fine moral sentiments but really a hypocrite, and his younger brother Charles, a cheerful spendthrift with a good heart. Their rich uncle, Sir Oliver, returns from India and tests them both in disguise, while old Sir Peter Teazle quarrels with his young, country-bred wife, who is being drawn into the scandal.
context: Richard Brinsley Sheridan (1751–1816), an Irish playwright who also ran the Drury Lane Theatre and sat in Parliament, wrote the comedy in 1777. Its 'screen scene', in which hidden characters are uncovered one by one in Joseph's library, is one of the most famous moments in English comedy. Read also his [The Rivals](/book/22035?lang=en).

about: Young Charles Marlow is painfully shy with well-bred ladies but bold with barmaids and servants. Sent to meet Kate Hardcastle, the girl his father hopes he will marry, he is tricked by her mischievous half-brother Tony Lumpkin into believing that the Hardcastles' country house is an inn, and he treats her father like an innkeeper. When Kate realises this she 'stoops to conquer', pretending to be a barmaid to win him, in one long night of mistakes.
context: Oliver Goldsmith wrote the comedy in 1773 as a reply to the sentimental comedies then in fashion, and it has been performed ever since. He is said to have based the central mistake on an adventure of his own youth, when he was directed to a private house as if it were an inn. Read also his [The Vicar of Wakefield](/book/2806?lang=en).

about: Dr Thomas Stockmann, the medical officer of a small Norwegian spa town, discovers that the waters of the new baths, on which the town's prosperity depends, are poisoned by waste from tanneries. Expecting to be thanked, he plans to publish his findings. But his brother, the mayor, warns that the repairs would ruin the town; the liberal newspaper and the property owners turn against him; and at a public meeting the crowd declares him an enemy of the people.
context: Henrik Ibsen wrote the play in 1882, partly as an angry reply to the attacks on his earlier play [Ghosts](/book/340?lang=en). Its closing line, that the strongest man in the world is the one who stands most alone, and its questions about truth, majority opinion and public health have kept it constantly relevant. See [Ibsen's life](/author/ibsen?lang=en).

about: Orgon, a wealthy Parisian, has fallen completely under the spell of Tartuffe, a penniless man who poses as a saint. He takes him into his house, praises his piety, promises him his daughter Mariane, who loves another man, and even signs his property over to him, while his family and their outspoken maid Dorine try in vain to open his eyes. Only when Orgon hides under a table and watches Tartuffe try to seduce his wife Elmire does he see the truth, and by then it may be too late.
context: Molière (1622–1673), the greatest French writer of comedy, first staged the play in 1664, and it was banned for five years after protests from powerful religious figures. Its title has become a word, in French and English, for a hypocrite. Compare the hypocrite Joseph Surface in [The School for Scandal](/book/2126?lang=en).

about: In 1885, during the war between Serbia and Bulgaria, a Swiss mercenary fighting for the Serbs escapes after a battle by climbing into the bedroom of Raina Petkoff, a young Bulgarian woman engaged to Sergius, the dashing hero of the cavalry charge that has just won the day. The fugitive, Captain Bluntschli, carries chocolates instead of bullets in his cartridge box, and his cheerful practicality punctures all Raina's romantic ideas about war and love.
context: Bernard Shaw's comedy was first performed in 1894, and its title comes from the opening of Virgil's [Aeneid](/book/541?lang=en), 'Arms and the man I sing'. Its mockery of military glory made it one of his first successes, and it was later turned into the operetta The Chocolate Soldier. Read also [Pygmalion](/book/3914?lang=en).

about: John Tanner, a wealthy revolutionary thinker who has written a 'Revolutionist's Handbook', finds himself made guardian of Ann Whitefield, a charming, determined young woman who has decided to marry him, though he is the last to realise it. When he does, he flees across Europe in a motor car with his chauffeur, and in the Spanish mountains he is captured by brigands; in the famous third-act dream, 'Don Juan in Hell', he becomes Don Juan, debating the Devil about the purpose of life.
context: Bernard Shaw wrote the play in 1903 as his own version of the Don Juan legend turned upside down: here the woman is the pursuer, driven by what Shaw called the Life Force. It is full of brilliant arguments, and the dream scene is often performed on its own. Read also [Arms and the Man](/book/3712?lang=en) and [Pygmalion](/book/3914?lang=en).

about: In France during the Hundred Years' War, a peasant girl from Domrémy who hears the voices of saints persuades a doubtful squire to give her a horse and armour, convinces the weak Dauphin Charles to let her lead his army, raises the siege of Orléans and sees him crowned at Reims. Then, captured by the Burgundians and sold to the English, she is tried for heresy by a church court in Rouen and burned at the stake in 1431. In an epilogue twenty-five years later, her spirit visits those who knew her.
context: Bernard Shaw wrote the play in 1923, three years after the Catholic Church declared Joan a saint, and soon afterwards he received the Nobel Prize for 1925. Shaw shows her judges not as villains but as sincere men defending order against an individual conscience, which makes the tragedy deeper. The play entered the public domain in the United States in 2020. See also [Pygmalion](/book/3914?lang=en).

about: One evening a frightened young stranger, Christy Mahon, stumbles into a remote pub on the wild coast of County Mayo and confesses that he has killed his father with a blow of a spade. Instead of handing him over, the villagers admire him as a hero, the publican's spirited daughter Pegeen Mike falls in love with him, and the Widow Quin competes for him, until his father, bandaged but very much alive, walks in at the door.
context: John Millington Synge (1871–1909) wrote the comedy in the rich, poetic English spoken in the west of Ireland, which he had studied on the Aran Islands. When it opened at Dublin's Abbey Theatre in 1907, riots broke out among nationalists who felt it insulted the Irish people. Read also his short tragedy [Riders to the Sea](/book/1254?lang=en).

about: This volume contains Sophocles' three Theban plays. In Oedipus the King, the ruler of Thebes sets out to find the murderer whose crime has brought plague on his city, and step by step discovers that he himself killed his father and married his mother, as an oracle foretold. In Oedipus at Colonus, the blind old exile, led by his daughter Antigone, finds a place to die near Athens. In Antigone, his daughter defies King Creon to bury her brother, choosing the law of the gods over the law of the state.
context: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC) wrote more than a hundred plays for the festivals of Athens, of which only seven survive complete. Aristotle, in his [Poetics](/book/2169?lang=en), treated Oedipus the King as the model of tragedy, and Freud took its name for his famous complex. Read also Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en).

about: In Corinth, Medea, a princess and sorceress from distant Colchis who betrayed her own family to help Jason win the Golden Fleece, learns that Jason is abandoning her to marry the daughter of King Creon, and that she and her two sons are to be banished. Humiliated and alone in a foreign land, she plans a terrible revenge on Jason, his new bride and the king, one that will destroy what she herself loves most.
context: Euripides (about 480–406 BC), the most modern of the Greek tragedians, first staged the play in Athens in 431 BC, where it won only third prize. Medea's speeches about the lot of women and of foreigners still sound startlingly fresh, and her story has inspired operas, films and countless new versions. Compare the tragedies of [Sophocles](/book/409?lang=en).

about: This is the Oresteia, the only complete trilogy of Greek tragedies to survive. In Agamemnon, the king returns from the Trojan War with the prophetess Cassandra and is murdered by his wife Clytemnestra, who has never forgiven him for sacrificing their daughter Iphigenia. In The Libation Bearers, their son Orestes returns from exile to avenge his father by killing his mother. In the last play, pursued by the Furies, Orestes is tried before a court of Athenians with the goddess Athena presiding, and the cycle of revenge gives way to justice.
context: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), who had fought the Persians at Marathon, won first prize with the trilogy in 458 BC. Its story of a law court replacing the blood feud is one of the founding myths of Western law. Read also Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en), the story of the war Agamemnon led.

about: Athens and Sparta have been at war for twenty years, and the Athenian woman Lysistrata has had enough. She gathers women from all over Greece, including the sturdy Spartan Lampito, and persuades them to refuse their husbands until the men make peace, while the older women seize the Acropolis and the treasury that pays for the war. As the men grow more desperate and ridiculous, the women hold firm.
context: Aristophanes (about 446–386 BC), the great comic poet of Athens, staged the play in 411 BC, during the Peloponnesian War described by [Thucydides](/book/7136?lang=en). Bawdy and outrageous, it is also a serious plea for peace, and it has been performed in protest against many modern wars; Spike Lee's film Chi-Raq (2015) moves its story to Chicago.

about: In 401 BC, ten thousand Greek mercenaries march deep into the Persian Empire to help the prince Cyrus the Younger seize the throne from his brother, King Artaxerxes. Cyrus is killed at the battle of Cunaxa, near Babylon in today's Iraq, and soon afterwards the Greek generals are lured to a meeting and murdered. Leaderless and surrounded, the soldiers elect new commanders, among them the young Athenian Xenophon, and fight their way north through the mountains of Kurdistan and Armenia, through snow and hostile tribes, until they see the Black Sea and cry out, 'The sea! The sea!'
context: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), a pupil of Socrates, wrote this account of the march, in which he played a leading part, years later. It is one of the great adventure stories of the ancient world, and Alexander the Great is said to have used it as a guide to the Persian Empire. Compare [Thucydides](/book/7136?lang=en).

about: In six books of Latin verse, the Roman poet Lucretius sets out the philosophy of Epicurus: everything in the universe, including the human soul, is made of tiny, indivisible atoms moving through empty space; the world was not made by the gods and is not governed by them; and death is simply the end of sensation, so there is nothing in it to fear. He uses this vision to explain thunder, magnets, disease and the origins of life and civilisation, and ends with a terrible description of the plague of Athens.
context: Almost nothing is known of Lucretius (about 99–55 BC). His poem was nearly lost until an Italian book hunter, Poggio Bracciolini, found a manuscript in a German monastery in 1417, and its rediscovery influenced the thinkers of the Renaissance and the scientific revolution. Compare the Stoic [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en) of Marcus Aurelius.

about: 'Some things are within our power, while others are not.' So begins this short handbook of Stoic philosophy, which teaches that our opinions, desires and actions are up to us, while our bodies, property, reputation and the actions of others are not, and that unhappiness comes from confusing the two. In brief chapters it gives practical advice for keeping calm through loss, insult and misfortune: people are disturbed not by things, but by the views they take of things.
context: Epictetus (about 50–135) was born a slave in Asia Minor, was freed and taught philosophy in Greece; he wrote nothing himself, and the Enchiridion, 'handbook', is a summary of his teaching made by his student Arrian. It deeply influenced Marcus Aurelius, whose [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en) quote Epictetus, and it is widely read today by people interested in Stoicism and in modern cognitive therapy.

about: In this short treatise, the first work of literary theory in the Western world, Aristotle asks what makes a good tragedy. He defines it as the imitation of a serious action that, through pity and fear, brings about a catharsis of those emotions; ranks its six elements, with plot first and character second; and explains the reversal of fortune, the moment of recognition and the tragic hero's error, hamartia, with frequent examples from Sophocles' Oedipus the King.
context: Probably based on Aristotle's lecture notes from the fourth century BC, the Poetics survives incomplete, and a second book on comedy is thought to be lost. It reached medieval Europe partly through Arabic translations and the commentary of Ibn Rushd, and it shaped the theory of drama for two thousand years. Read [Sophocles' plays](/book/409?lang=en), and see [Aristotle's life](/author/aristotle?lang=en).

about: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, as two great armies of kinsmen face each other, the warrior prince Arjuna loses heart at the thought of killing his own teachers and relatives, and lays down his bow. His charioteer, the god Krishna, answers him in a long dialogue about duty, the immortality of the soul, action without attachment to its rewards, devotion and the nature of the divine, and finally reveals himself in an overwhelming vision of his universal form.
context: The Bhagavad Gita, a section of the vast Indian epic the Mahabharata, probably took shape in the last centuries BC, and it is one of the most important scriptures of Hinduism. This is the 1885 verse translation by Sir Edwin Arnold (1832–1904), in which Mahatma Gandhi first read it as a student in London. Compare the Buddhist [Dhammapada](/book/2208?lang=en).

about: The Dhammapada, 'the path of the teaching', is a collection of 423 short verses attributed to the Buddha, arranged in twenty-six chapters on themes such as the mind, vigilance, anger, the fool and the wise, happiness and the path to freedom from suffering. It opens with the famous lines: 'All that we are is the result of what we have thought.' Its sayings are simple, direct and practical, meant to be memorised and lived.
context: Part of the Pali Canon of Theravada Buddhism, the verses were probably gathered in the third century BC. This translation by F. Max Müller (1823–1900), the German-born Oxford scholar who edited the great series Sacred Books of the East, was one of the first to bring the text to Western readers. Compare [The Song Celestial](/book/2540?lang=en) and [Tagore's Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: Writing in English for Western readers, Okakura Kakuzō uses the simple ritual of tea as a door into Japanese culture. He traces tea from a medicine in ancient China to its place in Zen Buddhism and Taoism, describes the tea-room, a small, bare hut for a few guests, and explains the ideals behind the tea ceremony: simplicity, the beauty of imperfect and incomplete things, respect for nature in the arrangement of flowers, and the art of living in the present.
context: Okakura (1863–1913), a Japanese art scholar who worked at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, published the book in New York in 1906, partly to answer Western misunderstandings of Asia.
