'Teaism', he wrote, 'is a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence.' Compare [Bushido](/book/10916?lang=en) and the [Tao Teh King](/book/531?lang=en).

about: What did the samurai believe? Nitobe Inazō explains the unwritten moral code of Japan's warrior class, which he calls bushido, 'the way of the warrior': rectitude, courage, benevolence, politeness, sincerity, honour, loyalty and self-control. He traces its roots in Buddhism, Shinto and Confucianism, describes the education of a samurai, the meaning of the sword and the ritual of seppuku, and compares these ideals with European chivalry.
context: Nitobe (1862–1933), a Japanese agricultural scientist, educator and Christian, wrote the book in English, published in 1900, after a Belgian scholar asked him how Japanese children were taught morals without religious education in schools. It became one of the most influential books shaping Western ideas of Japan, and Nitobe later served as an under-secretary-general of the League of Nations; his portrait appeared on the Japanese 5,000-yen note.

about: Kwaidan, 'strange tales', is a collection of Japanese ghost stories and legends retold in English: the blind musician Hoichi, whose body is covered with sacred texts to protect him from ghosts, except his ears; the Snow Woman, who spares a young woodcutter on condition that he never speak of her; the faceless Mujina met on a lonely road at night; and others, followed by short studies of butterflies, mosquitoes and ants.
context: Lafcadio Hearn (1850–1904), born on the Greek island of Lefkada to an Irish father and a Greek mother, settled in Japan in 1890, married a Japanese woman, Koizumi Setsu, who told him many of these tales, took the name Koizumi Yakumo, and became one of the first Western writers to interpret Japan for the world. Kwaidan appeared in 1904, the year of his death, and Masaki Kobayashi's 1964 film adapted several of its stories. Compare [The Book of Tea](/book/1051?lang=en).

about: On an uninhabited island near the equator, a baby boy, Hayy ibn Yaqzan, 'Alive, son of Awake', is raised by a gazelle. When she dies he opens her body to find what has left it, and from that moment he reasons his way alone through natural science and philosophy, to the nature of life, the heavens and the soul, and finally to the existence of a single Creator, whom he comes to know through contemplation. Only then does he meet another human being, Absal, who has come from a neighbouring island where religion is practised through laws and symbols.
context: Ibn Tufayl (about 1105–1185), a physician and philosopher at the Almohad court in Marrakesh who introduced Ibn Rushd to the caliph, wrote this philosophical tale in Arabic in the twelfth century. Translated into Latin in 1671 and into English soon after, it fascinated European thinkers of the Enlightenment and has been compared to [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en). This is Simon Ockley's English translation of 1708.

about: What makes an action morally right? In this short book Kant argues that it is not the consequences, nor our feelings, but the principle on which we act. A good will is the only thing good without qualification, and the supreme law of morality is the categorical imperative: act only on a rule that you could will to become a universal law, and treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. He tests it on examples such as a man who borrows money with a promise he knows he cannot keep.
context: Published in 1785 as the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, and translated here by T. K. Abbott as Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, it is the most accessible of Immanuel Kant's major works and remains central to every debate about human dignity and rights. Read also his [Perpetual Peace](/book/157?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/kant?lang=en).

about: Where do our ideas of good and evil come from? In three essays, Friedrich Nietzsche argues that they have a history. Noble, powerful people once called themselves 'good' and the weak 'bad'; then, he claims, the resentful weak overturned these values in a 'slave revolt in morality', calling meekness good and strength evil. He goes on to trace guilt and bad conscience to ancient relations of debt and cruelty, and asks why ideals of self-denial have had such power over human beings.
context: Published in 1887 as a sequel to [Beyond Good and Evil](/book/92?lang=en), it is the most systematic of Nietzsche's books and one of the most influential works of modern philosophy, though its ideas were later grossly distorted. This translation comes from the first complete English edition of his works, edited by Oscar Levy. See [Nietzsche's life](/author/nietzsche?lang=en).

about: Why do we dream, and what do dreams mean? In this short book, written for general readers, Sigmund Freud explains his theory that every dream is the disguised fulfilment of a wish, often a forbidden or forgotten one. He shows how the mind turns hidden thoughts into strange images through condensation, displacement and symbols, and why we forget our dreams on waking, using examples from his own dreams and those of his patients.
context: This is the English translation, published in 1920, of On Dreams (1901), the summary Freud wrote of his great [Interpretation of Dreams](/book/159?lang=en), and it is the easiest way into his ideas. Freud (1856–1939), the Viennese neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, fled from the Nazis to London in 1938. See [his life](/author/freud?lang=en).

about: 'Standing on the bare ground, my head bathed by the blithe air and uplifted into infinite space, all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eyeball.' In this short book Ralph Waldo Emerson argues that every person can have an original relation to the universe, not through books or churches but through direct experience of nature, which serves us as commodity, beauty, language and discipline, and leads us towards the spirit that lives in all things.
context: Published anonymously in 1836, Nature became the founding text of Transcendentalism, the movement of New England thinkers that included Henry David Thoreau. Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister, became the most influential American thinker of his age. Read his [Essays](/book/286?lang=en) and Thoreau's [Walden](/book/287?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/emerson?lang=en).

about: Thomas Carlyle tells the story of the French Revolution not as a dry history but as a vast drama in the present tense, from the death of Louis XV in 1774 through the storming of the Bastille, the flight of the king to Varennes, the September Massacres and the Terror, to the 'whiff of grapeshot' with which the young Napoleon Bonaparte put down a rising in Paris in 1795. Kings, crowds, orators and victims all pass before the reader in vivid scenes.
context: Carlyle (1795–1881), a Scottish writer, published the book in 1837 after a disaster: the only manuscript of the first volume was accidentally burned by a maid while on loan to John Stuart Mill, and he had to write it again from memory. Charles Dickens drew on it for [A Tale of Two Cities](/book/30?lang=en).

about: In the spring of 1846, the young Bostonian Francis Parkman, fresh from Harvard, set out from St Louis with his cousin Quincy Adams Shaw to see the American West before it vanished. They followed the emigrant trail across the plains to Fort Laramie, met settlers bound for Oregon, hunted buffalo and spent weeks living with a band of Oglala Sioux, whose daily life, hunts and preparations for war Parkman described in detail.
context: Published as a book in 1849, it is one of the classic accounts of the frontier, by a man who went on to become one of America's great historians, though his view of Native Americans reflects the prejudices of his day. Parkman (1823–1893) suffered from poor health and weak eyesight for the rest of his life. Compare Mark Twain's [Roughing It](/book/3302?lang=en).

about: Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing to an illness when she was nineteen months old and grew up a wild, frustrated child in Alabama, unable to communicate. Then, when she was almost seven, a young teacher, Anne Sullivan, arrived and began spelling words into her hand. One day at the water pump Helen suddenly understood that the letters w-a-t-e-r meant the cool something flowing over her hand, and a whole world opened. She tells how she learned to read, write and speak, and how she entered Radcliffe College.
context: Keller (1880–1968) wrote this autobiography while still a student at Radcliffe, and it was published in 1903 with her letters and an account of her education that includes Anne Sullivan's own reports. Keller became the first deaf-blind person to earn a university degree and a world-famous campaigner for the rights of disabled people. Compare [Up from Slavery](/book/2529?lang=en).

about: Benvenuto Cellini, a Florentine goldsmith and sculptor, tells the story of his life with tremendous energy and no modesty at all. He fights in the defence of Rome during the sack of 1527 and claims to have shot the Constable of Bourbon, works for popes, dukes and the King of France, kills several men in quarrels and is pardoned, escapes from the prison of Castel Sant'Angelo on a rope of bed sheets, and describes how he cast his great bronze Perseus, throwing his own pewter plates into the furnace when the metal would not flow.
context: Cellini (1500–1571) began dictating the book to a young assistant in 1558, and it circulated in manuscript until it was printed in 1728. Boastful, violent and unreliable, it is also one of the most vivid portraits of the Italian Renaissance, and Goethe translated it into German. This is the classic English translation by John Addington Symonds.

about: In 1793, at the height of the French Revolution, royalist peasants rise in rebellion in the Vendée and Brittany, led by the old Marquis de Lantenac, a ruthless aristocratic general. Against him the Republic sends his own great-nephew, Gauvain, a generous young commander, with a political commissioner at his side: Cimourdain, a former priest of iron principles who was once Gauvain's tutor and loves him like a son. The war is merciless on both sides, and at a besieged castle an act of mercy by Lantenac forces each man to choose between his cause and his conscience.
context: Ninety-Three, published in 1874, was Victor Hugo's last novel. It includes a famous scene in Paris with the revolutionary leaders Robespierre, Danton and Marat, and asks whether a revolution can be both just and humane. This translation is by Aline Delano. Read Hugo's [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en) and [Notre-Dame de Paris](/book/2754?lang=en).

about: On a freezing night in 1690, on the coast of England, a band of child-traffickers sails away and abandons a boy of about ten, Gwynplaine, whose face was cut into a permanent grin when he was a baby. Wandering through the snow, he rescues a blind baby girl from her dead mother's arms, and both are taken in by Ursus, a travelling philosopher and showman, and his tame wolf, Homo. Years later Gwynplaine is a famous clown, in love with the blind Dea, when a message from the sea reveals the secret of his birth and throws him into the world of the House of Lords.
context: Victor Hugo published the novel in 1869, while in exile on Guernsey, as an attack on the cruelty of aristocratic privilege. Its 1928 silent film inspired the look of the Joker in the Batman comics. Read also [Ninety-Three](/book/44577?lang=en) and [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en).

about: The novel opens in 1775 at the Maypole Inn near London, on the anniversary of a murder committed twenty-two years before. Barnaby Rudge, a gentle, simple-minded young man who wanders the countryside with his talking raven Grip, lives with his widowed mother, who hides a terrible secret about his father. Five years later, when the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots break out in London, Barnaby is swept into the mob that burns houses, chapels and Newgate Prison, while two romances, Joe Willet's and Dolly Varden's and Edward Chester's and Emma Haredale's, are torn apart by family hatreds.
context: Charles Dickens's first historical novel, published in 1841, gives a vivid and frightening picture of mob violence. Grip was based on Dickens's own pet raven, and Edgar Allan Poe, who reviewed the book, is thought to have been inspired by it to write [The Raven](/book/1321?lang=en). Dickens later wrote [A Tale of Two Cities](/book/30?lang=en); see [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: Young Martin Chuzzlewit, selfish and proud, quarrels with his rich grandfather and goes off to seek his fortune with his cheerful servant Mark Tapley, who is determined to stay jolly in the worst of circumstances. In America they are cheated into buying land in a swampy settlement called Eden, where Martin nearly dies and learns humility. Meanwhile in England the hypocritical architect Mr Pecksniff schemes for the grandfather's money, and Martin's cousin Jonas, a greedy brute, turns to murder.
context: Published in monthly parts in 1843 and 1844, the novel followed Dickens's disappointing first visit to America, and its satire of American boastfulness offended many readers there. It is famous for two of his greatest comic creations: Pecksniff, whose name became a word for a hypocrite, and the gin-loving nurse Mrs Gamp. Read [A Christmas Carol](/book/33?lang=en), written the same year, and see [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: In Yorkshire in 1811 and 1812, during the Napoleonic Wars, trade is ruined and new machines are taking the jobs of the cloth workers, who rise in the Luddite riots. Robert Moore, a determined mill owner of half-Belgian descent, brings in new machinery and faces an attack on his mill. Two very different young women love him: his quiet, sensitive cousin Caroline Helstone, who longs for useful work, and the bold, rich heiress Shirley Keeldar, who manages her own estate and speaks her mind like a man.
context: Charlotte Brontë published the novel in 1849, after [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en); she wrote it while her brother Branwell and her sisters Emily and Anne died one after another. Shirley was partly a portrait of Emily, and the book made Shirley, until then a man's name, popular for girls. Read also [Villette](/book/8744?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/cbronte?lang=en).

about: Mr Charles Pooter, a respectable, self-important City clerk, moves with his wife Carrie into a house in Holloway, north London, called The Laurels, and decides to keep a diary, for he fails to see why it should not be interesting just because he is not a 'Somebody'. He records his small triumphs and endless humiliations: rude tradesmen, the jokes of his friends Gowing and Cummings, his disastrous home improvements with red enamel paint, a ball at the Mansion House, and the antics of his fashionable son Lupin.
context: George Grossmith (1847–1912), a comic singer famous in Gilbert and Sullivan operas, wrote it with his brother Weedon, who drew the pictures; it first appeared in Punch and as a book in 1892. Gently mocking suburban snobbery, it remains one of the funniest books in English and gave the language the word 'Pooterish'. Compare [Three Men in a Boat](/book/613?lang=en).

about: Sir Willoughby Patterne, a handsome, rich young baronet admired by the whole county, believes himself the perfect English gentleman, but he is in fact a complete egoist who sees everyone around him only as a mirror of himself. Jilted once, he becomes engaged to Clara Middleton, a lively, intelligent young woman, who slowly realises with horror what marriage to him would mean and struggles to escape without scandal, helped by his quiet cousin, the scholar Vernon Whitford.
context: George Meredith (1828–1909) published this 'comedy in narrative' in 1879. Its witty, demanding style and its sympathy for a woman's right to choose her own life made it admired by many later writers, Virginia Woolf among them. Read Jane Austen's [Emma](/book/39?lang=en) for another clever comedy of courtship.

about: A young man looking for land to farm in a remote colony crosses an unexplored mountain range and discovers the hidden country of Erewhon, 'nowhere' spelled almost backwards. There everything is upside down: illness is punished as a crime, while crime is treated with sympathy as a sickness; the 'Musical Banks' issue a currency nobody really uses; the Colleges of Unreason teach 'hypothetics'; and all machines were destroyed centuries ago, for fear that they would evolve and enslave humanity.
context: Samuel Butler (1835–1902), who had been a sheep farmer in New Zealand, published the satire anonymously in 1872. Its 'Book of the Machines', which applies Darwin's theory of evolution to machines, is still quoted in debates about artificial intelligence. Read also Butler's novel [The Way of All Flesh](/book/2274?lang=en), and compare [Gulliver's Travels](/book/302?lang=en).

about: Through four generations of the Pontifex family, Samuel Butler shows how cruelty and hypocrisy are passed from parents to children in respectable Victorian homes. Ernest Pontifex is raised by his father Theobald, a clergyman who beats him into learning, and his self-deceiving mother, and is pushed into the Church himself. Naïve and unprepared for life, he goes from one disaster to another, including a spell in prison, before slowly learning to think for himself and break free, guided by his kindly godfather Overton, who tells the story.
context: Butler wrote the novel between 1873 and 1884, but it was so harsh a portrait of his own family that it was published only in 1903, after his death. Its attack on Victorian family life influenced Bernard Shaw and many writers of the twentieth century. Read Butler's satire [Erewhon](/book/2104?lang=en).

about: George Ponderevo, the son of a housekeeper on a great country estate, tells how his uncle Edward, a small-town chemist with big dreams, invents a patent medicine called Tono-Bungay, 'slightly injurious rubbish' sold through brilliant advertising. The tonic makes them enormously rich; the uncle becomes a famous financier, buys newspapers and builds a vast country house, while George turns to engineering and flying machines, until the whole empire of credit begins to collapse.
context: H. G. Wells published the novel in 1909 and called it the most finished novel he was ever likely to write. It is a sharp, comic satire of advertising, speculation and the decay of the old English social order. Read also Wells's [The History of Mr Polly](/book/7297?lang=en) and [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: Alfred Polly, a dreamy, shy shopkeeper of thirty-seven who loves books and invents comic words of his own, has been miserable for fifteen years in a small seaside town, with a failing shop, chronic indigestion and a discontented wife. One day he decides to end it all by setting fire to the shop and cutting his throat, but the fire turns into a heroic rescue, and instead of dying he simply walks away from his old life, to find happiness as a handyman at a riverside inn, where he must face its terrifying bully, Uncle Jim.
context: H. G. Wells published this comic novel in 1910, drawing on his own unhappy years as a draper's apprentice. It is a cheerful fable about the right to escape a wasted life, and it remains one of his most loved books. Read also [Tono-Bungay](/book/1005?lang=en) and [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: The last twelve Sherlock Holmes stories bring the great detective and Dr Watson some of their strangest cases: a Peruvian wife suspected of being a vampire, an illustrious client who wants to save a young woman from a seductive Austrian baron, a professor who behaves like a monkey after taking a mysterious serum, a woman found dead on a bridge with a note in her hand, and a veiled lodger whose face was mauled by a lion. Two of the stories are told by Holmes himself.
context: Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930) published the collection in 1927, three years before his death, ending a series that had run for forty years. Darker and more varied than the early stories, it is the last word on the most famous detective in fiction. Read [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) and [The Hound of the Baskervilles](/book/55?lang=en).

about: Three young American men, a sociologist, a doctor and a wealthy adventurer, hear rumours of a land without men hidden in the mountains of an unexplored region, and fly there in a biplane, each expecting something different: a paradise of women, a dull convent, or easy conquests. They find a peaceful, prosperous and highly organised society of women who have lived without men for two thousand years, bearing children without fathers and raising them in common, and who calmly study the three visitors as curiosities.
context: Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935), the American writer and feminist best known for [The Yellow Wallpaper](/book/2148?lang=en), serialised the novel in her own magazine, The Forerunner, in 1915, but it was published as a book only in 1979. Its gentle comedy turns the explorers' assumptions about women and men upside down. Compare [Looking Backward](/book/920?lang=en).

about: 'Patience, n. A minor form of despair, disguised as a virtue.' In alphabetical order, Ambrose Bierce redefines the words of the English language as a cynic sees them: 'Bore, n. A person who talks when you wish him to listen'; 'Politics, n. A strife of interests masquerading as a contest of principles'; 'Peace, n. In international affairs, a period of cheating between two periods of fighting.' Hundreds of short, savage entries mock politics, religion, marriage, money and human vanity.
context: Bierce (1842–about 1914), a Civil War veteran and San Francisco journalist known as 'Bitter Bierce', published the definitions in newspapers over many years and collected them in 1906 as The Cynic's Word Book, renamed in 1911. He disappeared in Mexico during its revolution and was never seen again. Read his story [An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge](/book/678?lang=en).

about: On Christmas Eve, Della Young has only one dollar and eighty-seven cents to buy a present for her husband Jim, a poorly paid clerk, in their shabby New York flat. The couple own just two treasures: Jim's gold watch, handed down from his father and grandfather, and Della's beautiful long hair. To buy Jim a chain worthy of his watch, Della has her hair cut off and sells it, and when Jim comes home he looks at her with a strange expression, because he too has made a sacrifice.
context: O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter (1862–1910), who began writing stories while in prison for embezzlement, published this tale in a New York newspaper in 1905, and it became the most famous of his hundreds of stories with their trademark twist endings. Its title recalls the wise men who brought gifts to the infant Jesus. Compare [A Christmas Carol](/book/33?lang=en).

about: Amory Blaine, a handsome, conceited young man from the Midwest raised by his eccentric, wealthy mother, goes to Princeton dreaming of becoming a great figure. Through his college years, the First World War and its aftermath, he falls in and out of love with a series of girls, among them the debutante Rosalind, who leaves him for a richer man, and drifts from ambition to disillusion, ending with the cry, 'I know myself, but that is all.'
context: F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) published his first novel in 1920, at twenty-three, and its picture of a new generation of restless, pleasure-seeking young Americans made him famous overnight; it also persuaded Zelda Sayre, on whom Rosalind was partly based, to marry him. Read his masterpiece, [The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en).

about: Anthony Patch, the idle grandson of a puritanical multimillionaire, lives in New York in elegant leisure, waiting to inherit his grandfather's fortune. He marries the beautiful, restless Gloria Gilbert, and the young couple devote themselves to parties, drinking and spending, while their money, their looks and their love slowly drain away. When the old man disinherits Anthony, they sink into a bitter legal fight over the will.
context: F. Scott Fitzgerald published this second novel in 1922, and its portrait of a glamorous couple destroying themselves drew on his own marriage to Zelda. It is a darker study of the Jazz Age than his first book. Read [This Side of Paradise](/book/1085?lang=en) and [The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en).

about: This slim book, printed in Paris in 1924 in an edition of only 170 copies, contains eighteen very short prose sketches, some only a paragraph long, written in a bare, exact style: six Greek cabinet ministers shot against a hospital wall at dawn, a bullfighter dying in the ring, refugees on a muddy road in a Greek retreat, soldiers shooting Germans as they climb a garden wall in the First World War, and a hanging in a Chicago jail.
context: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) was then an unknown young American journalist in Paris, and the book was edited by Ezra Pound for the small Three Mountains Press, with a portrait of the author by Henry Strater. In 1925 he placed these sketches between the stories of his first American collection, In Our Time. They are the laboratory of the style that later won him the Nobel Prize. Read [The Sun Also Rises](/book/61232?lang=en).

about: Born into slavery around 1797 in Ulster County, New York, in a Dutch-speaking household, the girl named Isabella was sold several times, beaten and separated from her children. In 1826 she walked away to freedom with her infant daughter, and later went to court to recover her young son, who had been illegally sold into slavery in Alabama, becoming one of the first Black women to win such a case against a white man. In 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth and began travelling as a preacher against slavery and for women's rights.
context: Sojourner Truth (about 1797–1883) could not read or write, and she dictated this story to her friend Olive Gilbert; it was published in 1850, and she sold copies at her meetings to support herself. Her speeches, above all the one remembered as 'Ain't I a Woman?', made her a legend. Read also [Frederick Douglass's Narrative](/book/403?lang=en) and [Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl](/book/10110?lang=en).

about: In a rough gold-mining camp in the California Sierra, the only woman, Cherokee Sal, dies giving birth to a baby boy, and the hundred hard-drinking, quarrelsome miners decide to raise the child themselves. They name him Thomas Luck and slowly transform their camp and themselves to make it fit for him. In 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat', a gambler, two disreputable women and a drunkard expelled from a mining town are trapped by a snowstorm in the mountains with an innocent young couple. The volume gathers these and many other tales, legends and parodies.
context: Bret Harte (1836–1902) published 'The Luck of Roaring Camp' in 1868 in the Overland Monthly, which he edited in San Francisco, and it made him one of the most famous writers in America, the creator of the colourful, sentimental Western tale. He was an early friend and later a rival of [Mark Twain](/author/twain?lang=en). Compare Twain's [Roughing It](/book/3302?lang=en).

about: Julian West, a wealthy young Bostonian, falls into a hypnotic sleep in his underground bedroom in 1887 and wakes in the year 2000. Boston has become a peaceful, beautiful city without poverty, crime, money or politics: the nation owns all industry, every citizen serves in an 'industrial army' from twenty-one to forty-five and receives an equal income on a credit card, goods are ordered from great central stores, and music is piped into homes by telephone. His host, Dr Leete, explains how it all came about.
context: Edward Bellamy (1850–1898) published the novel in 1888, and it was one of the best-selling American books of its century, inspiring hundreds of 'Nationalist' clubs devoted to its ideas. It is remembered today for predicting the credit card and broadcast music. Compare William Morris's reply, [News from Nowhere](/book/3383?lang=en).

about: Judah Ben-Hur, a young Jewish prince of Jerusalem, is falsely accused of trying to kill the Roman governor when a tile falls from his roof, and his boyhood friend Messala, now a proud Roman officer, has him sent as a slave to the galleys while his mother and sister vanish into prison. Saved during a sea battle, Judah is adopted by a Roman admiral, trains as a charioteer and returns to the East to defeat Messala in a great chariot race at Antioch, while his life crosses again and again with that of Jesus of Nazareth.
context: Lew Wallace (1827–1905), a Union general in the Civil War and later governor of New Mexico, published the novel in 1880, and it became the best-selling American novel of the nineteenth century after [Uncle Tom's Cabin](/book/522?lang=en). The 1959 film won eleven Oscars.

about: Henry Adams, great-grandson of one American president and grandson of another, tells his own life in the third person, as the story of an education that, he insists, never prepared him for the world he had to live in. He describes his Boston childhood, Harvard, his years in London as secretary to his father, the American minister, during the Civil War, his life as a historian and journalist in Washington, and his visit to the Paris Exposition of 1900, where he stood before the great electric dynamos and felt the force of a new age, which he compared to the power of the Virgin in the Middle Ages.
context: Adams (1838–1918) printed the book privately for friends in 1907; it was published only after his death, in 1918, and won the Pulitzer Prize in 1919. Its ironic, searching voice has made it one of the most admired American autobiographies. This is the edition of the Massachusetts Historical Society. Compare [The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin](/book/18052?lang=en).

about: In 1590, in the Austrian village of Eseldorf, 'Donkeytown', three boys meet a charming, handsome young stranger who calls himself Satan, a nephew of the fallen angel, and who can perform marvellous tricks: he makes tiny people out of clay and then crushes them without a thought. Through his eyes the boys see human cruelty, superstition and the 'moral sense' that, he argues, makes people worse than animals, and he shows them the future of those they love. This volume adds other stories by Mark Twain.
context: Twain worked on the story in several versions in his last, bitter years, after the deaths of his wife and two of his daughters, and never finished it; it was published in 1916, six years after his death, in a version put together by his literary executor Albert Bigelow Paine and the editor Frederick Duneka. Read [Pudd'nhead Wilson](/book/464?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: William Guest, a socialist in Victorian London, goes to bed after a heated political meeting and wakes up in a distant future, in an England transformed by revolution. Money, prisons, Parliament and great industrial cities have disappeared; London's factories have given way to gardens and villages, people work only at what they enjoy, things are made with craft and beauty, and men and women live as equals. He travels up the Thames with new friends to a haymaking festival, wondering whether he will be allowed to stay.
context: William Morris (1834–1896), the designer, poet and socialist, published the book in 1890 as a reply to Edward Bellamy's [Looking Backward](/book/920?lang=en), whose machine-run, centralised utopia he disliked. It is one of the most beautiful of all utopias, and the journey ends at Kelmscott Manor, Morris's own country house. Compare Thomas More's [Utopia](/book/2317?lang=en).

about: On a world called Mercury, a land of heroic kingdoms much like Homer's Greece or the Norse sagas, the noble lords of Demonland, Juss, Spitfire, Brandoch Daha and Goldry Bluszco, are challenged by King Gorice of Witchland, a sorcerer-king who demands their submission. When Goldry Bluszco is carried off by sorcery, Lord Juss leads a long and perilous quest over mountains and seas to rescue his brother, in a war of honour, magic and splendid battles.
context: E. R. Eddison (1882–1945), an English civil servant and translator of Icelandic sagas, published the novel in 1922, written in a rich, archaic English modelled on that of the sixteenth century. J. R. R. Tolkien read and admired it, and it is a founding work of heroic fantasy; its title, the serpent that eats its own tail, hints at its circular ending. Read also [Grettir's Saga](/book/650?lang=en).

about: The people of the little kingdom of Erl ask their lord to let them be ruled by a magic lord, so he sends his son Alveric beyond 'the fields we know' into Elfland, with a magic sword, to win the hand of Lirazel, the daughter of the King of Elfland. Alveric brings her home and they have a son, Orion, but Lirazel can never understand the ways of mortal men, and when her father sends a rune to call her back she drifts home to Elfland, and Alveric spends years wandering in search of a land that has moved away from him.
context: Lord Dunsany (1878–1957), an Anglo-Irish aristocrat, playwright and chess player, published the novel in 1924, and its dreamy, musical prose made it one of the most influential works of modern fantasy, admired by writers from Lovecraft to Neil Gaiman. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2020. Compare [The Worm Ouroboros](/book/61187?lang=en).

about: At a séance in London, a mysterious figure named Krag appears and invites a man called Maskull to travel with him to Tormance, a planet circling the double star Arcturus. Maskull wakes alone on Tormance, where he grows new sense organs that change how he sees and feels, and journeys across strange lands lit by two suns and coloured by two new primary colours, meeting beings who each embody a different philosophy of life and pleasure, as he searches for the truth behind Muspel, the source of all reality.
context: David Lindsay (1876–1945), a Scot who worked for years at Lloyd's in London before turning to writing, published the novel in 1920; it sold only a few hundred copies, but it later became a cult classic. C. S. Lewis called it a major influence on his own space trilogy, and critics count it among the strangest and most original novels of the century. Compare [The Worm Ouroboros](/book/61187?lang=en).

about: The idea Descartes summed up elsewhere as 'I think, therefore I am' is reached here by a famous path. He resolves to doubt everything that can possibly be doubted: his senses, which sometimes deceive him; whether he is awake or dreaming; even mathematics, since an evil demon might be deceiving him. One thing survives the doubt: while he doubts, he must exist as a thinking thing. From this foundation he argues for the existence of God, the distinction between mind and body, and the reality of the material world.
context: René Descartes (1596–1650) published the Meditations in Latin in 1641, together with objections from other philosophers and his replies. This is the first English translation, by William Molyneux, printed in London in 1680, and it includes the objections of Thomas Hobbes, the author of [Leviathan](/book/270?lang=en), with Descartes's answers. Read Descartes's [Discourse on the Method](/book/274?lang=en).

about: Having asked in his first Critique what we can know, Kant turns here to the question of what we ought to do. He argues that pure reason, without help from desire or experience, can give us a moral law, and that our awareness of this law shows that we are free. From morality he goes further: since we must hope that virtue and happiness will finally be united, practical reason leads us to believe in God and the immortality of the soul, which theoretical reason could never prove.
context: Published in 1788, three years after the [Groundwork](/book/5725?lang=en), the book ends with Kant's most famous words: two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, 'the starry heavens above and the moral law within'. This translation is by T. K. Abbott. Read his [Critique of Pure Reason](/book/4364?lang=en), and see [Kant's life](/author/kant?lang=en).

about: In the third of his great Critiques, Kant examines two kinds of judgement that seem to fall between knowledge and morality. The first is aesthetic: when we call something beautiful we expect everyone to agree, although we cannot prove it by concepts, and beauty pleases us without any interest in possessing it; he also analyses the sublime, the feeling of awe before vast mountains or storms. The second is our judgement of living things and of nature as if it had purposes, which science cannot prove but cannot do without.
context: Published in 1790, the book completes Kant's critical system, founded modern aesthetics and deeply influenced the Romantic poets and philosophers. This translation is by J. H. Bernard. Read first his [Critique of Practical Reason](/book/5726?lang=en), and see [Kant's life](/author/kant?lang=en).

about: How can we live as happily as possible in a world that Arthur Schopenhauer believed was, on the whole, full of suffering? In this practical essay he divides the good things of life into three kinds: what a person is, such as health, character and intelligence; what a person has, property; and how a person stands in the eyes of others, reputation, rank and fame. He argues that the first matters far more than the other two: a cheerful temperament and a rich inner life are worth more than any fortune.
context: The essay comes from Schopenhauer's Parerga and Paralipomena, published in 1851, whose popular essays at last made the old philosopher (1788–1860) famous after decades of neglect. This translation is by Thomas Bailey Saunders. Compare the Stoic [Enchiridion](/book/40729?lang=en) of Epictetus.

about: In this book of short aphorisms and essays, Friedrich Nietzsche breaks with his earlier admiration for Wagner and Schopenhauer and becomes a cool, scientific 'free spirit'. He examines morality, religion, art, the state, women, friendship and the psychology of human motives, arguing that what we call our highest feelings and values often grow from lower, all-too-human sources such as vanity, fear and habit, and can be understood without any appeal to the supernatural.
context: Nietzsche published the first part in 1878 and dedicated it to the memory of Voltaire on the hundredth anniversary of his death; the book marks the beginning of his mature philosophy. This translation is by Alexander Harvey. Read next [Beyond Good and Evil](/book/92?lang=en), and see [Nietzsche's life](/author/nietzsche?lang=en).

about: Written in a burst of recovered health and high spirits, this book of aphorisms, songs and poems, also known as The Gay Science, is Nietzsche at his most playful and lyrical. It contains the parable of the madman who runs into the marketplace with a lantern in broad daylight crying 'God is dead... and we have killed him', the first statement of the idea of eternal recurrence, and the first appearance of Zarathustra, as well as reflections on knowledge, art and how to live joyfully without illusions.
context: Published in 1882 and enlarged in 1887, the book prepared the way for [Thus Spake Zarathustra](/book/91?lang=en). This translation, by Thomas Common, with the verse translated by Paul Cohn and Maude Petre, comes from the complete English edition of Nietzsche's works edited by Oscar Levy. See [Nietzsche's life](/author/nietzsche?lang=en).

about: Nietzsche called this short book a great declaration of war, and its subtitle, 'how to philosophize with the hammer', means sounding out the 'idols', the great ideals of Western culture, to hear whether they ring hollow. In sharp chapters he attacks Socrates, the 'improvers' of mankind, German culture, free will and the idea of a 'true world' beyond this one, which he sums up in a famous page, 'How the True World Finally Became a Fable'. 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' comes from its opening maxims.
context: Written in 1888, the last year of Nietzsche's working life, it was published at the beginning of 1889, just after his mental collapse. This volume of the Oscar Levy edition, translated by Anthony M. Ludovici, also contains [The Antichrist](/book/96?lang=en). See [Nietzsche's life](/author/nietzsche?lang=en).

about: Drawing on the American anthropologist Lewis Henry Morgan's studies of the Iroquois and other peoples, Friedrich Engels traces how human society developed from early communal groups, in which descent was counted through the mother, to the monogamous family, private property and the state. He argues that the rise of private wealth brought about 'the world-historic defeat of the female sex', and that the state arose to protect the property of the ruling class.
context: Engels (1820–1895), Karl Marx's lifelong collaborator, wrote the book in 1884, after Marx's death, using Marx's notes on Morgan. Many of its anthropological claims are now outdated, but it remained central to socialist and feminist debates. This translation is by Ernest Untermann. Read [The Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en).

about: Against those who read Darwin's theory as a story of endless 'struggle for existence', in which only the most ruthless survive, the Russian naturalist Peter Kropotkin argues that cooperation is just as important a factor in evolution. Drawing on his own observations in Siberia, he describes mutual aid among ants, birds and mammals, and then traces it through human history: in tribes, village communities, medieval guilds and free cities, and in the unions and friendly societies of his own day.
context: Kropotkin (1842–1921), a prince who became an anarchist and spent years in prison and exile, published the essays as a book in 1902, in reply to an article by Thomas Huxley. Biologists studying cooperation have given his ideas new attention. Read also his [The Conquest of Bread](/book/20838?lang=en), and compare Darwin's [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en).

about: Why, asks Peter Kropotkin, should anyone go hungry in a world that can produce enough for everyone? In this book he describes how a society without government or private property might work after a revolution: the people would take over houses, land, food and factories and share them according to need, with everyone working four or five hours a day in freely organised cooperatives, leaving time for science, art and leisure.
context: Published in French in 1892, the book is the classic statement of anarchist communism, and it influenced movements from the Spanish Revolution of the 1930s to modern cooperatives. Kropotkin (1842–1921), born a Russian prince, was imprisoned in both Russia and France for his ideas. Read his [Mutual Aid](/book/4423?lang=en), and compare Proudhon's [What Is Property?](/book/663?lang=en).

about: 'Property is theft!' With this famous answer to the question of his title, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon attacks the right of owners to draw rent, interest and profit from land and capital without working, which he sees as a form of robbery that makes inequality inevitable. He examines and rejects, one by one, the arguments that property is a natural right or is justified by occupation or labour, and calls instead for a society of equals founded on justice, in which possession is limited to what a person uses.
context: Proudhon (1809–1865), a self-taught printer from a poor family in Besançon, published the book in 1840, and in it he became the first person to call himself an anarchist. Karl Marx first praised him and later attacked him. Read Kropotkin's [The Conquest of Bread](/book/20838?lang=en) and [The Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en).

about: What happens to a person in a crowd? The French social psychologist Gustave Le Bon argues that individuals in a crowd lose their sense of responsibility and their reasoning, and become part of a single 'collective mind' that is impulsive, credulous and suggestible, capable of both heroism and terrible violence. Crowds, he says, are moved not by facts but by images, slogans and the prestige of leaders who know how to affirm, repeat and spread ideas by contagion.
context: Published in 1895 as Psychologie des foules, the book was studied by Freud and by twentieth-century politicians, including Mussolini, and it remains a founding text of mass psychology. Le Bon (1841–1931) also wrote a famous study of Arab civilisation, La Civilisation des Arabes (1884), which has long been read in Arabic translation. See [Freud's life](/author/freud?lang=en).

about: In the title essay, William James defends the right to believe in something, religious faith for example, before there is enough evidence to prove it, when the choice is 'living, forced and momentous' and cannot be settled by the intellect alone; to refuse to decide, he argues, is itself a decision. Other essays in the volume ask 'Is Life Worth Living?' and discuss the moral philosopher and the moral life, the dilemma of determinism, great men and their surroundings, and psychical research.
context: James published the collection in 1897 and dedicated it to his old friend Charles Sanders Peirce. Written for general audiences, it is among his liveliest work, and the title essay is still debated wherever faith and reason meet. Read his [Pragmatism](/book/5179?lang=en) and [The Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/james?lang=en).

about: How did law begin? Studying Roman law, the Hindu laws of Manu, the Old Testament and other early codes, Henry Sumner Maine argues that the earliest societies were made up not of individuals but of families ruled by a father, and that law was at first a matter of custom, religion and paternal power. His most famous conclusion is that the movement of progressive societies has been 'from Status to Contract', from relationships fixed by birth to relationships freely chosen by agreement.
context: Maine (1822–1888), a Cambridge law professor who later served as legal adviser to the British government in India, published the book in 1861, and it helped to found the comparative and historical study of law, as well as modern anthropology. Compare Engels's [The Origin of the Family](/book/29597?lang=en).

about: Thomas Malthus argues that human population, when unchecked, grows geometrically, doubling every twenty-five years or so, while the supply of food can grow only arithmetically. Population must therefore always press against the means of subsistence, held down by misery, famine, disease and war, or, as he later stressed, by moral restraint. From this he concludes that the hopes of thinkers such as William Godwin and Condorcet for a future society of plenty and equality are doomed.
context: Malthus (1766–1834), an English clergyman and economist, published the essay anonymously in 1798 and greatly enlarged it in later editions. It was one of the most controversial books of its age, and both Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace said that reading it gave them the key to natural selection. Compare Adam Smith's [The Wealth of Nations](/book/3421?lang=en) and Darwin's [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en).

about: In eight books, Niccolò Machiavelli tells the history of his city from the fall of the Roman Empire to the death of Lorenzo de' Medici, the Magnificent, in 1492. He traces how Florence was torn by factions, Guelphs and Ghibellines, nobles and people, and how the Medici rose to power, and he describes vividly events such as the revolt of the wool workers, the Ciompi, in 1378, and the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, when Lorenzo's brother was murdered in the cathedral during Mass.
context: Machiavelli (1469–1527) was commissioned to write the history by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, and presented it to him in 1525, when he had become Pope Clement VII. Writing for the family that had removed him from office, he had to balance truth and tact. Read his [The Prince](/book/259?lang=en).

about: How did Islam spread across the world? In this history, the British scholar Thomas Walker Arnold argues, against the common European view of his time, that Islam spread far more through peaceful preaching, trade, the example of believers and the work of missionaries, Sufis and scholars than through the sword. He follows its growth region by region, in Western Asia, Africa, Spain, Persia and Central Asia, among the Mongols and the Turks, in India, China and the Malay Archipelago, drawing on a wide range of Arabic, Persian and European sources.
context: Arnold (1864–1930) taught for ten years at the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in India, and later in Lahore, where the young Muhammad Iqbal was his student and friend. He first published the book in 1896, and it remains a pioneering, much-cited study. Compare [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/14976?lang=en).

about: These eighty-five short poems of love and life, which Rabindranath Tagore translated into English prose himself, are lighter and more earthly than the devotional songs of [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en): a servant asks his queen for nothing but to be the gardener of her flower garden, lovers meet at the riverside and the village well, a girl hesitates at her door, and the poet reflects on youth, longing, parting and the passing of time.
context: Tagore (1861–1941), the Bengali poet, composer and educator who became the first non-European winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, published The Gardener that year, explaining that most of its lyrics had been written much earlier than those of Gitanjali. Read also [The Crescent Moon](/book/6551?lang=en) and [Stray Birds](/book/6554?lang=en), and his essays in [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: In these prose poems Rabindranath Tagore enters the world of childhood: a baby who could fly up to heaven if he wished but stays for his mother's love; a boy who dreams of being a sailor, or a hero rescuing his mother from robbers, or a champa flower playing hide-and-seek with her; questions about where babies come from; paper boats floated down the stream; and a mother's tender, sometimes sad thoughts as she watches her child grow.
context: Tagore translated the poems from Bengali himself, and the book was published in 1913, the year of his Nobel Prize. Simple and luminous, it is often read by parents and children together. Read also [The Gardener](/book/6690?lang=en) and [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en), and see Tagore's essays in [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: 'Stray birds of summer come to my window to sing and fly away.' This book gathers 326 very short poems and sayings, many only one or two lines long, in which Rabindranath Tagore captures a single thought or image: 'Let life be beautiful like summer flowers and death like autumn leaves'; 'The butterfly counts not months but moments, and has time enough'; 'Clouds come floating into my life, no longer to carry rain or usher storm, but to add colour to my sunset sky.'
context: Published in 1916, the collection was inspired partly by the Japanese haiku that Tagore encountered on his visit to Japan that year, and partly by Indian traditions of aphorism. This edition has illustrations by Willy Pogány. Compare [The Gardener](/book/6690?lang=en) and [The Crescent Moon](/book/6551?lang=en).

about: Kabir, a fifteenth-century weaver of Benares, was claimed by both Hindus and Muslims, and in these hundred short songs he rejects the outward forms of both religions, the temple and the mosque, the idol and the pilgrimage, to seek God within the heart: 'O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee. I am neither in temple nor in mosque.' His poems speak of love, of the body as a sacred place, and of the joy of union with the divine.
context: Rabindranath Tagore translated these songs into English in 1915, with the help of the scholar Evelyn Underhill, who wrote the introduction. Kabir (traditionally about 1440–1518) remains one of the best-loved poets of India, and his verses are sung by people of every faith. Compare Tagore's own [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en).

about: The Upanishads are the philosophical heart of the ancient Vedas: dialogues and meditations, composed in India over many centuries from around the eighth century BC, on the nature of the self and of ultimate reality. Their central teaching is that the innermost self of each person, Atman, is one with Brahman, the reality behind the whole universe. This volume presents the Isha, Kena and Katha Upanishads; in the Katha, the boy Nachiketas goes to Yama, the god of death, and asks him what happens after we die.
context: The translation, with a commentary, is by Swami Paramananda (1884–1940), an Indian monk of the Ramakrishna order who taught in the United States and founded the Vedanta Centre in Boston, where these translations began as classes. The Upanishads deeply influenced thinkers from Schopenhauer to Tagore. Compare [The Song Celestial](/book/2540?lang=en) and [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en).

about: Banished from the court of her usurping uncle, young Rosalind escapes into the Forest of Arden disguised as a boy named Ganymede, together with her loyal cousin Celia and the court jester Touchstone. In the forest she finds Orlando, a young man who has also fled persecution and is hanging bad love poems to her on the trees, and in her disguise she offers to 'cure' him of his love by letting him woo her as if she were Rosalind. Around them gather shepherds, a melancholy philosopher named Jaques, and her exiled father, the Duke, with his little court.
context: Written around 1599, the comedy contains Jaques's famous speech on the seven ages of man, beginning 'All the world's a stage'. Rosalind, witty and wise, has one of the longest parts for a woman in Shakespeare. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Read also [A Midsummer Night's Dream](/book/6?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: Soldiers return from war to the house of Leonato, governor of Messina, and two love stories begin. The young Claudio falls in love with Leonato's gentle daughter Hero, while Hero's cousin Beatrice and the soldier Benedick, who claim to despise each other, carry on a 'merry war' of insults until their friends trick each of them into believing the other is secretly in love. Meanwhile the villain Don John plots to ruin Hero's wedding with a cruel deception, which is uncovered, comically, by the bumbling constable Dogberry and his night watch.
context: Written around 1598 or 1599, the play is one of Shakespeare's most popular comedies, and the sparring of Beatrice and Benedick became the model for countless witty couples in literature and film. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Read also [As You Like It](/book/1365?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: 'Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by this sun of York.' At the end of the Wars of the Roses, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, deformed, brilliant and utterly without conscience, confides his plans to the audience and then carries them out: he arranges the death of his brother Clarence, woos the widow of a prince he killed, has his young nephews, the princes in the Tower, murdered, and seizes the crown. But his allies desert him, the ghosts of his victims visit him on the eve of battle, and at Bosworth Field he cries, 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!'
context: Written around 1592 or 1593, the play completes Shakespeare's first cycle of English history plays and created one of the great villains of the stage. Historians argue that the real Richard was far less wicked, but the play's portrait has proved unforgettable. Read also [Macbeth](/book/2?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: Mark Antony, one of the three men who rule the Roman world, has abandoned his duties in Rome for a life of pleasure in Alexandria with Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt. Called home by war and politics, he marries Octavia, the sister of his rival Octavius Caesar, to keep the peace, but he cannot stay away from Cleopatra. The quarrel between the two great men ends in war, the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra's fleet at Actium, and the lovers' deaths in Egypt.
context: Written around 1606, the play follows Plutarch's life of Antony closely, and the soldier Enobarbus's description of Cleopatra on her barge, with its line 'Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale her infinite variety', is among Shakespeare's most famous passages. It is a vast, sensual tragedy that moves between Rome and Egypt. Compare [Romeo and Juliet](/book/3?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: In Padua, the rich Baptista Minola will not let his gentle younger daughter Bianca marry until her elder sister Katherina, famous for her sharp tongue and temper, has found a husband. Bianca's many suitors are delighted when Petruchio, a bold fortune hunter from Verona, arrives determined to marry Katherina for her dowry and to 'tame' her by contradicting, starving and exhausting her. The play is framed by a joke played on a drunken tinker, Christopher Sly, who is persuaded that he is a lord watching the performance.
context: Written in the early 1590s, it is one of Shakespeare's most debated comedies: some read Katherina's final speech of obedience as sincere, others as ironic, and modern productions often turn it upside down. It inspired the musical Kiss Me, Kate and the film 10 Things I Hate About You. Read also [Much Ado About Nothing](/book/1363?lang=en).

about: Leontes, King of Sicilia, is suddenly seized by the jealous conviction that his pregnant wife Hermione has betrayed him with his oldest friend, Polixenes, King of Bohemia. He imprisons her, orders their newborn daughter abandoned in a wild place, and defies even the oracle of Apollo, with tragic results. Sixteen years later in Bohemia, the lost daughter, Perdita, raised by a shepherd, falls in love with Polixenes' son, and the play moves from tragedy towards a reunion that seems like a miracle.
context: Written around 1610 or 1611, it is one of Shakespeare's late romances, and it contains his most famous stage direction: 'Exit, pursued by a bear.' Its final scene, in which a statue of Hermione is unveiled, is one of the most moving in all his plays. Compare [The Tempest](/book/7?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: In St Petersburg, Razumov, a lonely, hard-working student with no family, wants only to win a university prize and a quiet career. Then a fellow student, Victor Haldin, who has just assassinated a hated government minister with a bomb, comes to his room and asks for help to escape. Fearing for his own future, Razumov betrays him to the police, and is then sent by the secret police to spy on Russian revolutionaries in exile in Geneva, among them Haldin's mother and his trusting sister Natalia, who believes Razumov was her brother's friend.
context: Joseph Conrad published the novel in 1911. Told by an elderly English teacher of languages in Geneva, the 'Western eyes' of the title, it is often read as Conrad's answer to Dostoevsky, whom he disliked, and it is a dark study of guilt, autocracy and revolution. Compare [Crime and Punishment](/book/12?lang=en) and Conrad's [The Secret Agent](/book/1235?lang=en).

about: Folly herself, dressed as a jester, climbs into the pulpit and delivers a speech in her own honour. Without her, she argues, nobody would marry, have children, make friends or enjoy life, and she claims as her followers almost everyone: lovers, hunters, gamblers, poets and philosophers, and above all the monks, theologians, bishops and popes of the Church, whose greed and empty arguments she mocks without mercy. At the end the joke turns serious, and Folly praises the holy foolishness of Christian faith.
context: Desiderius Erasmus (about 1466–1536), the great Dutch humanist, wrote the book in Latin in 1509 while staying with his friend Thomas More in London, and its Latin title, Moriae Encomium, is a pun on More's name. Its satire of Church corruption helped prepare the ground for the Reformation. This is John Wilson's translation of 1668. Read also More's [Utopia](/book/2317?lang=en).

about: The giant Gargantua is born from his mother's ear crying 'Drink! Drink!', and grows up to wage a comic war against a neighbouring king over some cakes, after which he founds the Abbey of Thélème for his friend Friar John, an abbey whose only rule is 'Do what you will'. His son Pantagruel, another giant, studies in Paris, befriends the witty, cowardly rogue Panurge, and sets out on a long voyage to consult the Oracle of the Holy Bottle on whether Panurge should marry.
context: François Rabelais (about 1494–1553), a French monk, physician and humanist, published the books between 1532 and 1564, the last after his death, and the theologians of the Sorbonne condemned them for their mockery of the Church and the schools. Bursting with bawdy jokes, lists, invented words and learning, the work gave English the word 'gargantuan'. This is the classic seventeenth-century translation by Sir Thomas Urquhart and Peter Motteux, with illustrations by Gustave Doré. Compare [Don Quixote](/book/168?lang=en).

about: 'Of Truth', 'Of Death', 'Of Revenge', 'Of Friendship', 'Of Studies': in some sixty short essays, Francis Bacon gives practical, worldly advice on how to live and how to succeed in public life, in sentences so compact that many have become proverbs. 'Revenge is a kind of wild justice'; 'Men fear death, as children fear to go in the dark'; 'Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.'
context: Bacon (1561–1626), lawyer, philosopher and Lord Chancellor of England until his fall for accepting bribes, published the first ten essays in 1597, borrowing the name from Montaigne's French Essais, and enlarged the collection to fifty-eight in 1625. They are among the first great essays written in English. Read also his [New Atlantis](/book/2585?lang=en), and compare [Machiavelli's The Prince](/book/259?lang=en).

about: A ship lost in the Pacific Ocean reaches an unknown island called Bensalem, where the sailors find a peaceful, Christian and well-governed people. Their greatest institution is Salomon's House, a college of scholars who study nature by experiment: they have towers for observing the weather, deep caves for preserving things, new metals and medicines, instruments for seeing small and distant things, engines that imitate the flight of birds and boats that travel under water, all devoted to 'the enlarging of the bounds of human empire'.
context: Francis Bacon left this short utopia unfinished, and it was published in 1627, a year after his death. Its picture of organised scientific research inspired the founders of the Royal Society in London in 1660. Compare Thomas More's [Utopia](/book/2317?lang=en), and read Bacon's [Novum Organum](/book/41517?lang=en).

about: Francis Bacon called for a 'great instauration', a complete renewal of human knowledge. In this book, written in Latin aphorisms, he argues that the old logic of Aristotle, which reasons downwards from general principles, has produced little that is new, and he proposes instead a method of careful observation, experiment and gradual induction from particular facts. He also describes the 'idols' that mislead the mind: those of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre, our natural, personal, verbal and inherited prejudices.
context: Published in 1620, the 'new instrument' of the title answers Aristotle's books on logic, known as the Organon. It is a founding document of the scientific method, and its account of the idols of the mind is still taught in courses on critical thinking. This edition was edited by Joseph Devey. Read also Bacon's [New Atlantis](/book/2585?lang=en) and his [Essays](/book/874?lang=en).

about: Over four evenings in 1507, at the court of the Duke of Urbino in Italy, a group of brilliant lords and ladies, led by the Duchess Elisabetta Gonzaga, play a game: they will describe the perfect courtier. They discuss his birth, his skill in arms and sports, his knowledge of letters, music and painting, the art of conversation and above all sprezzatura, the grace of doing difficult things as if without effort; then the perfect court lady; and finally, in a speech by the poet Pietro Bembo, the ladder of love that rises from beauty to the divine.
context: Baldassare Castiglione (1478–1529), a diplomat who had served at Urbino, published the book in 1528, and it became one of the most influential books of the Renaissance, shaping the manners of European gentlemen for two centuries. This is the 1901 translation by Leonard Eckstein Opdycke. Compare the very different advice of [Machiavelli's The Prince](/book/259?lang=en).

about: Lázaro, a poor boy born beside the river Tormes near Salamanca, tells how he survived by serving a string of masters, each worse than the last: a cruel blind beggar who teaches him cunning by knocking his head against a stone bull, a miserly priest who nearly starves him while he steals bread from a locked chest, and a proud but penniless squire whom his own servant must feed. He ends up, by his own account, a respectable town crier, married to a woman whose ties to an archpriest he prefers not to question.
context: Published anonymously in 1554, probably because of its satire of the clergy, Lazarillo de Tormes created the picaresque novel, the story of a rogue who lives by his wits, and influenced [Don Quixote](/book/168?lang=en) and countless later books. This translation by Robert S. Rudder also includes the continuation written by Juan de Luna in 1620.

about: Prince Segismundo of Poland has been kept chained in a tower in the mountains since birth, because the stars foretold that he would become a tyrant and humble his father, King Basilio. To test the prophecy, the king has him drugged and carried to the palace, where he wakes as a prince and behaves with violent cruelty; drugged again, he wakes in his chains and is told it was all a dream. Unsure what is real, Segismundo must decide how to act in a world where life itself may be a dream.
context: Pedro Calderón de la Barca (1600–1681), the great playwright of Spain's Golden Age, wrote the play in the 1630s, and it was first printed in 1636. This is the free English version by Edward FitzGerald, best known for his translation of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. Compare [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en), another prince who struggles with how to act.

about: In ten cantos, the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões tells the voyage of Vasco da Gama, who in 1497 and 1498 sailed around the Cape of Good Hope and across the Indian Ocean to Calicut in India, opening the sea route from Europe to Asia. Into the story he weaves the whole history of Portugal, the gods of Olympus quarrelling over the voyage, the terrifying giant Adamastor who embodies the stormy Cape, and the Isle of Love where Venus rewards the sailors on their way home.
context: Camões (about 1524–1580) lost an eye fighting in North Africa and spent years as a soldier in India and the Far East; he is said to have saved the manuscript by swimming ashore from a shipwreck at the mouth of the Mekong. Published in 1572, the epic is Portugal's national poem. This is William Julius Mickle's eighteenth-century verse translation. Compare Virgil's [Aeneid](/book/541?lang=en).

about: During an outbreak of plague in London, the gentleman Lovewit flees to the country and leaves his house in the care of his butler, Face. Face invites in a con man, Subtle, who poses as an alchemist, and a prostitute, Dol Common, and together they turn the house into a factory of fraud, promising a parade of greedy and gullible visitors the philosopher's stone, luck at gambling, a rich marriage or a meeting with the Queen of Fairies, until the master unexpectedly comes home.
context: Ben Jonson's comedy was first performed in 1610, and it keeps strictly to the classical unity of time, taking place in the space of a few hours. Samuel Taylor Coleridge counted it, with Oedipus the King and [Tom Jones](/book/6598?lang=en), among the three most perfect plots ever planned. Read also Jonson's [Volpone](/book/4126?lang=en).

about: The young widowed Duchess of Malfi is forbidden by her two brothers, the cruel Duke Ferdinand and the corrupt Cardinal, to marry again, since they want her fortune and her honour kept for the family. She secretly marries her honest steward, Antonio, and bears him children, while her brothers' spy, the bitter and brilliant Bosola, watches her. When the brothers discover the marriage, their revenge is terrible, and it destroys them too.
context: John Webster (about 1580–about 1632) wrote the tragedy around 1613, basing it on a real Italian story of the early sixteenth century. Dark, poetic and violent, it gives its heroine one of the most dignified deaths in English drama, with the famous line 'I am Duchess of Malfi still'. Compare Shakespeare's [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en).

about: God, angered that people have forgotten him, sends Death to summon Everyman to give an account of his life. Terrified, Everyman begs his companions to come with him on the journey, but Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin and Goods all refuse; only Good Deeds, too weak at first even to stand, will go with him to the grave, helped by Knowledge and Confession. This volume collects that famous play with other early English interludes and eight medieval miracle plays on stories from the Bible.
context: Everyman, a morality play of the late fifteenth century in which every character is an abstract quality, is still performed today. These plays, once acted by craft guilds in the streets of English towns, are the roots of English drama. The volume was edited by Ernest Rhys for Everyman's Library, the famous series that took its name and motto from the play. Compare [Doctor Faustus](/book/1061?lang=en).

about: Jonathan Swift's first great satire tells the story of three brothers, Peter, Martin and Jack, who each receive from their dying father a coat and a will forbidding them to change it in any way. Peter, who stands for the Catholic Church, covers his coat with fashionable ornaments and invents absurd excuses for it; Martin, the Church of England, removes them carefully; and Jack, the Puritans, tears his to rags in his zeal. Between the chapters come wild digressions mocking pedantic critics, modern learning and madness itself.
context: Published anonymously in 1704, when Swift (1667–1745) was a young clergyman, the book was so irreverent that it is said to have cost him a bishopric, since Queen Anne disliked it. This edition was edited by Henry Morley. Read Swift's [Gulliver's Travels](/book/302?lang=en).

about: 'Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man.' In four verse epistles addressed to his friend Lord Bolingbroke, Alexander Pope sets out to 'vindicate the ways of God to man': the place of human beings in the great chain of being, the balance of reason and passion within us, our place in society, and the nature of happiness, concluding that 'whatever is, is right'. This volume adds his Moral Essays and his satires.
context: Pope (1688–1744), the leading English poet of his century, published the Essay in 1733 and 1734. Its polished couplets made it famous across Europe, and Voltaire admired it, though he later mocked its optimism in [Candide](/book/279?lang=en). This edition was edited by Henry Morley. Read also Pope's [The Rape of the Lock](/book/9150?lang=en).

about: At a fashionable party at Hampton Court, a young baron snips off a lock of the beautiful Belinda's hair with a pair of scissors, and a social war breaks out. Alexander Pope tells this trivial quarrel in the grand style of Homer and Virgil, with a game of cards described like a battle, a heroic fight with fans and snuff, a journey to the gloomy Cave of Spleen, and an army of tiny guardian spirits, the sylphs, who have failed to protect her. This volume includes other poems by Pope.
context: The poem was based on a real incident: Lord Petre had cut a lock of Arabella Fermor's hair, and the two families fell out, so Pope's friend John Caryll asked him to write a light poem to laugh them into peace. First published in 1712 and enlarged in 1714, it is the finest mock-epic in English. Compare the real epic of Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en), and read Pope's [An Essay on Man](/book/2579?lang=en).

about: Micromegas, a young giant from a planet circling the star Sirius, eight leagues tall, is banished for writing a book about insects that the authorities consider heretical, and sets off to travel the universe. With a companion from Saturn, a mere dwarf a thousand fathoms high, he arrives on Earth, where at first they cannot even see the inhabitants. Through a microscope made from a diamond they discover a ship of philosophers returning from the Arctic, and are astonished that such tiny creatures can measure the heavens yet argue so foolishly about the soul.
context: Voltaire (1694–1778) published this short philosophical tale in 1752. It is one of the earliest works of science fiction, and its play with size, like that of [Gulliver's Travels](/book/302?lang=en), mocks human pride. This translation is by Peter Phalen. Read also [Candide](/book/279?lang=en).

about: Evelina Anville, a beautiful, sheltered girl of seventeen raised by a kind country clergyman, is unacknowledged by her aristocratic father. On her first visit to London she makes every possible social mistake at balls, theatres and pleasure gardens, is mortified by her vulgar grandmother, Madame Duval, and her cousins, the Branghtons, and is pursued by the rakish Sir Clement Willoughby, while she falls in love with the perfect gentleman, Lord Orville. She tells it all in letters to her guardian.
context: Fanny Burney (1752–1840) published the novel anonymously in 1778, and it was a sensation; when she was revealed as the author, Samuel Johnson became her friend. Its comedy of manners, seen through a young woman's eyes, prepared the way for Jane Austen, who admired her. Read [Pride and Prejudice](/book/38?lang=en).

about: These are the great medieval tales of Wales: the four branches of the Mabinogi, with Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, who changes places for a year with a king of the Otherworld, the giant Bendigeidfran wading across the sea to Ireland, and Blodeuwedd, the woman made of flowers who betrays her husband; and the Arthurian stories, among them Culhwch and Olwen, with its impossible tasks, and the romances of Owain, Peredur and Geraint.
context: The tales survive in Welsh manuscripts of the fourteenth century, though they are much older. Lady Charlotte Guest (1812–1895), an Englishwoman who learned Welsh and later became Lady Charlotte Schreiber on her second marriage, published the first English translation between 1838 and 1849 and gave the collection its name. Compare Tennyson's Arthurian [Idylls of the King](/book/907?lang=en).

about: In 778 the emperor Charlemagne is returning to France after seven years of war in Spain. Betrayed by Roland's stepfather, Ganelon, the rearguard led by Charlemagne's nephew Roland is ambushed by a vast Saracen army in the mountain pass of Roncevaux. Too proud to blow his horn, the Oliphant, to call for help, Roland fights on beside his friend Oliver and Archbishop Turpin until nearly all are dead; only then does he blow it, so hard that his temples burst, and Charlemagne returns to take revenge.
context: The oldest major work of French literature, composed around 1100 in some four thousand lines, the poem turned a small historical defeat, in which the real attackers were Basques, into a crusading epic against Muslims, and it reflects the outlook of the age of the First Crusade. This is the 1919 translation by C. K. Scott Moncrieff, later famous as the translator of Proust. Compare [The Nibelungenlied](/book/1390?lang=en).

about: Siegfried, the hero who killed a dragon, bathed in its blood and won the treasure of the Nibelungs, comes to the Burgundian court at Worms to win the beautiful Kriemhild, and by trickery helps her brother, King Gunther, to win the warrior queen Brunhild of Iceland. Years later a quarrel between the two queens leads to Siegfried's murder by the grim vassal Hagen, who sinks the treasure in the Rhine, and Kriemhild, now married to Etzel, king of the Huns, plans a revenge that ends in a massacre.
context: Composed in Middle High German around 1200 by an unknown poet, the epic draws on memories of the destruction of the Burgundian kingdom by the Huns in the fifth century. It became Germany's national epic and, in other forms, inspired Wagner's Ring cycle. This is the prose translation by Daniel Bussier Shumway. Compare [The Song of Roland](/book/694?lang=en) and [Beowulf](/book/14518?lang=en).

about: Grettir Asmundarson is the strongest man in Iceland and the unluckiest: proud, quarrelsome and brave, he wrestles with the walking dead and destroys a monstrous ghost named Glam, whose curse leaves him afraid of the dark for the rest of his life, and he is outlawed for deaths he never intended. For nearly twenty years he survives as an outlaw in the wilderness, until he takes refuge with his brother Illugi on the rocky island of Drangey.
context: Written down in Iceland in the early fourteenth century about a real man who died around 1031, Grettir's saga is one of the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas, and some of its episodes echo [Beowulf](/book/14518?lang=en). It is full of dark humour, ghosts and fate. Read also [The Nibelungenlied](/book/1390?lang=en).

about: Gilgamesh, the proud and restless king of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, the ancient city of Warka near today's Samawah in Iraq, oppresses his people until the gods create a rival for him, the wild man Enkidu, who lives among the animals. After a great wrestling match the two become inseparable friends and set out to kill Humbaba, the monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest. This book presents two Old Babylonian tablets of the epic, nearly four thousand years old, now in Philadelphia and at Yale, which tell of Enkidu's taming, his meeting with Gilgamesh and the friends' preparations for their journey.
context: The Gilgamesh epic, written on clay tablets in Akkadian after earlier Sumerian poems, is the oldest great work of world literature; its later version, found in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, opposite Mosul, includes a flood story strikingly like Noah's. Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay published these tablets in 1920 with the original text, a translation and notes, so this is a scholarly edition rather than a retelling. Compare Homer's [Odyssey](/book/173?lang=en).

about: What did the ancient Egyptians believe happened after death? In this short guide, E. A. Wallis Budge explains the great collection of spells, hymns and prayers that scribes wrote on tomb walls, coffins and papyrus rolls to help the dead on their journey: how the body was preserved, the role of Thoth, the god of wisdom, and of Osiris, king and judge of the underworld, the weighing of the heart in the Hall of Judgement, and the kingdom of the blessed dead, ending with a short description of the chapters themselves.
context: Budge (1857–1934) was keeper of Egyptian antiquities at the British Museum, home of the famous Papyrus of Ani.
