He explains that the name 'Book of the Dead' comes from the Egyptian tomb robbers, who called any papyrus found with a mummy 'Kitab al-Mayyit', 'the dead man's book'; the Egyptians' own title meant 'Coming Forth by Day'. Compare the Indian [Upanishads](/book/3405?lang=en).

about: Count Maximilian von Moor has two sons. The younger, Franz, ugly, envious and coldly rational, uses forged letters to turn their father against the elder, Karl, a generous, passionate student. Believing himself disowned, Karl becomes leader of a band of robbers in the Bohemian forests, a rebel against a corrupt society, while at home Franz seizes power, imprisons his father and tries to win Karl's beloved, Amalia. But Karl's band is full of real criminals, and his revolt soon turns into tragedy.
context: Friedrich Schiller (1759–1805) wrote the play as a young army doctor, and its first performance in Mannheim in 1782 caused a sensation, with spectators said to have fainted and strangers to have embraced in tears. It is a landmark of the Sturm und Drang movement, and Verdi made it into an opera. Compare Goethe's [The Sorrows of Young Werther](/book/166?lang=en).

about: Hermann, a poor, ambitious young officer of German descent in St Petersburg, watches others gamble every night but never plays himself. Then he hears that an old countess knows a secret of three cards that will always win, a secret she learned in Paris sixty years before. Determined to get it, he courts her young ward, Lizaveta, to gain entry to the house at night, and confronts the old woman with a pistol, with consequences that follow him all the way to the card table.
context: Alexander Pushkin (1799–1837), Russia's greatest poet, published this short story in 1834, and Tchaikovsky later turned it into an opera. Dostoevsky called it a masterpiece of fantastic fiction. This translation is by H. Twitchell. Read also Dostoevsky's [The Gambler](/book/18?lang=en), and see [Pushkin's life](/author/pushkin?lang=en).

about: Eugene Onegin, a bored young dandy from St Petersburg, inherits his uncle's country estate and befriends his neighbour, the romantic young poet Lensky, who is in love with Olga Larina. Olga's quiet, bookish sister Tatyana falls in love with Onegin and writes him a passionate letter; he coldly lectures her in reply. A trivial quarrel at Tatyana's name-day party leads to a duel between the friends. Years later Onegin meets Tatyana again in Petersburg, now a married princess, and it is his turn to fall hopelessly in love.
context: Alexander Pushkin wrote this 'novel in verse' between 1823 and 1831, in a fourteen-line stanza of his own invention, and it is often called the foundation of modern Russian literature. Tchaikovsky made it into an opera. This is the 1881 translation by Henry Spalding. Compare Lermontov's [A Hero of Our Time](/book/1180?lang=en), and see [Pushkin's life](/author/pushkin?lang=en).

about: In a small, corrupt provincial town, the mayor learns that a government inspector is coming from St Petersburg in disguise. Panic spreads among the officials, who all have something to hide: the judge takes bribes in hunting puppies, the hospital is a disgrace, the postmaster opens everyone's letters. When they hear that a young man from Petersburg has been staying at the inn without paying, they take him for the inspector. Khlestakov, a penniless, empty-headed clerk, happily accepts their bribes, flirts with the mayor's wife and daughter, and leaves just in time.
context: Nikolai Gogol (1809–1852) wrote the comedy in 1836, reportedly from an idea given to him by Pushkin, and Tsar Nicholas I laughed at its first performance. Its epigraph, 'Don't blame the mirror if your face is crooked', sums up its satire of bureaucracy. This translation is by Thomas Seltzer. Read Gogol's [Dead Souls](/book/331?lang=en).

about: Old Taras Bulba, a fierce Cossack colonel, welcomes his two sons home from the academy in Kiev and takes them straight to the Zaporozhian Sich, the island stronghold of the Cossacks on the Dnieper, to learn the life of warriors. In a war against the Poles, the elder son, Ostap, proves a hero, but the younger, Andriy, falls in love with a Polish noblewoman inside a besieged city and goes over to the enemy, and Taras must face his own son. The volume adds other tales by Gogol.
context: Nikolai Gogol, born in Ukraine, published the story in 1835 and expanded it in 1842; it is a romantic, violent epic of the seventeenth-century Cossacks, and it also carries the prejudices of its age. Compare Tolstoy's [The Cossacks](/book/4830?lang=en), and read Gogol's [Dead Souls](/book/331?lang=en).

about: Sixteen-year-old Vladimir, spending the summer of 1833 at his family's country house near Moscow, falls in love with the beautiful, capricious Princess Zinaida, who lives next door and amuses herself by tormenting a whole circle of admirers. He is happy just to be her page, until he begins to suspect that she loves someone else, and discovers who it is in a night scene he will never forget. This volume adds other stories by Turgenev.
context: Ivan Turgenev (1818–1883) published 'First Love' in 1860 and said it was the most autobiographical of his works. It is one of the most delicate stories about adolescence in any language. This translation is by Isabel Hapgood. Read Turgenev's [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en).

about: Nikolenka Irtenev, a sensitive ten-year-old boy on a Russian country estate in the early nineteenth century, describes his world with intense feeling: his beloved mother, his kind German tutor Karl Ivanych, a holy fool who visits the house, a hunt with the dogs, a children's dance in Moscow, his first loves and quarrels, and finally the death of his mother, which brings his childhood to an end.
context: This was Leo Tolstoy's first published work, appearing in a magazine in 1852, when he was twenty-four and serving as a soldier in the Caucasus, and it made him famous at once. Its close attention to feelings and memory already shows the author of [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en). This translation is by C. J. Hogarth. See also [The Cossacks](/book/4830?lang=en).

about: On a freezing winter afternoon, Vasili Brekhunov, a greedy, self-satisfied village merchant, sets off by sleigh with his patient, good-natured servant Nikita to buy a grove at a bargain price before a rival can. Impatient to close the deal, he refuses to wait out a gathering snowstorm, and the two men lose their way again and again in the blizzard. As night falls and the cold closes in, the master faces a choice that will show what his life has been worth.
context: Leo Tolstoy wrote the story in 1895, in the years after his religious conversion, and it is one of the finest of his late works, a simple parable about death and love for one's neighbour. This translation is by Louise and Aylmer Maude. Read also his [The Kingdom of God Is Within You](/book/39159?lang=en).

about: Dmitri Olenin, a rich young Muscovite tired of society, joins the army as a cadet and is posted to a Cossack village on the Terek River in the Caucasus. Living among the Cossacks, he is enchanted by their free, natural life, hunting in the forest with the old hunter Eroshka, a magnificent storyteller, and falling in love with Maryanka, a proud, beautiful Cossack girl who is engaged to the young warrior Lukashka. But Olenin discovers that he can never truly become one of them.
context: Leo Tolstoy, who served in the Caucasus himself in the early 1850s, worked on the novel for ten years and published it in 1863. It is a fresh, lyrical picture of the region and its people. This translation is by Louise and Aylmer Maude. Read also his [Childhood](/book/2329?lang=en) and [Sevastopol](/book/42623?lang=en).

about: In three sketches, Leo Tolstoy describes the siege of Sevastopol in the Crimean War, where he served as a young artillery officer. 'Sevastopol in December' leads the reader through the besieged city and its field hospitals, where the wounded lie in terrible suffering; 'Sevastopol in May' follows officers whose vanity and ambition carry on even under fire; and 'Sevastopol in August' tells of two brothers in the final assault, as the city falls. 'The hero of my tale,' he writes, 'is truth.'
context: Published in 1855 and 1856 while the war was still being fought, the sketches made Tolstoy's name and were among the first works of literature to show modern war without glory; the tsar is said to have asked that the young officer be kept out of danger. This translation is by Isabel Hapgood. They prepare the way for [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en).

about: In The Kingdom of God Is Within You, Leo Tolstoy argues that the heart of Jesus' teaching is the command not to resist evil by force, so that a true Christian must refuse military service, violence and the power of the state, whatever the churches teach. In What Is Art? he asks what art is for and gives a startling answer: true art passes on genuine feeling and unites people, and by this test he rejects much of the most admired art of his day, including most of his own novels.
context: The Kingdom of God Is Within You was banned in Russia and published abroad in 1893; it deeply moved the young Mohandas Gandhi in South Africa, who later corresponded with Tolstoy. What Is Art? followed in 1897 and 1898. This volume collects both, translated by Aline Delano. Read Tolstoy's late story [Master and Man](/book/1247?lang=en).

about: Pelageya Nilovna, a timid, devout working-class woman in a factory town, has spent her life being beaten by her drunken husband. After his death her son Pavel, a young factory worker, stops drinking, begins reading forbidden books and gathers revolutionary friends in their house. Frightened at first, his mother slowly comes to understand and share their cause, and when Pavel is arrested after a May Day march, she herself begins to carry leaflets and speak out.
context: Maxim Gorky (1868–1936), the pen name of Alexei Peshkov, who grew up in poverty and wandered across Russia doing odd jobs, wrote the novel in 1906 while in the United States, basing it on real events in the factory town of Sormovo. It became a model for Soviet 'socialist realism', and Vsevolod Pudovkin filmed it in 1926. Compare Zola's [Germinal](/book/327?lang=en).

about: In 1819, in a shabby boarding house in Paris run by Madame Vauquer, live a strange collection of lodgers: Eugène de Rastignac, a poor, ambitious law student from the provinces; Vautrin, a mysterious, cynical man who offers him a criminal shortcut to fortune; and old Goriot, a retired vermicelli maker, once rich and now mocked by everyone. Rastignac discovers that Goriot has given all his money to his two daughters, who married into high society and are ashamed of him, and watches a father's love being exploited to the end.
context: Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) published the novel in 1835. It was the first in which he brought back characters from earlier books, creating the huge linked world of his Human Comedy, and Rastignac's challenge to Paris on its last page, 'À nous deux maintenant!', became famous. This translation is by Ellen Marriage. Compare [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en), and read Balzac's [Eugénie Grandet](/book/323?lang=en).

about: Gervaise Macquart, a young laundress with two small sons, is abandoned in a Paris slum by her lover Lantier. She marries Coupeau, a kind, sober roofer, and through hard work and thrift saves enough to open a laundry of her own, which prospers. Then Coupeau falls from a roof, and during his long recovery he takes to drink at the local bar, the Assommoir; idleness, debt and alcohol slowly drag the family down, and when Lantier returns, everything Gervaise has built begins to fall apart.
context: Émile Zola (1840–1902) published the novel in 1877 as part of his Rougon-Macquart cycle, and its frank picture of working-class life and drink, written in the slang of the Paris streets, caused a scandal and made him rich. Gervaise's daughter is the heroine of Nana, and her son Étienne the hero of [Germinal](/book/327?lang=en). See also [Thérèse Raquin](/book/329?lang=en).

about: Tartar rebels under the ruthless Feofar Khan, helped by the traitor Ivan Ogareff, have invaded Siberia and cut the telegraph lines. The Tsar must warn his brother, the Grand Duke, besieged in the city of Irkutsk, that Ogareff is coming to betray him, and he chooses Michael Strogoff, a young courier of extraordinary strength and courage, who must cross more than five thousand kilometres of Siberia in disguise, through rivers, forests and enemy armies, together with a brave young woman, Nadia, and two quarrelling foreign journalists.
context: Jules Verne published the novel in 1876. Though it has no science fiction, it is one of his most exciting adventures and was a huge success on the stage; the scene in which Strogoff is condemned to be blinded with a red-hot blade is a classic of suspense. Read Verne's [Around the World in Eighty Days](/book/122?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/verne?lang=en).

about: A young writer, nameless and starving, wanders the streets of Kristiania, today's Oslo, trying to sell articles to newspapers. Too proud to beg and too stubborn to give up, he pawns his waistcoat, chews wood shavings, tells absurd lies to strangers and swings between despair and wild exaltation, as hunger sharpens his mind into strange, feverish states. He tells it all in the first person, with a frankness never seen before.
context: Knut Hamsun (1859–1952) based the novel, published in 1890, on his own years of poverty, and it is often called the first modern psychological novel; Isaac Bashevis Singer said that the whole modern school of fiction stems from Hamsun. He won the Nobel Prize in 1920, but later disgraced himself by supporting the Nazi occupation of Norway. This is George Egerton's translation of 1899, in a slightly shortened later printing.

about: Nils Holgersson, a lazy, mischievous fourteen-year-old farm boy in southern Sweden who torments animals, is shrunk by an elf to the size of a thumb. When the family's tame white gander flies off to join a flock of wild geese, Nils clings to its neck, and he travels with the flock, led by the wise old goose Akka, the whole length of Sweden to Lapland and back, learning the speech of the animals, the history and geography of his country and, slowly, kindness.
context: Selma Lagerlöf (1858–1940) wrote the book in 1906 and 1907 at the request of Swedish teachers who wanted a geography reader for schools, and it became a classic of children's literature around the world. In 1909 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. This translation is by Velma Swanston Howard. Compare [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en).

about: Emil Sinclair, a boy from a respectable, pious family, is drawn into lies and fear by a bully, and is rescued by a mysterious older schoolmate, Max Demian, who teaches him to question everything he has been told about good and evil. As Sinclair grows into a young man, through loneliness, drink and religious searching, Demian's ideas, and the image of a bird breaking out of its egg towards the god Abraxas, in whom good and evil are united, guide him towards his true self, until the First World War breaks out.
context: Hermann Hesse published the novel in 1919 under the pen name Emil Sinclair, after undergoing Jungian psychoanalysis, and it became a cult book for the generation that came home from the war: 'The bird fights its way out of the egg. The egg is the world. Who would be born must first destroy a world.' This is the first English translation, of 1923. Read [Siddhartha](/book/2649?lang=en).

about: In 1628, in a village near Lake Como, the young silk weaver Renzo and the gentle Lucia are about to marry when the village priest, Don Abbondio, is threatened by the thugs of a powerful nobleman, Don Rodrigo, who has made a bet that he will have Lucia, and the wedding is called off. The lovers flee and are separated: Lucia takes refuge in a convent under the protection of a mysterious nun, while Renzo is caught up in the bread riots of Milan, and both must survive famine, war and the great plague of 1630.
context: Alessandro Manzoni (1785–1873) published the novel in 1827 and revised it in 1840, rewriting it in the Florentine Italian that became the model for the modern language. It is the most widely read novel in Italian, studied by every Italian schoolchild, and its account of the plague is unforgettable. Compare Scott's [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en) and Defoe's [A Journal of the Plague Year](/book/679?lang=en).

about: Olenka, 'the darling', is a gentle, loving woman who cannot live without someone to love and who takes on all the opinions of whoever she loves: first a theatre manager, then a timber merchant, then a veterinary surgeon, and at last a little schoolboy. Tolstoy loved the story and read it aloud again and again. This first volume of Constance Garnett's translations of Anton Chekhov's tales also includes 'Ariadne', 'Anyuta', 'The Two Volodyas', 'An Artist's Story' and the short novel 'Three Years'.
context: Chekhov (1860–1904), a doctor who wrote hundreds of stories as well as plays such as The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard, changed the short story for ever with his quiet, open endings and his refusal to judge his characters. Constance Garnett (1861–1946) brought him and the other great Russian writers to English readers. Read also Turgenev's [First Love](/book/51638?lang=en).

about: Imprisoned at Pavia and awaiting execution on a charge of treason he denied, the Roman statesman Boethius is visited in his cell by a majestic woman, Lady Philosophy, who drives away the Muses of poetry that have been feeding his self-pity. In five books of alternating prose and verse, she reminds him that Fortune is a turning wheel that gives and takes away, that true happiness lies not in wealth, power or fame but in the highest good, which is God, and she reconciles God's foreknowledge with human free will.
context: Boethius (about 477–524), a scholar who had served the Ostrogothic king Theodoric in Italy, wrote the book shortly before his death. It became one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages, translated into English by King Alfred and by Chaucer, and its image of Fortune's wheel echoes through medieval literature. This Loeb edition by H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand also contains his theological tractates. Compare the Stoic [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en).

about: In On Old Age, Cato the Elder, in his eighty-fourth year, talks with two young friends and answers the four reasons people give for thinking old age miserable: that it withdraws us from active life, weakens the body, takes away pleasures and brings death near. With warmth and wit he shows that each can be met with dignity. In On Friendship, Laelius, mourning his great friend Scipio, explains what true friendship is: a bond possible only between good people, founded on virtue rather than usefulness.
context: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Rome's greatest orator and a statesman later killed on the orders of Mark Antony, wrote both dialogues in 44 BC, in the troubled months around the murder of Julius Caesar. They have been among the best-loved works of Latin prose for two thousand years. This translation is by Evelyn Shuckburgh. Compare the [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en) of Marcus Aurelius.

about: In the Tusculan Disputations, written at his country house at Tusculum after the death of his beloved daughter Tullia, Cicero discusses in five books how to face death, endure pain, master grief and the other disturbances of the mind, and whether virtue alone is enough for a happy life. On the Nature of the Gods sets an Epicurean, a Stoic and a sceptic arguing over whether the gods exist and whether they care for humanity. The volume also includes what survives of On the Commonwealth, with its famous 'Dream of Scipio'.
context: Cicero wrote the Disputations and On the Nature of the Gods in 45 BC, when he had been pushed out of politics, to make Greek philosophy available in Latin, and in doing so he created much of the philosophical vocabulary of Latin, and through it of modern European languages. On the Commonwealth, written a decade earlier, was largely lost until parts were found in a Vatican manuscript in 1819. This translation is chiefly by C. D. Yonge. Read also his [Treatises on Friendship and Old Age](/book/2942?lang=en).

about: In the Germania, Tacitus describes the tribes living beyond the Rhine and the Danube: their land, their warriors and assemblies, their gods, marriages and hospitality, often holding up their simple, hardy virtues as a reproach to the luxury of Rome. The Agricola is a short life of his father-in-law, Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the general who completed the Roman conquest of much of Britain, and it contains the famous speech of the Caledonian chieftain Calgacus against Rome: 'They make a desert and call it peace.'
context: Cornelius Tacitus (about 56–120), the greatest Roman historian, wrote both works around AD 98. The Germania later became enormously important, sometimes dangerously so, to Germans looking for a portrait of their ancestors, and the Agricola is one of the earliest accounts of Britain. This is the revised Oxford translation, with an introduction by Edward Brooks Jr. Compare [Caesar's Gallic War](/book/9772?lang=en).

about: 'All Gaul is divided into three parts.' In these clear, rapid commentaries, written in the third person, Julius Caesar tells the story of his conquest of Gaul between 58 and 50 BC: his campaigns against the Helvetii and the Germans, his bridge across the Rhine, his two expeditions to Britain, and finally the great revolt led by Vercingetorix, which ended with the siege of Alesia. The volume also contains the commentaries on the civil war that followed, in which Caesar fought Pompey for control of Rome.
context: Caesar (100–44 BC) wrote the commentaries both as a record of his deeds and as political propaganda for readers in Rome, and their plain, elegant Latin made them the first book read by generations of students. This translation is by W. A. McDevitte. Compare Xenophon's [Anabasis](/book/1409?lang=en) and [Tacitus](/book/7510?lang=en).

about: Flavius Josephus tells the history of the great Jewish revolt against Rome: its background under the Maccabees and Herod the Great, the outbreak of war in AD 66, the campaigns of Vespasian in Galilee, where Josephus himself commanded the rebel forces until his surrender at Jotapata, and the terrible siege of Jerusalem by Titus in AD 70, which ended with the burning of the Temple. It closes with the fall of the desert fortress of Masada.
context: Josephus (37–about 100), born into a priestly family in Jerusalem, went over to the Romans, took the family name of the emperors and wrote the book in Rome as a witness to events he had lived through. It is the main source for the history of the region in the first century. This is the classic translation of 1737 by William Whiston. Compare [Tacitus](/book/7510?lang=en).

about: This short treatise traces how the government of Athens developed, from the early kings and archons through the reforms of Draco, Solon, Cleisthenes and Pericles to the full democracy of the fourth century BC, and then describes how that democracy worked: how citizens were registered, how officials were chosen by lot, how the council and the law courts operated, and how jurors were paid.
context: Long known only from quotations, the work was recovered from papyrus rolls found in Egypt and published in 1891 by Frederic Kenyon of the British Museum, whose translation this is, to the excitement of scholars everywhere. It is thought to have been written by Aristotle or one of his students around 330 BC, as one of 158 studies of the constitutions of Greek states. Read Aristotle's [Politics](/book/84?lang=en).

about: Three friends discuss whether we can know anything about God from the world around us. Cleanthes argues that the order of nature, like a great machine, proves the existence of an intelligent designer; Demea, a pious believer, insists that God's nature lies beyond human understanding; and Philo, a sceptic, takes the argument from design apart piece by piece, asking why an imperfect, suffering world should point to a perfect and all-good creator.
context: David Hume (1711–1776), the Scottish philosopher, worked on the Dialogues for more than twenty-five years but held them back, fearing the scandal they would cause; they were published in 1779, three years after his death. They remain the classic critique of the argument from design. Read Hume's [Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding](/book/277?lang=en).

about: Hylas, who believes in the ordinary idea of material things existing outside the mind, meets Philonous, whose name means 'lover of mind', on three morning walks. Step by step Philonous leads him to admit that colours, sounds, heat, shape and even solidity exist only as they are perceived, and argues that there is no need for any unperceived 'matter' at all: to be is to be perceived, and the world exists continuously in the mind of God.
context: George Berkeley (1685–1753), an Irish philosopher and later Bishop of Cloyne, published the dialogues in 1713 to present in a readable form the startling theory he had set out in his Principles of Human Knowledge. Samuel Johnson famously kicked a large stone and declared, 'I refute it thus.' Compare [Hume's Enquiry](/book/277?lang=en), and read Descartes's [Meditations](/book/63980?lang=en).

about: If God is all-good and all-powerful, why is there evil in the world? Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz answers that God, choosing among all possible worlds, created the best one possible: a world in which some evils are the necessary price of greater goods, such as freedom. He defends the harmony of faith and reason, examines free will and necessity, and argues at length against the French sceptic Pierre Bayle.
context: Leibniz (1646–1716), the German philosopher and mathematician who invented the calculus at the same time as Newton, published the book in French in 1710, and it gave the word 'theodicy' to the language. Voltaire mocked its optimism in [Candide](/book/279?lang=en) through the tutor Pangloss, who insists that all is for the best. This translation is by E. M. Huggard.

about: What is the best form of government? John Stuart Mill argues that it is representative democracy, because it protects people's rights and helps them grow into active, thoughtful citizens. He then examines its dangers, the tyranny of the majority, incompetent rulers and the influence of narrow class interests, and proposes remedies, among them proportional representation, extra votes for the educated and the vote for women.
context: Published in 1861, between [On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en) and [The Subjection of Women](/book/266?lang=en), the book is one of the founding texts of modern democratic theory. Mill (1806–1873) later sat in Parliament, where in 1867 he proposed giving women the vote. Read also his [Autobiography](/book/9548?lang=en).

about: John Stuart Mill tells the story of the most famous education of the nineteenth century: taught at home by his father, the philosopher James Mill, he began Greek at three and Latin at eight, and had read much of classical literature, history and logic before he was twelve. At twenty he fell into a deep depression, from which he recovered partly by reading Wordsworth's poetry, and learned that feeling must be cultivated as well as reason. He describes his friendship and marriage with Harriet Taylor, whom he calls the greatest influence on his thought.
context: Mill wrote the book in his last years, and it was published in 1873, the year of his death. It is a classic of intellectual autobiography. Read his [On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en) and [Utilitarianism](/book/265?lang=en).

about: Four years after Darwin's [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en), Thomas Henry Huxley took on the question Darwin had avoided: where do human beings fit in nature? Comparing the skeletons, brains and development of humans with those of gorillas, chimpanzees and other apes, he argues that the differences between humans and the great apes are smaller than those between the great apes and the lower monkeys, so that humans share a common ancestry with them. He also discusses the fossil skull recently found in the Neander valley in Germany.
context: Huxley (1825–1895), the biologist known as 'Darwin's bulldog' for his fierce defence of evolution, published the book in 1863, and its frontispiece showing the skeletons of apes and a man in a row became one of the most reproduced images in science. Read Darwin's [The Descent of Man](/book/146?lang=en).

about: In the winter of 1609 and 1610, Galileo Galilei turned a telescope he had built himself to the night sky and saw what no one had seen before: mountains and valleys on the Moon, which was not a perfect sphere; countless stars invisible to the naked eye, which make up the Milky Way; and four 'stars' near Jupiter that moved night after night, which he realised were moons circling the planet. This short book, published in March 1610, announces those discoveries.
context: Galileo (1564–1642) named Jupiter's moons the 'Medicean stars' after the Medici, who soon became his patrons. The discovery that bodies could circle something other than the Earth was strong evidence for the Sun-centred system of Copernicus, and set Galileo on the road to his trial by the Inquisition. This is the 1880 translation by Edward Stafford Carlos. Compare Einstein's [Relativity](/book/5064?lang=en).

about: Sartor Resartus, 'the tailor re-tailored', presents itself as an English editor's commentary on a vast, chaotic German book about the philosophy of clothes, written by an eccentric professor, Diogenes Teufelsdröckh, of the University of Weissnichtwo, 'Know-not-where'. Clothes, it argues, are only symbols: institutions, customs and even the body are garments of the spirit. Through the professor's confused life story, the book tells of a passage from the 'Everlasting No' of despair to the 'Everlasting Yea' of faith and work.
context: Thomas Carlyle published the book as a magazine serial in 1833 and 1834. Strange, comic and visionary, it influenced Emerson and the American Transcendentalists, who brought it out as a book before it appeared in Britain. Read Carlyle's [The French Revolution](/book/1529?lang=en).

about: In the winter of 1878 and 1879, Lady Anne Blunt and her husband, the poet Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, set out from Damascus with a small caravan across the Nafud, the great red-sand desert of northern Arabia, to reach the oasis town of Ha'il, capital of the powerful Emir Muhammad ibn Rashid of the Shammar. She describes Bedouin hospitality, the dangers of the desert crossing, the emir's court and his famous horses, with drawings of her own. This is the first of two volumes; the second tells of their return through Iraq and Persia.
context: Lady Anne Blunt (1837–1917), a granddaughter of Lord Byron, was among the first European women to travel in central Arabia, and she learned Arabic thoroughly. She and her husband founded the Crabbet Arabian Stud in England, which preserved bloodlines of Arabian horses still bred today. Compare Lane's [Arabian Society in the Middle Ages](/book/36996?lang=en).

about: Khalid, a young dreamer from Baalbek in Lebanon, emigrates to New York with his friend Shakib at the end of the nineteenth century. In the cellars of lower Manhattan they peddle trinkets and holy pictures; Khalid reads hungrily, turns to poetry and politics and is drawn into the corruption of American elections. Returning home, he preaches a new faith that would unite East and West, the spirituality of the Orient with the science and freedom of the West, and his preaching stirs up trouble in the Ottoman lands.
context: Ameen Rihani (1876–1940), born in Freike in Mount Lebanon, published the book in New York in 1911 with illustrations by Kahlil Gibran, and it is considered the first novel in English by an Arab author. Rihani, who also wrote in Arabic and travelled widely in Arabia, is often called the father of Arab-American literature. Read Gibran's [The Prophet](/book/98?lang=en).

about: This is Abu Hamid al-Ghazali's famous spiritual autobiography, known in Arabic as al-Munqidh min al-Dalal, 'Deliverance from Error'. He tells how, as a celebrated professor in Baghdad, he was seized by doubt about whether anything could be known with certainty, and examined in turn the theologians, the philosophers, the Batinis who followed a hidden teacher, and the Sufis. After a crisis in which he could no longer speak to teach, he left his post and his wealth to follow the Sufi path, where he found certainty through direct experience.
context: Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), born in Tus in Khorasan, is one of the most influential thinkers in the history of Islam, known as Hujjat al-Islam, 'the Proof of Islam'. This short English version by Claud Field was published in 1909 in the Wisdom of the East series. Compare Ibn Tufayl's [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/14976?lang=en) and Saint Augustine's [Confessions](/book/3417?lang=en).

about: In two long stays between 1825 and 1835, the English scholar Edward William Lane lived in Cairo, dressing as an Egyptian, speaking Arabic and living among the people under the name Mansur Effendi. This book is his detailed record of their daily life: houses and dress, childhood and education, religion and law, the government of Muhammad Ali Pasha, manners and etiquette, festivals and the month of Ramadan, superstitions, music, the storytellers of the coffee houses, weddings and funerals, illustrated with his own drawings.
context: Lane (1801–1876) first published the book in 1836, and it remains one of the most valuable descriptions of Egyptian life before modern times, although it reflects the views of a European observer. He later translated the Thousand and One Nights and compiled a great Arabic–English Lexicon. This is a Ward, Lock edition of 1890. Read his [Arabian Society in the Middle Ages](/book/36996?lang=en).

about: While translating the Thousand and One Nights, Edward William Lane wrote long notes explaining the world behind the stories, and in this book his great-nephew Stanley Lane-Poole gathered them into a portrait of medieval Arab society: belief in jinn, magic, astrology and alchemy, religion and the festivals of Islam, literature and storytellers, food and drink, music, slaves and women, marriage, the education of children, and funeral rites.
context: Lane-Poole (1854–1931), himself a historian of the Muslim world, published the collection in 1883. It is sometimes criticised for using the Egyptian customs of Lane's own day to explain the medieval past, but it is still a vivid guide to the background of the Nights. Compare [The Arabian Nights Entertainments](/book/479?lang=en) and Lane's [Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians](/book/64633?lang=en).

about: 'We all have strength enough to bear the misfortunes of others.' In some five hundred short maxims, François de La Rochefoucauld strips the masks from human behaviour to show self-love, amour-propre, hidden behind almost every virtue: our generosity is often vanity, our humility a way of being praised, our gratitude a hope of future favours. 'Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised.'
context: La Rochefoucauld (1613–1680), a French nobleman who had fought and plotted against Cardinal Mazarin in the civil wars of the Fronde, polished his maxims in the literary salons of Paris and published them in 1665. Witty, cynical and exact, they influenced moralists from Voltaire to Nietzsche. This translation is by J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell. Compare [Pascal's Pensées](/book/16334?lang=en).

about: The grasshopper who sang all summer and must beg from the ant in winter; the crow who drops his cheese when the fox praises his voice; the tortoise who beats the hare; the wolf who finds an excuse to eat the lamb, because 'the reason of the strongest is always the best'. In some 240 verse fables, Jean de La Fontaine retells and reinvents tales from Aesop and Phaedrus, turning animals into sharp portraits of the courtiers, kings and ordinary people of seventeenth-century France.
context: La Fontaine (1621–1695) published his Fables in twelve books between 1668 and 1694, and generations of French children have learned them by heart. Several of his later fables come from Kalila wa Dimna, the fables that Ibn al-Muqaffa' carried into Arabic from the Indian Panchatantra, which reached him through a French version of a Persian retelling. This is the American translation by Elizur Wright. Compare [The Arabian Nights Entertainments](/book/479?lang=en).

about: The Chevalier des Grieux, a promising seventeen-year-old student from a noble family, meets the beautiful young Manon Lescaut at an inn in Amiens as she is being sent to a convent, and elopes with her to Paris the same day. Manon loves him, but she loves pleasure and money even more, and again and again she leaves him for richer men, while he, unable to give her up, sinks into cheating at cards, prison and disgrace, until she is deported to the French colony of Louisiana and he follows her.
context: Antoine François Prévost (1697–1763), known as the abbé Prévost, a former monk and adventurer, published the story in 1731 as part of a longer novel, and it was seized in Paris as immoral. It became one of the most famous love stories in French literature and inspired operas by Massenet and Puccini. Compare [Camille](/book/1825?lang=en) by Dumas fils.

about: On the tropical island of Mauritius, then the French Île de France, two young mothers living apart from French society raise their children, Paul and Virginia, together in a remote valley, far from the corruption of civilisation. The two grow up in innocent love among the forests and mountains, until Virginia is sent to France by a rich aunt to be educated and married, and her voyage home brings the story to its famous storm.
context: Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre (1737–1814), a disciple of Rousseau who had lived on Mauritius, published the novel in 1788, and it was one of the best-selling books of its age, admired by Napoleon. Its lush descriptions of tropical nature influenced the Romantic writers. Compare [Atala](/book/40111?lang=en) by Chateaubriand.

about: In the forests of Louisiana in the early eighteenth century, the old blind Natchez chief Chactas tells a young Frenchman, René, the story of his youth: captured by an enemy tribe and condemned to death, he was freed by Atala, the beautiful Christian daughter of the enemy chief, and the two fled together through the wilderness. They found refuge with an old missionary, Father Aubry, but Atala was bound by a vow made by her dying mother, which stood between them.
context: François-René de Chateaubriand (1768–1848), who had travelled in America in 1791, published the short novel in 1801, and its dreamy, exotic descriptions of nature and its mixture of passion and Christian feeling made it a founding work of French Romanticism. This edition has illustrations by Gustave Doré. Compare [Paul and Virginia](/book/2314?lang=en).

about: Raphaël de Valentin, a ruined young man in Paris, is about to throw himself into the Seine when he wanders into an antique shop, where a mysterious old dealer offers him a talisman: a piece of wild ass's skin inscribed with the promise that it will grant his every wish. But each wish makes the skin shrink, and with it the length of his life. Raphaël becomes immensely rich overnight, and then, terrified, tries to stop wishing for anything at all.
context: Honoré de Balzac published the novel in 1831, and it made him famous; he later placed it at the head of the 'philosophical studies' of his Human Comedy, as a fable about the price of desire. This translation is by Ellen Marriage. Read also [Father Goriot](/book/1471?lang=en) and [Lost Illusions](/book/11818?lang=en).

about: Lucien Chardon, a handsome, gifted young poet in the provincial town of Angoulême, is taken up by an aristocratic lady, Madame de Bargeton, and follows her to Paris, dreaming of literary fame. There he discovers a world of journalism where reviews are bought and sold and reputations are made and destroyed overnight, and talent counts for less than intrigue. Torn between a circle of honest young writers who befriend him and the corrupt press, he chooses success and pays dearly, while at home his loyal friend David Séchard, a printer and inventor, is ruined.
context: Honoré de Balzac published the three parts of the novel, Two Poets, A Distinguished Provincial at Paris and Eve and David, all included here, between 1837 and 1843, and he considered it the centrepiece of his Human Comedy. Its portrait of the press is among the sharpest ever written. This translation is by Ellen Marriage. Read also [Father Goriot](/book/1471?lang=en).

about: Sylvain Pons, an elderly, ugly and kind-hearted musician who was once a minor composer, has two passions: good dinners, for which he depends on invitations from his rich relatives, and his collection of paintings and fine objects, bought cheaply over a lifetime. His relatives despise him and close their doors to him, until they discover that his collection is worth a fortune, and then, as Pons falls ill in the care of his devoted friend, the German pianist Schmucke, a crowd of greedy schemers gathers around his bed.
context: Published in 1847, this was one of the last novels Balzac completed, written together with Cousin Bette under the title The Poor Relations. It is a moving tale of friendship and a ferocious satire of greed. This translation is by Ellen Marriage. Read also [Father Goriot](/book/1471?lang=en).

about: Marguerite Gautier, the most beautiful and expensive courtesan in Paris, who always carries a bouquet of camellias, falls truly in love with Armand Duval, a young man of good family and modest means. She gives up her luxurious life to live quietly with him in the country, until Armand's father comes to her in secret and begs her to give him up for the sake of his family's honour. Already gravely ill with tuberculosis, she makes the sacrifice, and Armand, believing she has betrayed him, takes a cruel revenge.
context: Alexandre Dumas fils (1824–1895), son of the author of The Three Musketeers, based the novel, published in 1848, on his own affair with the courtesan Marie Duplessis, who died at twenty-three. His stage version inspired Verdi's opera La Traviata. Compare [Manon Lescaut](/book/768?lang=en).

about: In the Egyptian desert of the fourth century, Paphnuce, a holy hermit who has renounced the world, is haunted by the memory of Thaïs, the most celebrated actress and courtesan of Alexandria, and resolves to save her soul. He goes to the city, converts her and leads her to a convent in the desert. But back in his solitude he cannot stop thinking of her beauty, and his faith gives way to an obsession that consumes him.
context: Anatole France (1844–1924), the ironic French master who won the Nobel Prize in 1921, published the novel in 1890. Its picture of late Roman Alexandria, with a famous banquet at which philosophers of every school debate, and its gentle mockery of fanaticism inspired Massenet's opera. This translation is by Robert B. Douglas. Read also France's [Penguin Island](/book/2127?lang=en).

about: A short-sighted old saint, Maël, drifting at sea in a stone trough, lands on an island of great auks and, mistaking them for people, baptises them. The baptism causes such confusion in heaven that God turns the birds into human beings, and Anatole France then tells the whole history of the Penguins, a parody of the history of France: its legends and saints, kings and revolutions, wars, a scandal that is a thinly disguised Dreyfus Affair, and finally a modern world of financiers and anarchists.
context: Published in 1908, the satire is one of France's most celebrated books, and its mockery of nationalism, the Church and the army has lost little of its bite. Read also his [Thaïs](/book/2268?lang=en), and compare [Gulliver's Travels](/book/302?lang=en).

about: Jean des Esseintes, the last, sickly descendant of an ancient noble family, disgusted with Paris and with people, retires to a house outside the city to live entirely for refined sensations. He decorates his rooms in exotic colours, sets precious stones into the shell of a living tortoise, builds an 'organ' of liqueurs that he plays on his tongue, collects strange flowers and perfumes, and reads only the decadent Latin poets and the most refined modern writers, until his nerves give way.
context: Joris-Karl Huysmans (1848–1907) published the novel, À rebours, in 1884, and it became the bible of the Decadent movement; it is the poisonous yellow book that corrupts the hero of Oscar Wilde's [The Picture of Dorian Gray](/book/62?lang=en). This translation is by John Howard. Compare Baudelaire's [The Flowers of Evil](/book/32375?lang=en).

about: Charles Baudelaire's poems move from the poet's spleen, boredom and sense of exile in a fallen world, through love, beauty and sensual pleasure, to the streets of modern Paris, wine, revolt and finally death, which he greets as a last voyage into the unknown. In them perfumes, colours and sounds answer one another, the poet is an albatross mocked on the deck of a ship, and the reader is addressed as 'hypocrite reader, my likeness, my brother'.
context: When the book appeared in 1857, Baudelaire (1821–1867) and his publisher were prosecuted for offending public morals, and six poems were banned. It is now seen as the first great book of modern poetry. This edition is a selection translated by the composer Cyril Scott in 1909. Compare [Against the Grain](/book/11135?lang=en), and T. S. Eliot's [The Waste Land](/book/1549?lang=en), which quotes it.

about: Jerusalem, during the Third Crusade. A young Knight Templar, spared by Sultan Saladin because he resembles the sultan's lost brother, rescues Recha, the adopted daughter of the rich Jewish merchant Nathan, from a fire. Saladin, short of money, summons Nathan and tries to trap him with a question: which of the three religions, Judaism, Christianity or Islam, is the true one? Nathan answers with the parable of the three rings, in which a father who cannot choose between his three sons has two perfect copies made of his precious ring, so that no one can tell which is the original.
context: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781), a leading figure of the German Enlightenment, published the play in 1779 as a plea for religious tolerance, and it was not staged until after his death. The ring parable comes from Boccaccio's Decameron. This translation is by William Taylor, edited by Henry Morley. Compare Scott's [The Talisman](/book/1602?lang=en), which also portrays Saladin.

about: Gustav von Aschenbach, a famous, disciplined German writer in his fifties, worn out by years of work, takes a holiday in Venice. At his hotel on the Lido he sees a beautiful Polish boy of about fourteen, Tadzio, and falls into a silent, consuming fascination with him, which he dresses up in thoughts of Greek ideals of beauty. Although he learns that cholera is spreading secretly through the city, he cannot bring himself to leave.
context: Thomas Mann (1875–1955), who won the Nobel Prize in 1929, published the novella in 1912; it is a study of an artist's discipline breaking down before passion and death. This translation, by the American critic Kenneth Burke, appeared in 1925. Visconti filmed it in 1971 and Britten made it an opera. Compare Hesse's [Steppenwolf](/book/69207?lang=en).

about: Harry Haller, a lonely, middle-aged intellectual who feels split between a refined bourgeois man and a savage 'wolf of the steppes', takes rooms in a respectable house and contemplates suicide. Then he is handed a strange little 'Treatise on the Steppenwolf' that describes his own soul, and meets Hermine, a young woman who teaches him to dance, introduces him to jazz, pleasure and the saxophonist Pablo, and finally leads him into the Magic Theatre, 'for madmen only', where the many selves within him are revealed.
context: Hermann Hesse published the novel in 1927, at fifty, out of his own crisis, and it became a cult book again in the 1960s, even giving its name to a rock band. This is Basil Creighton's translation of 1929. Read [Siddhartha](/book/2649?lang=en) and [Demian](/book/67930?lang=en).

about: Paul Bäumer and his classmates are persuaded by their patriotic schoolmaster to volunteer for the German army in the First World War. At the front in France, under shelling, gas attacks and hunger, their youth and their illusions are destroyed, and the only things that matter are survival and comradeship, above all with the resourceful older soldier Katczinsky. When Paul goes home on leave, he finds he can no longer talk to anyone who has not been there.
context: Erich Maria Remarque (1898–1970), who was wounded in the war, published the novel in 1929, and it sold millions of copies within months. The Nazis burned it and later stripped him of his German citizenship. This is A. W. Wheen's English translation of the same year. Compare Wilfred Owen's [Poems](/book/1291?lang=en) and Hemingway's [A Farewell to Arms](/book/68678?lang=en).

about: While Charlemagne's Christian knights defend Paris against the Saracen armies of Agramante, king of Africa, the beautiful princess Angelica of Cathay is pursued by half the knights of Europe. When she marries a humble Saracen soldier, Medoro, the great paladin Orlando goes mad with jealousy and runs naked across Europe and Africa, until his friend Astolfo travels to the Moon to bring back his lost wits in a flask. Around them weave dozens of tales of love, magic and war, above all the love of the Christian warrior maiden Bradamante for the Saracen knight Ruggiero.
context: Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) published the poem, a continuation of Boiardo's unfinished Orlando Innamorato, in its final form of 46 cantos in 1532. Ironic, inventive and endlessly entertaining, it was the bestseller of the Italian Renaissance and inspired Spenser, Cervantes and countless painters and composers. This is the complete verse translation by William Stewart Rose. Compare [The Song of Roland](/book/694?lang=en).

about: In the last year of the First Crusade, the Christian army under Godfrey of Bouillon besieges Jerusalem. Torquato Tasso's epic follows the campaign and the loves and adventures of its heroes: Rinaldo, who is lured away by the enchantress Armida to her magic garden; Tancredi, who loves the Muslim warrior maiden Clorinda and fights her in a night duel without recognising her; and Erminia, a Muslim princess who loves Tancredi. On the other side the defenders are led by the fierce Argante and the Sultan Solimano.
context: Tasso (1544–1595) published the poem in 1581, and it inspired operas by Monteverdi, Handel and Rossini. It tells the Crusade from the Christian point of view of its age, though its Muslim heroes are drawn with nobility. This is the celebrated English translation of 1600 by Edward Fairfax. Compare [Orlando Furioso](/book/912?lang=en) and Lessing's [Nathan the Wise](/book/3909?lang=en).

about: Enrico, a boy in the third grade at a school in Turin, keeps a diary through one school year in the early 1880s. He writes about his classmates, rich and poor, the brave, the bullies and the boy whose father is in prison; about his teachers; and he copies the letters of advice his parents write in his notebook. Each month his teacher reads a 'monthly story' of heroic children from every part of Italy, among them the famous 'From the Apennines to the Andes', about a boy who crosses the ocean to Argentina in search of his mother.
context: Edmondo De Amicis (1846–1908), a former army officer and journalist, published the book in 1886, and for generations it was one of the most read books in Italy, meant to unite the children of the newly unified country; it has been translated into many languages, Arabic among them. This translation is by Isabel Hapgood. Compare [Tom Brown's School Days](/book/1703?lang=en).

about: These twelve short novels by the author of Don Quixote are set in the Spain of his day: 'The Little Gipsy Girl', about a beautiful dancer for whom a young nobleman joins a band of gypsies; 'Rinconete and Cortadillo', two boy thieves who join a guild of criminals in Seville; 'The Licentiate Vidriera', a scholar who goes mad and believes he is made of glass; 'The Dialogue of the Dogs', in which two dogs in a hospital talk all night about their masters; and others of love, adventure and satire, among them 'The Generous Lover', set among the Turks in Cyprus.
context: Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) published the novels in 1613, between the two parts of [Don Quixote](/book/168?lang=en), and called them 'exemplary' because each, he said, held a useful lesson. Cervantes had himself been a captive in Algiers for five years, and the Mediterranean world of his life appears in several stories. This translation is by Walter K. Kelly.

about: Julio Desnoyers, the handsome, idle son of a rich Franco-Argentine family, lives a life of tango and love affairs in Paris with no interest in politics, while his German cousins are proud officers of the Kaiser. Then in August 1914 war breaks out, and the German armies sweep over the family's château on the Marne. A mysterious Russian philosopher, Tchernoff, sees in the war the four horsemen of the Apocalypse, conquest, war, plague and death, riding over Europe, and the family is torn apart as its members fight on opposite sides.
context: Vicente Blasco Ibáñez (1867–1928), a Spanish novelist and republican politician, published the novel in 1916, and in this English translation by Charlotte Brewster Jordan it became the best-selling novel in the United States in 1919. The 1921 film made Rudolph Valentino a star. Compare [All Quiet on the Western Front](/book/68493?lang=en).

about: Pepe Rey, a brilliant young engineer from Madrid with modern scientific ideas, comes to the old cathedral town of Orbajosa to marry his cousin Rosario, daughter of his aunt Doña Perfecta, a wealthy widow admired for her piety. But the town, ruled by tradition and by the canon Don Inocencio, sees him as an atheist and an intruder; his aunt, outwardly gentle, turns against him with ruthless determination, and the conflict between progress and fanaticism ends in tragedy.
context: Benito Pérez Galdós (1843–1920), the greatest Spanish novelist since Cervantes, published the novel in 1876, and its portrait of religious intolerance in provincial Spain caused a stir. This translation is by Mary J. Serrano. Compare Manzoni's [The Betrothed](/book/31509?lang=en).

about: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, a kind, intelligent and wealthy young landowner, lives in a flat in St Petersburg and hardly ever gets up from his sofa; the whole first part of the novel passes while he tries, and fails, to get out of bed. His energetic friend Stolz, half German, tries to rouse him, and he falls in love with the lively Olga, who wants to bring him back to life, but the pull of idleness and of his childhood dreams of the peaceful family estate, Oblomovka, is stronger than love.
context: Ivan Goncharov (1812–1891) published the novel in 1859, and 'Oblomovism' became the Russian word for idle, dreamy apathy. It is both a comedy and a sad portrait of a whole class of Russian gentry. This translation is by C. J. Hogarth. Compare Turgenev's [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en).

about: A rich American, never named, sets out at fifty-eight with his wife and daughter on a luxurious voyage to the Old World, having worked all his life and decided it is time to enjoy himself. On the great liner Atlantis and in the hotels of Naples and Capri everything is arranged for his comfort, until one evening, dressing for dinner in Capri, he suddenly collapses, and the hotel that served him so eagerly hurries to hide him away. This volume adds other stories by Ivan Bunin.
context: Bunin (1870–1953), who left Russia after the Revolution, became in 1933 the first Russian writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. This 1922 translation is by S. S. Koteliansky together with D. H. Lawrence and Leonard Woolf, and it was published by the Hogarth Press of Leonard and Virginia Woolf. Compare Tolstoy's [Master and Man](/book/1247?lang=en).

about: A poor shoemaker, Simon, finds a naked stranger shivering by a roadside shrine in winter and brings him home, though his wife is furious. The stranger, Michael, becomes his apprentice and smiles only three times in six years, each time when he learns one of the truths that God sent him to discover: what dwells in man, what is not given to man, and what men live by. The volume gathers other short tales Tolstoy wrote for ordinary readers in his later years.
context: Leo Tolstoy wrote these simple parables in the 1880s, after his religious conversion, drawing on folk tales and the Gospels, and they are among his most widely read works. This translation is by Louise and Aylmer Maude. Read also his [Master and Man](/book/1247?lang=en).

about: In the summer of 1853, at a country house near Moscow, Elena Stakhova, a serious, idealistic young woman, is courted by two young Russians: Bersenev, a gentle scholar, and Shubin, a talented, flighty sculptor. But she chooses Dmitri Insarov, a poor, determined Bulgarian student with one aim in life, to free his country from Ottoman rule. Against her family's wishes she marries him in secret and follows him towards the war that is about to begin.
context: Ivan Turgenev published the novel in 1860, on the eve of the great reforms in Russia, and its portrait of a woman choosing a life of purpose over comfort influenced a generation. This translation is by Constance Garnett. Read Turgenev's [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en).

about: At the fashionable German spa of Baden-Baden in 1862, Grigory Litvinov, a sensible young Russian who has studied agriculture abroad, is waiting for his fiancée, Tatyana, when he meets again Irina, the beautiful woman who jilted him ten years before and is now married to a general. Their old passion flares up again, while around them Russian expatriates talk endlessly about Russia's future, words that seem to Litvinov like so much smoke.
context: Ivan Turgenev published the novel in 1867, and its satire of both Slavophile conservatives and Westernising radicals angered almost everyone in Russia, Dostoevsky among them, who quarrelled with him over it. This translation is by Constance Garnett. Read also [On the Eve](/book/6901?lang=en).

about: In the 1870s, young Russian radicals 'go to the people', trying to rouse the peasants to revolution. Alexei Nezhdanov, the illegitimate son of a nobleman and a sensitive poet torn between art and politics, becomes a tutor in the house of a liberal official, falls in love with Marianna, a young relative of the family, and runs away with her to work for the cause. But the peasants do not understand them, and Nezhdanov comes to doubt everything.
context: Published in 1877, Turgenev's last and longest novel is a sympathetic but sceptical portrait of the populist movement; its title comes from its epigraph, which says that virgin soil must be turned up not by a plough that skims the surface but by one that digs deep. This translation is by R. S. Townsend. Read also [On the Eve](/book/6901?lang=en).

about: After years abroad and the betrayal of his frivolous wife, Fyodor Lavretsky returns to his country estate in provincial Russia, where he finds a 'nest of gentlefolk' still living in the old ways, and falls in love with Liza Kalitina, a pure, deeply religious young woman. Her old German music teacher, Lemm, composes music for their love. When news comes that his wife has died, happiness seems possible at last, but the past has not finished with him.
context: Ivan Turgenev published the novel in 1859, and it was his greatest popular success in Russia. This is W. R. S. Ralston's translation of 1869, published under the title Liza. Read [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en) and [On the Eve](/book/6901?lang=en).

about: This volume contains Anton Chekhov's last two great plays and six of his comic one-act 'vaudevilles'. In The Three Sisters, Olga, Masha and Irina, stranded in a provincial garrison town, dream endlessly of returning to Moscow while their lives slip away. In The Cherry Orchard, the charming, careless Madame Ranevsky returns from Paris to her family estate, which is about to be sold for debt, and cannot bring herself to save it by cutting down the beloved orchard. The farces include The Proposal, The Bear and The Wedding.
context: Chekhov wrote The Three Sisters in 1900 and The Cherry Orchard in 1903, the year before his death, and both were first staged by Stanislavsky's Moscow Art Theatre. Bernard Shaw said that every time he saw a Chekhov play he wanted to throw his own into the fire. This translation, with an introduction, is by Julius West. Read Chekhov's stories in [The Darling](/book/12036?lang=en).

about: Tamburlaine, a Scythian shepherd of boundless ambition, rises by force and charm to conquer the kingdoms of Asia: he wins over the Persian commander sent against him, overthrows the Persian king, defeats the Turkish emperor Bajazeth and carries him about in a cage, and takes as his bride Zenocrate, daughter of the Sultan of Egypt, whose city of Damascus he besieges. In thundering blank verse he declares that nothing can limit a man who aspires to 'the sweet fruition of an earthly crown'.
context: Christopher Marlowe wrote the play around 1587, and its 'mighty line' transformed English drama and prepared the way for Shakespeare. It is loosely based on the real Turkic conqueror Timur (1336–1405), who defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I near Ankara in 1402. This edition was edited by Alexander Dyce. Read Marlowe's [Doctor Faustus](/book/1061?lang=en).

about: At the court of Spain, after a war with Portugal, the young courtier Horatio, son of the old marshal Hieronimo, is murdered in a garden by his rivals in love and hanged from a tree, where his father finds him. Unable to obtain justice from the king, Hieronimo, half mad with grief, plans his revenge, which he carries out through a play performed before the whole court. The story is watched throughout by the ghost of a dead soldier and the spirit of Revenge.
context: Thomas Kyd (1558–1594) wrote the tragedy in the late 1580s, and it was one of the most popular plays of the Elizabethan stage, creating the revenge tragedy and the play within a play that [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en) would make immortal. Compare Marlowe's [Tamburlaine](/book/1343?lang=en).

about: This volume gathers John Milton's finest early poems. 'L'Allegro' and 'Il Penseroso' are a matching pair describing a day spent by the cheerful man and by the thoughtful man, from the morning lark to the music of the night. Comus is a masque, a court entertainment, in which a virtuous lady lost in a wood resists the enchanter Comus. Lycidas is an elegy for a drowned college friend, Edward King, which becomes a meditation on early death, fame and the corruption of the Church.
context: Milton wrote these poems in his twenties, between about 1631 and 1637, long before [Paradise Lost](/book/297?lang=en), and Lycidas is often called the greatest short poem in English. See [Milton's life](/author/milton?lang=en).

about: Parson Yorick, the hero of [Tristram Shandy](/book/1330?lang=en), sets off for France on an impulse, because someone has told him 'they order this matter better in France'. Instead of describing cathedrals and monuments, he records the small encounters and feelings of the road: a monk at Calais whom he treats unkindly and then regrets, a pretty glover's wife in Paris, a caged starling crying 'I can't get out', a lost passport, and many moments of tenderness, comedy and gentle flirtation.
context: Laurence Sterne published the book in 1768, a few weeks before his death, and it made 'sentimental' a fashionable word all over Europe. It is a playful answer to the stiff travel books of its day, especially Tobias Smollett's, whom Sterne mocks as 'Smelfungus'.

about: Rasselas, a prince of Abyssinia, lives with his brothers and sisters in the Happy Valley, a paradise enclosed by mountains where every pleasure is provided, yet he is not happy. With his sister Nekayah, her maid and the poet-philosopher Imlac, he escapes through a passage in the mountain and travels to Cairo to discover how to make the choice of a happy life. They meet philosophers, shepherds, hermits, the rich and the powerful, visit the pyramids and the catacombs, and learn that no way of life brings perfect happiness.
context: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784), the great English writer and lexicographer, is said to have written the tale in the evenings of a single week in 1759 to pay for his mother's funeral. A wise, melancholy fable, it appeared the same year as Voltaire's [Candide](/book/279?lang=en), which it often resembles. Compare [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/14976?lang=en).

about: Caleb Williams, a clever, curious young man of humble birth, becomes secretary to Ferdinando Falkland, a refined and generous country gentleman admired by everyone, who is nevertheless haunted by a secret sorrow. Caleb's curiosity leads him to uncover Falkland's terrible secret, and from that moment Falkland, using his wealth and the law, pursues him across England, framing him as a thief and hounding him through prisons and disguises.
context: William Godwin (1756–1836), the radical philosopher who married Mary Wollstonecraft and was the father of Mary Shelley, published the novel in 1794 to show how the laws and power of the rich crush the poor. It is often called one of the first crime thrillers. Read [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en), by his daughter.

about: In a gloomy, half-ruined abbey in the Lincolnshire fens live the melancholy Mr Glowry and his son Scythrop, a young man who reads German tragedies, drinks from a skull and plans to reform the world through secret societies, while hopelessly in love with two women at once. The house fills with guests who each embody a fashionable gloom of the day: Mr Flosky, a mystic philosopher no one can understand, Mr Cypress, a poet bitter about the world, and others.
context: Thomas Love Peacock (1785–1866) published this short comic novel in 1818, satirising the Romantic moods of his friends: Scythrop is a portrait of Percy Bysshe Shelley, Mr Flosky of Coleridge and Mr Cypress of Byron, and Shelley enjoyed the joke. Compare Jane Austen's [Northanger Abbey](/book/42?lang=en), another parody of Gothic fashion.

about: In early eighteenth-century Scotland, Robert Wringhim is raised by a fanatical Calvinist minister who teaches him that he is one of the elect, predestined for salvation whatever he does. Soon after he learns this, Robert meets a mysterious, charming stranger, Gil-Martin, who can take on the face of anyone and who persuades him that killing sinners is God's work. The story is told twice: first by an editor piecing together the events, then in Robert's own confession, found in his grave a century later.
context: James Hogg (1770–1835), known as 'the Ettrick Shepherd' because he had worked as a shepherd in the Scottish Borders, published the novel anonymously in 1824. Neglected for a century, it is now hailed as a masterpiece of psychological horror and a forerunner of [Jekyll and Hyde](/book/419?lang=en).

about: In four essays, John Ruskin attacks the economics of his day, which treated human beings as machines driven only by self-interest. He argues that 'there is no wealth but life', that employers owe duties to their workers just as soldiers and doctors owe duties to the public, and that a fair wage, not the lowest possible one, is a matter of justice. The title comes from the Gospel parable of the vineyard, in which the last workers hired are paid the same as the first. The volume adds other essays on political economy.
context: Ruskin (1819–1900), the great art critic, published the essays in a magazine in 1860, which stopped them after protests from readers. The book later inspired founders of the British Labour Party and changed the life of Mohandas Gandhi, who read it on a train in South Africa and translated it into Gujarati as Sarvodaya. Compare Adam Smith's [The Wealth of Nations](/book/3421?lang=en).

about: What can hold a society together when old authorities are weakening and everyone insists on 'doing as one likes'? Matthew Arnold's answer is culture, 'the best which has been thought and said in the world', a pursuit of 'sweetness and light' that should shape both individuals and the state. He divides the English classes into the aristocratic 'Barbarians', the middle-class 'Philistines', narrow and money-minded, and the 'Populace', and contrasts the 'Hebraism' of strict moral conscience with the 'Hellenism' of free, flexible thought.
context: Arnold (1822–1888), poet, critic and inspector of schools, published the essays as a book in 1869, during the debates over giving the vote to working men. Its phrases have shaped arguments about education and culture ever since. Compare [Mill's On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en).

about: John Henry Newman, the most famous English clergyman of his century to leave the Church of England for the Catholic Church, tells the history of his religious opinions: his evangelical boyhood, his years at Oxford as a leader of the Oxford Movement, which tried to recover the Catholic roots of Anglicanism, his growing doubts and his reception into the Catholic Church in 1845. He writes to show that he was honest at every step.
context: Newman (1801–1890) wrote the book in a few weeks in 1864, in reply to Charles Kingsley, the author of [The Water-Babies](/book/1276?lang=en), who had accused him of not caring for truth; its sincerity won over many readers who disagreed with him. He became a cardinal in 1879 and was declared a saint in 2019. Compare [The Confessions of St. Augustine](/book/3417?lang=en).

about: In sixty-three short lyrics, simple in form and haunting in effect, A. E. Housman speaks through a young man of the Shropshire countryside: of spring blossom and summer fairs, love and friendship, and above all of the brevity of youth, the soldiers who march away and do not return, and the young men who die before their time. 'Loveliest of trees, the cherry now / Is hung with bloom along the bough.'
context: Housman (1859–1936), a brilliant classical scholar who taught Latin in London and later at Cambridge, published the book at his own expense in 1896. Slow to sell at first, it became enormously popular, especially during the First World War, and many of its poems were set to music. Compare Wilfred Owen's [Poems](/book/1291?lang=en).

about: Wilfred Owen wrote almost all of these poems in the last year and a half of his life, as an officer on the Western Front and in hospital: 'Dulce et Decorum Est', with its soldier dying in a gas attack and its bitter rejection of 'the old Lie' that it is sweet to die for one's country; 'Anthem for Doomed Youth'; 'Strange Meeting', in which a dead soldier meets the enemy he killed; and others. 'My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.'
context: Owen (1893–1918) was killed in action a week before the Armistice, at twenty-five, when only five of his poems had been published. This first collection, of 1920, was edited by his friend Siegfried Sassoon, who wrote the introduction. Compare [All Quiet on the Western Front](/book/68493?lang=en).

about: Picking up where Typee left off, the narrator, rescued from the valley of the cannibals, joins the crew of an Australian whaler, the Julia, a leaky, run-down ship with a sick captain and a drunken mate. When the crew refuses to sail any further, they are thrown into a calabooza, a jail, on Tahiti, and the narrator and his eccentric friend Doctor Long Ghost wander the islands of Tahiti and Eimeo as beachcombers, observing the islanders, the missionaries and the European sailors.
context: Herman Melville (1819–1891) drew on his own adventures of 1842, including a real mutiny, and published the book in 1847 as a sequel to [Typee](/book/143?lang=en); 'omoo' is a Polynesian word for a wanderer from island to island. Read Melville's [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en).

about: In the title essay, an Old Man argues with a Young Man that human beings are machines, driven entirely by temperament, training and outside influences, and that every act, even the most generous, springs from the desire for one's own approval. The collection also includes 'The Death of Jean', Twain's grieving account of his youngest daughter's death on Christmas Eve 1909; 'Is Shakespeare Dead?', in which he doubts that the man from Stratford wrote the plays; and comic pieces on tobacco, the bicycle and bees.
context: Mark Twain printed 'What Is Man?' anonymously in 1906, so dark were its ideas, and this volume was published in 1917, after his death. Read his [The Mysterious Stranger](/book/3311?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: In 1895, bankrupt after bad investments, Mark Twain set off on a lecture tour around the world to pay his debts. This book records the journey: across the Pacific to Fiji, through Australia and New Zealand, then to India, where he marvels at Benares and the Taj Mahal, and on to South Africa, mixing comic stories, history and sharp observation with growing anger at the cruelties of colonialism. Each chapter opens with a maxim from 'Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar'.
context: Published in 1897, after the death of his daughter Susy in 1896 while he was abroad, it is the last and most serious of Twain's travel books. Read [The Innocents Abroad](/book/52?lang=en) and [Roughing It](/book/3302?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: Silas Lapham, a rough, honest Vermont farm boy who has made a fortune from a mineral paint found on his father's land, wants to rise in Boston society, and begins building a grand house in the fashionable Back Bay. His family becomes entangled with the Coreys, an old, cultured and impoverished Boston family, whose son Tom seems to be courting the pretty younger Lapham daughter, Irene, but in fact loves the plain, witty elder one, Penelope. Meanwhile a business deal tests Lapham's conscience.
context: William Dean Howells (1837–1920), editor of The Atlantic Monthly and the great champion of American realism, published the novel in 1885, and its story of a self-made man's moral test is his best-known book. Compare Trollope's [The Way We Live Now](/book/5283?lang=en).

about: In the San Joaquin Valley of California in the 1880s, wheat farmers led by the proud rancher Magnus Derrick have built prosperous ranches on land they expected to buy cheaply from the railroad, which controls freight rates, politicians and newspapers like an octopus. When the railroad raises the price of the land and sends marshals to evict them, the conflict ends in bloodshed. A young poet, Presley, who has come to write an epic of the West, watches it all.
context: Frank Norris published the novel in 1901, basing it on the real Mussel Slough tragedy of 1880, when settlers were killed in a land dispute with the Southern Pacific Railroad. It is a powerful work of American naturalism. Compare Norris's [McTeague](/book/503?lang=en) and Upton Sinclair's [The Jungle](/book/486?lang=en).

about: As a teenager in the 1890s, Jack London left home to ride the rails across America as a hobo, and here he tells how it was done: begging for meals at back doors with invented life stories, 'holding down' trains by riding underneath the carriages and on their roofs, dodging brakemen and railway police, and joining Kelly's army of unemployed men on its way to Washington in 1894. He also tells of thirty days in the brutal Erie County Penitentiary in New York for vagrancy.
context: London published these sketches in 1907, and they inspired later writers of the road such as Jack Kerouac. They show the experiences that made him a socialist. Read [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en) and [The Iron Heel](/book/1403?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/london?lang=en).

about: Jennie Gerhardt, the gentle, beautiful daughter of a poor German immigrant family in Columbus, Ohio, works with her mother cleaning in a hotel, where she attracts the attention of a kind, middle-aged senator, who promises to marry her but dies suddenly, leaving her pregnant. Later she becomes the companion of Lester Kane, the son of a rich carriage manufacturer, who loves her but cannot marry her without losing his inheritance.
context: Theodore Dreiser published the novel in 1911, his second after [Sister Carrie](/book/546?lang=en). Like that book, it shocked readers by refusing to punish its heroine for breaking moral rules, and it is one of the most compassionate portraits of a woman in American fiction.

about: In a small railway town on the Nebraska prairie, the elegant, charming Marian Forrester, much younger wife of the old railroad builder Captain Forrester, makes their house a place of brilliance and grace for visitors from the East, and the boy Niel Herbert worships her. But as the Captain loses his fortune and his health, and the pioneer age gives way to a meaner one of shrewd businessmen, Niel watches with dismay as Mrs Forrester, determined to survive, compromises with men he despises.
context: Willa Cather published the novel in 1923, and F. Scott Fitzgerald admired it so much that he wrote to her, worried that a passage in [The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en) resembled one of hers. Read Cather's [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en) and [Death Comes for the Archbishop](/book/63659?lang=en).

about: In 1851 a French priest, Jean Marie Latour, arrives in the vast territory of New Mexico, newly taken by the United States, as its first bishop, together with his old friend Father Joseph Vaillant. Over nearly forty years they travel thousands of miles on horse and mule through deserts and mountains, visiting Mexican villages, Hopi and Navajo country and the ancient pueblos, struggling with corrupt local priests and building a cathedral in Santa Fe, until the archbishop, old and at peace, prepares to die.
context: Willa Cather published the novel in 1927, basing her heroes on the real Bishop Jean-Baptiste Lamy and his vicar Joseph Machebeuf. Written in calm, luminous episodes, it is often considered her masterpiece. Read also [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en).

about: Godfrey St Peter, a historian at a Midwestern university, has won a prize for his great work on the Spanish explorers of America and moved with his family into a fine new house, but he cannot bring himself to leave his shabby study in the attic of the old rented house where he wrote it. Around him his family grows rich from the invention of his brilliant dead student, Tom Outland, and in the middle of the novel Tom's own story is told: his discovery of an ancient cliff city hidden in a mesa in the Southwest.
context: Willa Cather published the novel in 1925, comparing its structure, with a story set inside a story, to a Dutch painting of a room with a window open on to the sea. It is a quiet study of loneliness and middle age. Read also [The Song of the Lark](/book/420?lang=en) and [A Lost Lady](/book/59836?lang=en).

about: Martin Arrowsmith, a doctor's son from a small Midwestern town, is inspired as a medical student by the stern German bacteriologist Max Gottlieb to devote his life to pure science.
