But the world keeps pulling him away: country practice, public health politics, a fashionable clinic, and finally a research institute in New York, where he discovers a virus that destroys bacteria and is sent to fight an outbreak of plague on a Caribbean island, where he must choose between saving lives and completing his experiment.
context: Sinclair Lewis wrote the novel with the help of the microbiologist Paul de Kruif and published it in 1925; it was awarded the Pulitzer Prize, which Lewis refused. It is one of the first great novels about scientific research. Read Lewis's [Main Street](/book/842?lang=en) and [Babbitt](/book/1395?lang=en).

about: Elmer Gantry, a loud, handsome, hard-drinking college football player with no real faith, drifts into the ministry because he enjoys an audience. He becomes a travelling evangelist alongside the passionate revivalist Sharon Falconer, then a Methodist preacher who climbs the ladder of success with sensational sermons and campaigns against vice, while secretly drinking, chasing women and betraying everyone who trusts him.
context: Sinclair Lewis published the novel in 1927, and its savage portrait of religious hypocrisy caused an uproar; it was banned in several American cities and denounced from pulpits. The 1960 film won Burt Lancaster an Oscar. Read also [Arrowsmith](/book/64711?lang=en) and [Babbitt](/book/1395?lang=en).

about: Instead of one hero, this novel follows dozens of New Yorkers from the 1890s to the 1920s: Ellen Thatcher, an actress who rises through marriages and affairs; Jimmy Herf, a disillusioned reporter; Congo, a French sailor who becomes a rich bootlegger; a milkman, a lawyer, a union organiser, immigrants and drifters, as the city grows into a roaring, merciless metropolis. Their stories are cut together like scenes in a film, with newspaper headlines, songs and street noises.
context: John Dos Passos (1896–1970) published the novel in 1925, the same year as [The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en), and its collage technique made him one of the leading experimental writers of his generation. Compare Sherwood Anderson's [Winesburg, Ohio](/book/718?lang=en).

about: The decline of the Compson family, once great landowners in Jefferson, Mississippi, is told four times. First through the mind of Benjy, a man with a severe mental disability for whom past and present are mixed together; then through his brother Quentin, a Harvard student, on a single day in June 1910, haunted by memories of their sister; then through the bitter, greedy brother Jason; and finally through a narrator who follows Dilsey, the family's Black cook, whose strength holds the house together. At the centre of all of them is their lost sister, Caddy.
context: William Faulkner (1897–1962), who won the Nobel Prize in 1949, published the novel in 1929, and its title comes from Macbeth's speech about life as 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury'. Difficult but rewarding, it is one of the great experimental novels of the century. Read [Macbeth](/book/2?lang=en), and compare Joyce's [Ulysses](/book/347?lang=en).

about: Frederic Henry, a young American serving as an ambulance officer in the Italian army in the First World War, falls in love with Catherine Barkley, an English nurse, while recovering from a wound in a hospital in Milan. Back at the front, he is caught up in the chaotic retreat from Caporetto, where military police are shooting officers, and he deserts, makes his 'separate peace' and escapes with Catherine across the lake into Switzerland.
context: Ernest Hemingway, who had himself been wounded as an ambulance volunteer in Italy in 1918 and fallen in love with a nurse, published the novel in 1929, and its spare style and tragic ending made it his first great best-seller. Read [The Sun Also Rises](/book/61232?lang=en), and compare [All Quiet on the Western Front](/book/68493?lang=en).

about: Cane is a book unlike any other, mixing short stories, poems and a final piece written almost like a play. Its first part is set among Black farmers in rural Georgia, where women such as Karintha, Becky and Fern live and suffer among cane fields, sawmills and dusk; its second moves north to the cities of Washington and Chicago; and its third returns south with Ralph Kabnis, an educated Black teacher from the North, who struggles to face the legacy of slavery.
context: Jean Toomer (1894–1967) wrote the book after working as a teacher in Georgia in 1921, and it was published in 1923. Hailed as a masterpiece, it became one of the founding works of the Harlem Renaissance. Compare Langston Hughes's [The Weary Blues](/book/68231?lang=en) and Sherwood Anderson's [Winesburg, Ohio](/book/718?lang=en), which Toomer admired.

about: 'I've known rivers: I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins.' In his first book of poems, Langston Hughes writes in the rhythms of jazz and the blues about the lives of Black Americans: a pianist playing the blues late at night on Lenox Avenue in Harlem, cabarets and dancers, working people, the dream of Africa, and the proud declaration 'I, too, sing America'.
context: Hughes (1901–1967) published the book in 1926, at twenty-four, after its title poem won a prize from the magazine Opportunity, and he became the best-known poet of the Harlem Renaissance. In 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' he bathes in the Euphrates 'when dawns were young' before the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi. Compare [Cane](/book/54587?lang=en).

about: The unnamed narrator, son of a white Southern gentleman and a Black mother, grows up in Connecticut believing he is white, until a day at school reveals that the world counts him as Black. A gifted pianist, he works in a cigar factory in Florida, plays ragtime in New York clubs and tours Europe with a rich patron, dreaming of composing music from Black folk songs. After witnessing a lynching in the South, he decides to 'pass' as a white man, and wonders what he has sold.
context: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938), a writer, diplomat, civil rights leader and author of the song 'Lift Every Voice and Sing', published the novel anonymously in 1912, and many readers took it for a real memoir. It is a landmark of African American literature. Compare Du Bois's [The Souls of Black Folk](/book/710?lang=en).

about: A Northern couple, John and his wife Annie, buy an old vineyard in North Carolina after the Civil War, and the formerly enslaved Uncle Julius McAdoo, who works for them, entertains them with stories of plantation days: tales of conjuring, of a man turned into a tree, of a bewitched grapevine and of a slave changed into a mule. Behind the folk humour the stories reveal the cruelty of slavery, and Julius, it turns out, always has a practical reason of his own for telling them.
context: Charles W. Chesnutt (1858–1932), a writer of mixed race from Ohio and North Carolina, published the collection in 1899, and it was one of the first books by a Black American author to be widely read by white readers. Compare [Uncle Tom's Cabin](/book/522?lang=en) and [The Souls of Black Folk](/book/710?lang=en).

about: In essays, stories, poems and autobiographical pieces, W. E. B. Du Bois looks at the world after the First World War through the eyes of the colonised and the oppressed: 'the souls of white folk' who claim to rule the world by right, the colonial greed in Africa that he saw as a root of the war, the riots against Black workers in East St Louis in 1917, the dignity of Black women, and the hope of a future in which all races share in work and culture.
context: Du Bois (1868–1963) published the book in 1920 as a kind of sequel to [The Souls of Black Folk](/book/710?lang=en), and its essays on race and empire are among his most powerful. Compare Booker T. Washington's [Up from Slavery](/book/2529?lang=en).

about: Lorelei Lee, a pretty blonde from Little Rock, Arkansas, keeps a diary of her adventures, written with dreadful spelling and a perfect head for business. Supported by Gus Eisman, the 'Button King' of Chicago, she sails to Europe with her sharp-tongued friend Dorothy, and in London, Paris and Vienna collects diamonds from gentlemen, outwits a pair of French swindlers and meets 'Dr Froyd', who finds she has no inhibitions, all the while claiming to be a girl who wants to improve her mind.
context: Anita Loos (1889–1981), a Hollywood screenwriter, published the comic novel in 1925, and it was a huge best-seller, admired by readers as different as James Joyce and Edith Wharton. The 1953 film with Marilyn Monroe made 'Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend' famous. Compare [The Diary of a Nobody](/book/1283?lang=en).

about: At noon on Friday, 20 July 1714, the finest bridge in all Peru, a rope bridge woven by the Incas, breaks and throws five travellers into the gorge below. Brother Juniper, a Franciscan friar who sees it happen, sets out to discover whether their deaths were an accident or part of God's plan by investigating the lives of the victims: an eccentric old marquesa who writes brilliant letters to her daughter, a young orphan girl, a grieving twin brother, an old man of the theatre and a small boy.
context: Thornton Wilder (1897–1975) published the novel in 1927, and it won the Pulitzer Prize the following year. Its last line, 'There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love', is often quoted. Compare Cather's [Death Comes for the Archbishop](/book/63659?lang=en).

about: In San Francisco, the private detective Sam Spade, cool, cynical and loyal to his own code, takes a case from a beautiful, nervous young woman calling herself Miss Wonderly. That night his partner, Miles Archer, is shot dead, and Spade finds himself among a gang of rival crooks, the perfumed Joel Cairo, the enormous, genial Casper Gutman and his young gunman Wilmer, all hunting for a jewelled statuette of a falcon made, legend says, by the Knights of Malta in 1539.
context: Dashiell Hammett (1894–1961), who had worked as a Pinkerton detective, published the novel in 1930, and it shaped the hard-boiled detective story as we know it; the 1941 film with Humphrey Bogart is a classic. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2026. Compare Agatha Christie's [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: In 1915, as the Lusitania sinks, a man hands a packet of secret papers to a young American woman. Four years later, in post-war London, two old friends, the cheerful, penniless Tommy Beresford and the bold Prudence 'Tuppence' Cowley, set up as 'Young Adventurers', willing to go anywhere and do anything, and are soon caught up in the hunt for the missing papers and the girl who had them, pursued by a criminal mastermind known only as Mr Brown.
context: Published in 1922, this was Agatha Christie's second novel and the first featuring Tommy and Tuppence, who would appear in her books until 1973. It is a fast, light-hearted thriller rather than a puzzle. Read also [The Mysterious Affair at Styles](/book/1134?lang=en).

about: 'Anyone who murdered Colonel Protheroe would be doing the world at large a service,' remarks the vicar of St Mary Mead at lunch, and that same evening the colonel, the most disliked man in the village, is found shot dead at the writing desk in the vicar's own study. There are far too many suspects, and two people confess, but it is the vicar's elderly neighbour, Miss Jane Marple, who watches everything from her garden and knows human nature from village life, who sees the truth.
context: Published in 1930, this was the first novel featuring Miss Marple, and it entered the public domain in the United States in 2026. Agatha Christie later thought its plot too crowded, but its picture of village gossip is a delight. Read also [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: In the second and last book of stories about the Hundred Acre Wood, a new friend arrives: Tigger, a bouncy, boastful animal who does not know what Tiggers like to eat. Pooh and Piglet build a house for Eeyore, Pooh invents the game of Poohsticks from a bridge, Owl's house is blown down in a gale, and Rabbit tries to 'unbounce' Tigger. At the end Christopher Robin, who is growing up and going away to school, takes Pooh to an enchanted place at the top of the forest to say goodbye.
context: A. A. Milne published the book in 1928 with drawings by E. H. Shepard, and it entered the public domain in the United States in 2024. Read the first book, [Winnie-the-Pooh](/book/61195?lang=en), and Milne's poems [When We Were Very Young](/book/64136?lang=en).

about: These forty-four poems for children, written for and about Milne's small son, Christopher Robin, include 'Buckingham Palace', in which Christopher Robin and his nurse Alice watch the changing of the guard; 'Vespers', with the little boy kneeling at the foot of his bed saying his prayers; 'The King's Breakfast'; 'Disobedience', about James James Morrison Morrison Weatherby George Dupree; and the first appearance of a teddy bear, not yet called Pooh.
context: A. A. Milne published the book in 1924 with drawings by E. H. Shepard, two years before [Winnie-the-Pooh](/book/61195?lang=en), and it was an immediate best-seller. Read also [The House at Pooh Corner](/book/66760?lang=en).

about: Bambi, a roe deer fawn, is born in a thicket deep in the forest and learns from his mother about the meadow, the other animals and the changing seasons. As he grows he meets his cousins Faline and Gobo, learns to fight rival bucks, and is taught by an old, solitary stag, the prince of the forest, the hardest lesson of all: how to survive the terrifying creature the animals call 'He', the hunter with his gun.
context: Felix Salten (1869–1945), an Austrian writer, published the novel in 1923 as Bambi: A Life in the Woods; it is far more serious than Disney's 1942 film, a quiet meditation on life, loss and death. The Nazis banned it, reading it as an allegory of the persecution of the Jews, and Salten, who was Jewish, fled to Switzerland. This is a modern translation by David Wyllie.

about: Doctor John Dolittle of Puddleby-on-the-Marsh loves animals so much that his house fills up with them and his human patients stop coming. Then his parrot, Polynesia, teaches him the language of animals, and he becomes the most famous animal doctor in the world. When the monkeys of Africa fall sick in a terrible epidemic, he sails off to cure them with his household, Dab-Dab the duck, Jip the dog, Gub-Gub the pig, Chee-Chee the monkey and Too-Too the owl, and meets the rare two-headed pushmi-pullyu.
context: Hugh Lofting (1886–1947) invented the doctor in illustrated letters to his children while serving as a soldier in the First World War, and published the book in 1920. Its picture of an African kingdom contains racist caricatures that later editions removed. Compare [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en).

about: A stuffed velveteen rabbit is given to a little boy as a Christmas present, and is soon forgotten among the expensive mechanical toys, which look down on him. The wise old Skin Horse explains what it means to become Real: 'Real isn't how you are made. It's a thing that happens to you,' when a child loves you for a long, long time, even if your fur is loved off. The rabbit becomes the boy's favourite and goes everywhere with him, until the boy falls ill with scarlet fever.
context: Margery Williams (1881–1944) published the tale in 1922 with illustrations by William Nicholson, and it has become one of the best-loved children's stories about love and growing old. Compare [Winnie-the-Pooh](/book/61195?lang=en).

about: King Dushyanta, hunting in the forest, comes to a hermitage and falls in love with Shakuntala, the foster daughter of a sage, marries her secretly and gives her his ring. But Shakuntala, lost in thoughts of him, fails to greet a short-tempered holy man, who curses her: the king will forget her until he sees the ring again. When she comes to his court, pregnant, he does not know her, for the ring has been lost in a river, until a fisherman finds it inside a fish.
context: Kalidasa, the greatest poet of classical Sanskrit, probably lived in the fifth century, and Shakuntala is his masterpiece. When it was translated into European languages in 1789 it amazed readers, and Goethe wrote a famous verse in its praise. This volume, translated by Arthur W. Ryder, also includes Kalidasa's other works. Compare [The Song Celestial](/book/2540?lang=en).

about: This small anthology brought classical Chinese poetry to English readers in a new way. Its first part ranges over many centuries, including poems by Tao Yuanming (T'ao Ch'ien), who gave up office to farm, drink wine and write about his garden, while the second is devoted to the Tang poet Bai Juyi (Po Chü-i), with his simple, humorous poems about growing old and going bald, drinking with friends, his years in exile and the sufferings of ordinary people.
context: Arthur Waley (1889–1966), a largely self-taught scholar who worked at the British Museum and never visited China, published the book in 1918, translating into plain, rhythmic English without rhyme, and it had a deep influence on modern poetry in English. Compare [The Analects](/book/258?lang=en) and the [Tao Teh King](/book/531?lang=en).

about: In these essays and sketches, Lafcadio Hearn tries to show the 'heart' of the Japanese, which is what kokoro means: their sense of duty and self-control, their feeling for the dead, Buddhist ideas of pre-existence and karma, and the life of ordinary people in a country changing very fast. Among the pieces are the story of Kimiko, a geisha who gives up the man she loves, a blind street singer whose song moves a crowd to tears, the tale of a nun of the temple of Amida, and reflections on the strength of Japanese civilisation.
context: Hearn published the book in 1896, the year he became a Japanese citizen under the name Koizumi Yakumo. It is one of his most thoughtful books about Japan, though some of its generalisations now seem dated. Read his [Kwaidan](/book/1448?lang=en).

about: This collection retells twenty-two traditional Japanese tales: Momotaro, the Peach Boy, who sets off with a dog, a monkey and a pheasant to defeat the ogres of Ogre Island; Urashima Taro, the fisherman who visits the palace of the Dragon King under the sea and returns to find that three hundred years have passed; the tongue-cut sparrow; the old man who made withered trees blossom; the moon princess found inside a bamboo; and many others.
context: Yei Theodora Ozaki (1870–1932), born in London to a Japanese father and an English mother, first published her retellings in 1903 and reissued them in 1908 as Japanese Fairy Tales, adapting them freely for Western children. Compare Lafcadio Hearn's [Kwaidan](/book/1448?lang=en) and [Kokoro](/book/8564?lang=en).

about: During the Mexican Revolution, the peasant Demetrio Macías, driven from his home by federal soldiers who burn his house, takes to the mountains and becomes the leader of a band of rebels. At first they fight bravely for justice, and they are joined by Luis Cervantes, an idealistic, opportunistic young medical student; but as they win battles and rise in rank, the revolution turns into looting, cruelty and confusion, and Demetrio no longer knows why he is fighting. When his wife asks him, he throws a stone into a canyon and watches it fall.
context: Mariano Azuela (1873–1952), a doctor who served with the forces of Pancho Villa, published the novel in 1915, and it is the most famous novel of the Mexican Revolution. This is the English translation of 1929 by Enrique Munguía. Compare [All Quiet on the Western Front](/book/68493?lang=en).

about: In the voice of an imagined Spanish monk, Fray Antonio Agapida, a zealous chronicler, Washington Irving tells the ten-year war, from 1482 to 1492, in which the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella conquered the last Muslim kingdom in Spain: the surprise capture of Alhama, the battles in the mountains, the quarrels within the Nasrid family between the sultan Abu al-Hasan, his brother al-Zaghal and his son Boabdil, the sieges of Málaga and Baza, and finally the surrender of Granada and Boabdil's departure.
context: Irving published the chronicle in 1829 after studying the archives in Spain, and he chose the voice of the fanatical monk so that, through irony, the cruelty and bigotry of the crusade would speak for themselves. Read it with his [The Alhambra](/book/45043?lang=en), written in the palace itself.

about: King Henry IV, who seized the crown from Richard II, faces a rebellion led by the fiery young Henry Percy, called Hotspur, and his allies from the north and from Wales. Meanwhile the king's son and heir, Prince Hal, wastes his days in the taverns of Eastcheap with a band of thieves and drinkers led by Sir John Falstaff, a fat, witty and cowardly old knight who is one of the greatest comic characters in literature. At the battle of Shrewsbury, Hal must prove himself against Hotspur.
context: Written around 1596 or 1597, the play mixes history and comedy as no play before it had, and Falstaff became so popular that Shakespeare brought him back in two more plays. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Continue with [Henry IV, Part 2](/book/1362?lang=en) and [Henry V](/book/1364?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: The rebellion against King Henry IV goes on, now led by the Archbishop of York, while the king, sick and sleepless ('uneasy lies the head that wears a crown'), worries about his heir. Prince Hal still spends time with Falstaff, who travels into the country to recruit soldiers, takes bribes to release the fittest ones and reminisces with his old friend Justice Shallow about their wild youth. When the old king dies, Hal becomes Henry V and must decide what to do about Falstaff.
context: Written around 1597 or 1598, the play is darker and more autumnal than Part 1, full of age, sickness and memory, and its ending, the new king's rejection of his old friend, is one of the most painful moments in Shakespeare. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Read [Henry V](/book/1364?lang=en) next.

about: 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more.' The young King Henry V, once the wild Prince Hal, claims the crown of France and invades it. Through the siege of Harfleur, a night spent in disguise among his soldiers before the battle, and the great English victory at Agincourt in 1415 against a much larger French army, he proves himself a leader of men, inspiring them with the famous speech of 'we few, we happy few, we band of brothers'. The play ends with his courtship of the French princess Katherine.
context: Written in 1599, the play is introduced by a Chorus who asks the audience to imagine the fields of France inside the 'wooden O' of the theatre. It can be read as a celebration of heroism or as a darker look at war, and both Laurence Olivier and Kenneth Branagh filmed it. Read [Henry IV, Part 1](/book/1360?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: King Richard II, a graceful and poetic but vain and extravagant ruler, banishes his cousin Henry Bolingbroke and then seizes his inheritance to pay for a war in Ireland. While Richard is away, Bolingbroke returns with an army, the nobles desert the king, and Richard, in a series of beautiful, self-pitying speeches about the sacred right of kings, is forced to give up his crown. He is imprisoned in Pomfret Castle, and Bolingbroke becomes Henry IV.
context: Written around 1595, entirely in verse, the play contains John of Gaunt's famous praise of England as 'this sceptred isle'. The scene of the king's deposition was considered so dangerous that it was left out of the early printed editions, and supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance on the eve of his rebellion in 1601. Continue with [Henry IV, Part 1](/book/1360?lang=en).

about: King John of England holds his crown against the claim of his young nephew Arthur, who is backed by the King of France. Into the court strides Philip the Bastard, the illegitimate son of Richard the Lionheart, a witty, outspoken soldier who becomes the play's commentator on 'commodity', the self-interest that drives kings. John orders his servant Hubert to blind and kill Arthur, and the boy's fate turns the nobles against their king.
context: Written in the mid-1590s, it is one of Shakespeare's least performed histories, but the Bastard is one of his liveliest characters, and Constance, Arthur's grieving mother, has some of his most powerful laments. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [Richard II](/book/1359?lang=en).

about: The Duke of Vienna, pretending to leave the city, hands power to his strict deputy Angelo, then stays on disguised as a friar to watch what happens. Angelo revives an old law and condemns the young Claudio to death for getting his fiancée pregnant before their marriage. Claudio's sister Isabella, about to become a nun, pleads for his life, and Angelo offers to spare him if she will sleep with him, setting up a dark comedy of hypocrisy, mercy and justice.
context: Written around 1603 or 1604, it is one of Shakespeare's 'problem plays', whose ending leaves many questions open, and its title comes from the Sermon on the Mount: 'with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again'. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [The Merchant of Venice](/book/8?lang=en).

about: Caius Marcius, a proud and brilliant Roman general, wins the name Coriolanus by capturing the Volscian city of Corioli almost single-handed. But when he stands for the office of consul, his contempt for the common people, whom he refuses to flatter, lets the tribunes stir up the crowd against him, and he is banished from Rome. In fury he joins his old enemy, the Volscian leader Aufidius, and marches on his own city, where only his mother, Volumnia, can stop him.
context: Written around 1608 and based on Plutarch's life of Coriolanus, the play is Shakespeare's most political tragedy, and every age has read it differently: a Paris production caused riots in 1934, and Bertolt Brecht adapted it. Compare [Julius Caesar](/book/9?lang=en) and [Antony and Cleopatra](/book/1370?lang=en).

about: Two pairs of identical twins separated in a shipwreck as babies, both masters named Antipholus and both servants named Dromio, find themselves by chance in the same city, Ephesus, on the same day. The Antipholus from Syracuse is greeted as a husband by a wife he has never met, his servant is claimed by a kitchen maid, gold chains and beatings go to the wrong men, and everyone begins to think the town is bewitched, while the twins' old father, Egeon, waits to be executed.
context: Written in the early 1590s, it is Shakespeare's shortest play and one of his earliest, based on a Roman comedy by Plautus, and it remains one of the funniest farces ever written. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [Twelfth Night](/book/10?lang=en), another comedy of twins.

about: Titus Andronicus, a Roman general returning victorious from war against the Goths, sacrifices the eldest son of their captive queen, Tamora, and so begins a chain of revenge more violent than any other in Shakespeare. Tamora marries the new emperor and, with her lover Aaron the Moor, a brilliant and gleeful villain, takes terrible vengeance on Titus's family, until Titus, half mad with grief, plans a revenge of his own, ending in a banquet no audience forgets.
context: Shakespeare's first tragedy, written in the early 1590s, it was hugely popular in its time, in the fashion set by Kyd's [The Spanish Tragedy](/book/31670?lang=en). Long dismissed for its horrors, it has been revived with success in modern times, and Julie Taymor filmed it in 1999. This text follows the First Folio of 1623.

about: Sir John Falstaff, short of money in the town of Windsor, sends identical love letters to two respectable married women, Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, hoping to get at their husbands' money. The two wives compare letters and decide to punish him: he is hidden in a basket of dirty laundry and tipped into the Thames, disguised as an old woman and beaten, and finally lured to Windsor Forest at midnight, while the jealous Master Ford, in disguise, tries to catch his wife out.
context: Tradition says Shakespeare wrote the comedy around 1597 because Queen Elizabeth wished to see Falstaff in love. It is his only comedy set in the England of his own day, and Verdi made it into his last opera, Falstaff. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Read [Henry IV, Part 1](/book/1360?lang=en).

about: During the Trojan War, the young Trojan prince Troilus falls in love with Cressida, helped by her uncle Pandarus, a go-between, but after one night together she is handed over to the Greeks in an exchange of prisoners, and Troilus watches her give herself to a Greek warrior. Around them the heroes of Homer appear in a bitter light: the sulking Achilles, the boastful Ajax, the scheming Ulysses with his great speech on order, and the foul-mouthed Thersites, who sees in the war nothing but 'wars and lechery'.
context: Written around 1602, the play is the darkest of Shakespeare's 'problem plays', a cynical view of love and heroism that has found many admirers in modern times. Chaucer had told the same story in his Troilus and Criseyde. Compare Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en), and see [Shakespeare's life](/author/shakespeare?lang=en).

about: In ancient Britain, Imogen, the daughter of King Cymbeline, secretly marries the poor but noble Posthumus, who is banished. In Italy, Posthumus is tricked by the boastful Iachimo, who hides in a trunk in Imogen's bedroom, into believing that she has been unfaithful, and orders his servant to kill her. Disguised as a boy, Imogen flees into the Welsh mountains, where she finds shelter with two young men who are, unknown to all, her own lost brothers, while war breaks out between Britain and Rome.
context: Written around 1610, it is one of Shakespeare's late romances, with an astonishing final scene in which one revelation follows another, and its song 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' is among his most beautiful. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [The Winter's Tale](/book/1374?lang=en).

about: Helena, the orphaned daughter of a famous doctor, loves Bertram, the young Count of Rousillon, who looks down on her humble birth. When she cures the dying King of France with one of her father's remedies, the king rewards her with the husband of her choice, and she chooses Bertram, who marries her against his will and runs off to the wars in Italy, declaring that he will never be her husband until she wears his ring and carries his child. Helena sets out to meet his conditions.
context: Written around 1604 or 1605, it is another of Shakespeare's 'problem plays', a fairy-tale plot told with uncomfortable realism, and its title is a proverb. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [Measure for Measure](/book/1368?lang=en), which uses the same 'bed trick'.

about: The King of Navarre and three of his lords vow to spend three years in study, fasting and sleeping little, and to see no women. At once the Princess of France arrives with three ladies on a diplomatic mission, and the four men fall in love, each secretly writing sonnets, until they are all found out. Around them a crowd of comic characters, a fantastical Spaniard, a pedantic schoolmaster and a clown, show off their absurd wordplay, until a messenger brings sudden news that changes everything.
context: Written in the mid-1590s, it is Shakespeare's wittiest and wordiest comedy, full of puns, sonnets and verbal fireworks, and unusually it ends without the weddings: 'Jack hath not Jill.' This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [Much Ado About Nothing](/book/1363?lang=en).

about: Two close friends from Verona, the faithful lover Valentine and the fickle Proteus, travel to the court of Milan, where both fall in love with the duke's daughter, Silvia. Proteus betrays his friend and forgets his own sweetheart, Julia, who follows him disguised as a page. Valentine, banished, becomes the leader of a band of outlaws in the forest, while Proteus's servant Launce supplies the comedy with his complaints about his ungrateful dog, Crab.
context: Probably one of Shakespeare's very first plays, written around 1590, it introduces many devices of his later comedies, the heroine in boy's clothes, the forest of outlaws and the comic servant, and its song 'Who is Silvia?' is famous. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [As You Like It](/book/1365?lang=en).

about: Timon, a rich Athenian lord, gives away his fortune in lavish gifts and banquets to a crowd of flatterers. When his money runs out and his creditors close in, he asks his friends for help, and every one of them refuses. Turning against all humanity, Timon gives a last banquet of warm water and stones, then leaves the city to live in a cave in the woods, where, digging for roots, he finds gold, which he gives to anyone who will use it to destroy Athens.
context: Written around 1605 or 1606, probably together with Thomas Middleton, the play may have been left unfinished. Karl Marx quoted Timon's speech on gold in his analysis of money. This text follows the First Folio of 1623. Compare [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en).

about: In 1745 Edward Waverley, a dreamy young English officer raised on romantic books, takes leave to visit his uncle's old friend, the Baron of Bradwardine, in the Scottish Lowlands, and is drawn north into the Highlands, where he is captivated by the Jacobite chieftain Fergus Mac-Ivor and his passionate sister Flora. Accused of treason by his own army, Waverley joins the rising of Bonnie Prince Charlie and fights at Prestonpans, until he must choose between romance and reality, and between Flora and the gentle Rose Bradwardine.
context: Published anonymously in 1814, Waverley was Sir Walter Scott's first novel and is often called the first historical novel in the modern sense; it was so successful that his later books were known as the 'Waverley novels'. Its subtitle, ''Tis Sixty Years Since', marks the distance between reader and past. Read Scott's [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en).

about: Henry Esmond, an orphan believed to be the illegitimate son of a nobleman, grows up as a page in the household of his kinsman Lord Castlewood in the reign of William III, devoted to the gentle Lady Castlewood and later in love with her proud, dazzling daughter Beatrix. Through the wars in Flanders under the Duke of Marlborough, duels and Jacobite plots to bring the exiled Stuart prince to the throne, Esmond tells his story in the elaborate style of the early eighteenth century.
context: William Makepeace Thackeray published the novel in 1852 and thought it the best he could do; it is a remarkable imitation of the prose of Queen Anne's age, with appearances by Addison, Steele and Swift. Read Thackeray's [Vanity Fair](/book/896?lang=en).

about: In Florence in the 1490s, after the death of Lorenzo de' Medici, the noble, serious Romola, daughter of a blind old scholar, marries Tito Melema, a charming, clever young Greek who has arrived in the city after a shipwreck. But Tito is selfish and cowardly: he has abandoned the adoptive father who raised him, now a captive, and betrays everyone who trusts him as he rises in the dangerous politics of the city, while the fiery Dominican friar Savonarola preaches against the vanities of Florence.
context: George Eliot spent years researching Renaissance Florence for the novel, published in 1862 and 1863, and said that she began it a young woman and finished it an old one. It is a rich historical portrait and a study of moral corruption. Read [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en) and [Adam Bede](/book/807?lang=en).

about: These three stories of country clergymen in the English Midlands were George Eliot's first fiction. In 'The Sad Fortunes of the Reverend Amos Barton', a dull, poor curate is gossiped about by his parish until tragedy awakens their sympathy; in 'Mr Gilfil's Love-Story', an old vicar's past love for an Italian orphan girl is revealed; and in 'Janet's Repentance', a woman beaten by her drunken husband is saved from despair by the evangelical clergyman Mr Tryan.
context: The stories appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in 1857 and as a book in 1858 under the pen name George Eliot, used here for the first time by Mary Ann Evans; Charles Dickens guessed from them that the author must be a woman. Read her first novel, [Adam Bede](/book/807?lang=en), and [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en).

about: In the Scottish Lowlands at the end of the seventeenth century, Edgar Ravenswood, the proud, impoverished heir of an ancient family, lives in his ruined tower of Wolf's Crag, hating Sir William Ashton, the lawyer who acquired his family's lands. But when he saves Ashton and his gentle daughter Lucy from a wild bull, Edgar and Lucy fall in love and secretly pledge themselves to each other. Lucy's ambitious, domineering mother has other plans, and an old prophecy hangs over the house of Ravenswood.
context: Sir Walter Scott published the tragic novel in 1819, basing it on a real case of 1669, and wrote much of it while seriously ill, dictating to secretaries. Donizetti made it into the opera Lucia di Lammermoor, famous for its mad scene. Read Scott's [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en) and [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en).

about: In 1780, in the 'Neutral Ground' of Westchester County, New York, between the British and American lines during the Revolutionary War, a humble pedlar named Harvey Birch is suspected and hated by the Americans as a British spy. In fact he is working secretly for George Washington himself, who appears in disguise as 'Mr Harper', and he risks his life again and again, unable to reveal the truth even to save his own name, while the Wharton family, divided between the two sides, is caught up in the war.
context: James Fenimore Cooper published the novel in 1821, and it was the first great American best-seller and one of the first spy novels; Cooper based Birch partly on a story told him by John Jay. Read Cooper's [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en).

about: In 1793, in the new settlement of Templeton on Lake Otsego in upstate New York, Judge Marmaduke Temple presides over a frontier community that is felling forests, netting fish by the thousand and shooting pigeons by the flock. On the edge of the town lives the old hunter Natty Bumppo, Leatherstocking, with his aged Mohican friend Chingachgook, now called Indian John, and a mysterious young man, Oliver Edwards, who seems to bear a grudge against the judge.
context: Published in 1823, The Pioneers was the first of James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales, though it tells of Natty's old age, and it drew on the life of Cooper's own father, who founded Cooperstown. Its scenes of wasteful slaughter of wildlife make it one of the first American novels with an environmental conscience. Read [The Deerslayer](/book/3407?lang=en), which tells of Natty's youth.

about: Miles Coverdale, a minor poet, joins a group of idealists who have founded Blithedale, a farm community near Boston where they hope to build a better society by sharing work and living simply. There he is drawn to three remarkable people: the brilliant, beautiful feminist Zenobia, the fragile, mysterious young Priscilla, and the forceful reformer Hollingsworth, who wants to use the community for his own scheme for reforming criminals. Coverdale watches, half involved, as their relationships tangle towards tragedy.
context: Nathaniel Hawthorne based the novel, published in 1852, on his own months at the utopian community of Brook Farm in 1841. Read Hawthorne's [The Scarlet Letter](/book/411?lang=en) and [The House of the Seven Gables](/book/444?lang=en).

about: On April Fool's Day, a Mississippi steamboat called the Fidèle sets off down the river towards New Orleans, carrying a crowd of passengers from every walk of American life. Among them moves a mysterious stranger, or perhaps a series of strangers, who in one disguise after another, a deaf-mute, a crippled beggar, a charity agent, a herb doctor and a cosmopolitan in fancy clothes, asks each passenger for one thing: confidence, in him, in humanity and in God.
context: Herman Melville published the novel on April Fool's Day 1857, and it was the last novel published in his lifetime; its dark, philosophical comedy baffled readers then and fascinates them now. Read Melville's [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en) and [Bartleby, the Scrivener](/book/142?lang=en).

about: Arthur Gordon Pym, a restless young man from Nantucket, stows away aboard the whaling ship Grampus, hidden in the hold by his friend Augustus. A bloody mutiny breaks out, followed by shipwreck, starvation and cannibalism among the survivors. Rescued by another ship, Pym sails further and further south into the Antarctic, where the sea grows warm, the water is strange, the islanders are hostile, and at the very end a vast white figure rises before him.
context: Edgar Allan Poe's only complete novel, published in 1838, it inspired Jules Verne to write a sequel and influenced H. P. Lovecraft's [At the Mountains of Madness](/book/64499?lang=en). Read Poe's [The Fall of the House of Usher](/book/128?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/poe?lang=en).

about: When her parents divorce bitterly, the little girl Maisie Farange is passed between them, six months with each, and each uses her to carry messages of hatred to the other. Both parents remarry and take lovers, and Maisie, with her innocent, observant eyes, watches the adults around her lie, quarrel and betray one another, until she must make a choice of her own about where, and with whom, she will live.
context: Henry James published the novel in 1897, telling it through the point of view of a child who sees more than she understands, and it is one of his most daring experiments in narration. Read James's [Washington Square](/book/3001?lang=en) and [The Turn of the Screw](/book/353?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/jamesh?lang=en).

about: Charity Royall, an orphan brought down as a child from a poor, lawless community on the mountain above the village, lives in the small, dull New England town of North Dormer with her guardian, the lonely lawyer Mr Royall. One summer a young architect from the city, Lucius Harney, comes to study the old houses of the region, and Charity falls passionately in love with him, in a summer that will change her life.
context: Edith Wharton published the novel in 1917 and called it her 'hot Ethan', because it is set in the same New England landscape as [Ethan Frome](/book/4598?lang=en), but in summer and with a heroine awakening to love; its frankness about desire was daring for its time. Read also [The Age of Innocence](/book/840?lang=en).

about: Two distant cousins, both named Allan Armadale, are bound together by a terrible family secret: the father of one killed the father of the other. Growing up, they become close friends, one cheerful and rich, the other, who calls himself Ozias Midwinter, haunted by guilt and by a prophetic dream. Into their lives comes Lydia Gwilt, a beautiful, red-haired adventuress with a criminal past, who plots to marry the rich Armadale and inherit his fortune.
context: Wilkie Collins published the novel in 1866, and Lydia Gwilt, a scheming but strangely sympathetic villainess, shocked Victorian critics. It is one of the most intricate sensation novels of the age. Read Collins's [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en) and [The Moonstone](/book/497?lang=en).

about: Magdalen and Norah Vanstone grow up happily in a comfortable country house, until their parents die within days of each other and the sisters discover that their parents were not legally married when they were born. By the harsh law of the time they are 'nobody's children', with no name and no claim on their father's fortune, which passes to a hard-hearted uncle. Norah accepts her fate, but the spirited Magdalen, a gifted actress, sets out to win the money back by disguise and deception.
context: Wilkie Collins published the novel in 1862, between [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en) and [The Moonstone](/book/497?lang=en), as an attack on the law's treatment of children born outside marriage. Captain Wragge, the cheerful swindler who helps Magdalen, is one of his best comic creations.

about: Ruth Hilton, a beautiful, innocent orphan apprenticed to a dressmaker, is seduced at sixteen by a wealthy young gentleman, Henry Bellingham, who abandons her, pregnant, in a Welsh village. She is rescued by a kind Dissenting minister, Thurstan Benson, and his sister, who take her into their home in a northern town and pass her off as a young widow so that her child can grow up free of shame. For years the lie protects her, until the truth comes out.
context: Elizabeth Gaskell published the novel in 1853, and its sympathy for a 'fallen woman' outraged many readers; members of her husband's own congregation burned copies. Read Gaskell's [Mary Barton](/book/2338?lang=en) and [North and South](/book/4360?lang=en).

about: Stephen Smith, a young architect's assistant, is sent to restore the church tower of the remote parish of Endelstow on the wild coast of Cornwall, and falls in love with the vicar's daughter, the lively, blue-eyed Elfride Swancourt. Her father refuses his consent when he learns that Stephen's parents are humble villagers, and Elfride's feelings are tested when she meets the older, more sophisticated critic Henry Knight, who has fixed ideas of his own about women.
context: Thomas Hardy published the novel in 1873, drawing on his own courtship of his first wife, Emma Gifford, whom he met while restoring a church in Cornwall. It contains a famous scene in which Knight hangs from the edge of a sea cliff, sometimes said to be the origin of the word 'cliffhanger'. Read Hardy's [Far from the Madding Crowd](/book/307?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: Captain MacWhirr, the stolid, literal-minded master of the steamer Nan-Shan, has no imagination at all and does not believe in steering round a storm just because the books say so. Carrying two hundred Chinese labourers home with their savings across the China Sea, he sails straight into a typhoon. While the ship is battered for hours, the labourers' boxes break open below decks, their silver dollars scatter, and a fight breaks out in the hold.
context: Joseph Conrad published the story in 1902, and its description of the storm is one of the most powerful in literature; the captain's unimaginative courage turns out to be exactly what the crisis needs. Read Conrad's [Youth](/book/824?lang=en) and [Lord Jim](/book/343?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/conrad?lang=en).

about: Marlow, the narrator of Heart of Darkness, tells a group of friends over a bottle of wine about his first voyage to the East, at twenty, as second mate of the Judea, an old barque carrying coal to Bangkok under the motto 'Do or Die'. Everything goes wrong: storms, leaks, a collision, and finally the coal catches fire and the ship burns at sea, leaving young Marlow to command a small boat on the way to Java. Yet he remembers it all with joy, because he was young.
context: Joseph Conrad based the story, published in 1898, on his own voyage in the Palestine between 1881 and 1883, and it was the first story told by Marlow. Read [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en), and see [Conrad's life](/author/conrad?lang=en).

about: A young officer abruptly gives up his berth on a steamer in an Eastern port, restless and bored, and then unexpectedly receives his first command: a sailing ship at Bangkok whose captain has died. At sea the ship is trapped by a dead calm in the Gulf of Siam, fever spreads through the crew, and the young captain discovers that the quinine he relied on has been replaced by worthless powder, while the sick first mate believes the dead captain's ghost is cursing the ship.
context: Joseph Conrad based the story, published in 1917, on his own first command, the Otago, in 1888, and dedicated it to his son Borys, then fighting in the First World War. It is a tale of crossing the line from youth into maturity. Read [Typhoon](/book/1381?lang=en) and [Youth](/book/824?lang=en).

about: In 1366, young Alleyne Edricson, raised by monks in a Hampshire abbey, goes out into the world at twenty and falls in with a band of English archers and soldiers of fortune, the White Company, recruited for a war in Spain. With the huge, rough archer Hordle John and the veteran bowman Samkin Aylward, he becomes squire to the brave little knight Sir Nigel Loring and follows him through adventures in France and Spain, falling in love with Sir Nigel's daughter, Maude.
context: Arthur Conan Doyle thought his historical novels, above all this one, published in 1891, better than his Sherlock Holmes stories, and it was hugely popular in its day. Read [The Exploits of Brigadier Gerard](/book/10280?lang=en) and [The Hound of the Baskervilles](/book/55?lang=en).

about: Etienne Gerard, a brave, vain and gloriously boastful hussar of Napoleon's army, now an old man, tells the stories of his greatest exploits in the wars across Europe: how he went to the Castle of Gloom to rescue a friend's beloved, defended the Emperor against Corsican assassins, was taken prisoner by the English and escaped from Dartmoor, and carried secret messages through enemy lines. The joke is that Gerard never notices how ridiculous his vanity makes him, yet his courage is real.
context: Arthur Conan Doyle published the stories in The Strand Magazine and collected them in 1896; many readers prefer the boastful Gerard to Sherlock Holmes. Doyle based him partly on the memoirs of the real Baron de Marbot. Read [The White Company](/book/1171?lang=en) and [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en).

about: These eight stories are among the last adventures of Sherlock Holmes. In 'The Bruce-Partington Plans', Holmes and his brother Mycroft hunt for stolen plans of a secret submarine; in 'The Dying Detective', Holmes appears to be wasting away from a rare tropical disease; in 'The Devil's Foot', a strange poison drives a Cornish family to madness; and in the title story, set on the eve of the First World War in 1914, an older Holmes comes out of retirement to trap a German spy.
context: Arthur Conan Doyle collected the stories in 1917, during the war. The title story, told in the third person, ends with Holmes's famous words about the 'east wind' that is coming over England. Read [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) and [The Hound of the Baskervilles](/book/55?lang=en).

about: These forty short stories, many only a few pages long, portray the British in India in the 1880s: officers and civil servants, their wives and flirtations at the hill station of Simla, young men who fall in love with Indian women, drunkards and misfits, and the gossip of a small, closed society. They include the first appearances of Mrs Hauksbee, the witty queen of Simla society, and of the three soldiers Mulvaney, Ortheris and Learoyd.
context: Rudyard Kipling wrote most of the stories as a young journalist in Lahore for the Civil and Military Gazette and published them as a book in 1888, at twenty-two; they made his name in India and then in England. Read [Kim](/book/356?lang=en) and [The Man Who Would Be King](/book/8060?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: In the voices and slang of ordinary British soldiers, the 'Tommy Atkins' of the Victorian army, these poems tell of barrack life, of fighting in India, Burma, Afghanistan and the Sudan, and of a public that cheers its soldiers in war and despises them in peace. They include 'Gunga Din', about an Indian water-carrier who dies saving a soldier's life; 'Mandalay', with its longing for the East; 'Danny Deever', about a military hanging; and 'Fuzzy-Wuzzy', a tribute to the Sudanese warriors who broke a British square.
context: Rudyard Kipling published the collection in 1892, and its music-hall rhythms made the poems enormously popular, though their imperial outlook is now much debated. Read [Plain Tales from the Hills](/book/2057?lang=en) and [Kim](/book/356?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: On Midsummer Eve, two children, Dan and Una, act scenes from A Midsummer Night's Dream in a meadow below Pook's Hill in Sussex, and accidentally summon Puck, the last of the fairies left in England. Through the summer he brings them visitors from the past who lived on the same land: Sir Richard, a Norman knight of the Conquest; Parnesius, a Roman centurion guarding Hadrian's Wall against the Picts; and others, who tell their stories, after which Puck makes the children forget.
context: Rudyard Kipling published the book in 1906, inspired by the history of the country around his house, Bateman's, in Sussex, and it contains 'A Tree Song', with its refrain of 'Oak and Ash and Thorn'. The story continues in Rewards and Fairies. Read [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: Dick Heldar, a brilliant young war artist, makes his name sketching the British campaign in the Sudan, where he receives a sword cut to the head. Back in London, famous and successful, he falls in love again with Maisie, his childhood companion, now a struggling painter more interested in her own art than in him. Then Dick begins to lose his sight, a late result of the old wound, and races to finish his masterpiece before darkness falls.
context: Published in 1891, it was Rudyard Kipling's first novel, and he wrote two endings for it, one happy and one tragic. Its picture of the artist's life and of war correspondents drew on his own early fame in London. Read [Plain Tales from the Hills](/book/2057?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/kipling?lang=en).

about: Much as the caliph Harun al-Rashid wanders Baghdad in disguise in the Arabian Nights, Prince Florizel of Bohemia roams modern London and Paris incognito with his loyal friend Colonel Geraldine in search of adventure. In 'The Suicide Club' they join a secret society whose members draw cards each night to decide which of them will die and who will kill him; in 'The Rajah's Diamond', a great stolen jewel passes from hand to hand, bringing ruin to each owner.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson published the collection in 1882, and it also includes the eerie Scottish tale 'The Pavilion on the Links'. Its witty, fantastic stories influenced later detective and spy fiction. Compare the [Arabian Nights Entertainments](/book/479?lang=en), and read [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en).

about: Picking up where Kidnapped ended, young David Balfour, now an heir, goes to Edinburgh to give the evidence that would save James Stewart of the Glens, a Highlander falsely accused of the Appin murder. But powerful men want James hanged, and David is kidnapped again and held on a lonely rock in the sea until the trial is over. Meanwhile he falls in love with Catriona Drummond, the proud, spirited daughter of a treacherous Highland chief, and meets her again later in Holland.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson published this sequel to [Kidnapped](/book/187?lang=en) in 1893, and the trial of James Stewart in 1752 was real. Published in America as David Balfour, it is a story of loyalty, justice and first love. See [his life](/author/stevenson?lang=en).

about: Arthur Kipps, an orphan raised by his aunt and uncle in a seaside town, is apprenticed to a draper and leads a dull, cramped life, until he unexpectedly inherits a fortune from the grandfather he never knew. Suddenly a gentleman, he tries desperately to learn the manners of polite society and becomes engaged to the refined Helen Walsingham, who sets about improving him, while he still loves his childhood sweetheart, Ann Pornick, now a housemaid.
context: H. G. Wells published the comic novel in 1905, drawing on his own years as a draper's apprentice, and it was later turned into the musical Half a Sixpence. Read [The History of Mr Polly](/book/7297?lang=en) and [Tono-Bungay](/book/1005?lang=en).

about: Graham, a Victorian Englishman who cannot sleep, falls at last into a trance in 1897 and wakes two hundred years later in a gigantic London of glass-roofed streets, moving roadways and flying machines. He discovers that his savings, growing for two centuries, have made him the legal owner of half the world, ruled in his name by a council of trustees while the masses toil in misery below. Hailed by the people as their saviour, he finds himself at the centre of a revolution.
context: H. G. Wells first published the novel as When the Sleeper Wakes in 1899 and revised it in 1910 as The Sleeper Awakes, which is this text. It is one of the first great dystopias of the modern city and influenced films such as Metropolis. Read [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: In the title story, a mountaineer named Nunez falls into a hidden valley in the Andes, cut off from the world for generations, whose people have all been born blind and have forgotten that sight exists. Remembering the saying 'In the country of the blind the one-eyed man is king', he expects to rule them, but finds that they think him mad, and that to marry the girl he loves he must give up his eyes. The collection includes more than thirty other stories by H. G. Wells.
context: Wells published 'The Country of the Blind' in 1904 and gathered what he thought the best of his short stories in this volume in 1911, among them 'The Door in the Wall' and 'The Star'. Read [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en) and [The War of the Worlds](/book/180?lang=en).

about: Two travellers walking in the Swiss Alps suddenly find themselves on another planet exactly like Earth, except that humanity has organised itself into a single peaceful world state. In a mixture of story and essay, H. G. Wells explores how such a society would work: a world government, freedom of movement, a minimum wage, the end of poverty, and a voluntary order of 'samurai' who govern through discipline and service, while his companion, a botanist, can think only of a woman he once loved.
context: Wells published the book in 1905, trying to imagine a utopia that is not fixed and perfect but changing and modern. Compare Thomas More's [Utopia](/book/2317?lang=en) and Edward Bellamy's [Looking Backward](/book/920?lang=en).

about: William Crimsworth, an orphan of good family, refuses to become a clergyman and goes to work as a clerk for his harsh elder brother, a mill owner in the north of England. Escaping to Brussels, he becomes a teacher in a boys' school and then in the neighbouring girls' school, where he resists the charms of the scheming headmistress, Mademoiselle Reuter, and falls in love with a poor, serious Anglo-Swiss pupil teacher, Frances Henri.
context: This was Charlotte Brontë's first novel, written in 1846, but publishers rejected it and it appeared only in 1857, after her death. She later reworked its Brussels material into [Villette](/book/8744?lang=en). Read [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/cbronte?lang=en).

about: In 1660, years after The Three Musketeers, d'Artagnan, still a lieutenant of the King's Musketeers, is tired of serving a young Louis XIV dominated by Cardinal Mazarin. Hearing that the exiled Charles II of England needs help to regain his throne, he sets off on a daring private adventure, while his friend Athos's son, Raoul, the Vicomte de Bragelonne, a noble, loyal young man, loves the gentle Louise de la Vallière. This volume contains the first seventy-five chapters of the vast novel.
context: Alexandre Dumas published the final part of the d'Artagnan trilogy between 1847 and 1850, and its later volumes include the story of the Man in the Iron Mask. Read [The Three Musketeers](/book/133?lang=en) and [Twenty Years After](/book/135?lang=en).

about: Pamela Andrews, a pretty, pious fifteen-year-old maidservant, is left without protection when her kind mistress dies, and the lady's son, the young squire Mr B., begins to pursue her. In letters to her poor, honest parents, and later in a journal, she records his attempts to seduce her, from hiding in her closet to offering money, and finally his kidnapping of her to his country house in Lincolnshire, where she is guarded by a monstrous housekeeper. Pamela resists every attempt, until Mr B., reading her journal, is moved to change.
context: Samuel Richardson (1689–1761), a London printer, published this novel in letters in 1740; it was a sensation and one of the first great English novels, and its message that virtue is rewarded by marriage to the master provoked Henry Fielding's parodies Shamela and Joseph Andrews. Read Fielding's [Tom Jones](/book/6598?lang=en).

about: The town of Hadleyburg is so proud of its reputation as the most honest, incorruptible place in the country that it once insulted a passing stranger. Years later the stranger takes his revenge: he leaves a sack of gold coins, supposedly for the townsman who once did him a kindness, a man who will be known by a remark he made. Nineteen of the town's leading citizens are secretly told the 'remark', and every one of them claims the gold, until a public meeting exposes them all.
context: Mark Twain published the story in 1899, one of his sharpest satires of hypocrisy; the town learns that virtue untested is worth little and changes its motto to 'Lead us into temptation'. The volume adds other stories and essays. Read [Pudd'nhead Wilson](/book/464?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/twain?lang=en).

about: In the summer of 1902, Jack London bought old clothes, took a room in the East End of London and lived for weeks among its poorest people, sleeping in workhouses, queuing for charity meals and walking all night with homeless men, because the police would not let them sleep on the benches. He describes the overcrowded rooms, the sweatshops, the hunger and the despair at the heart of the richest empire in the world.
context: London published the book in 1903 and later said it was the one of all his books he loved most. It is a pioneering work of undercover reporting, and it influenced George Orwell's Down and Out in Paris and London. Read [The Road](/book/13088?lang=en) and [The Iron Heel](/book/1403?lang=en).

about: In the reign of Elizabeth I, Amyas Leigh, a big, brave young man from Bideford in Devon, sails with Francis Drake around the world and then to the Spanish Main in search of his brother and of the beautiful Rose Salterne, whom many young men love and who has run away with a Spanish nobleman. Through battles in Ireland, adventures in the jungles of South America and the fight against the Spanish Armada in 1588, his hatred of Spain grows until it nearly destroys him.
context: Charles Kingsley published the novel in 1855, during the Crimean War, as a patriotic adventure, and it was so popular that a new seaside town in Devon was named after it. Its hostility to Catholic Spain reflects the prejudices of its age. Read Kingsley's [The Water-Babies](/book/1276?lang=en).

about: In the London of 1984, democracy has been replaced by a king chosen at random, and the lot falls on Auberon Quin, a joker who decides, for fun, to give each borough of London its own medieval pageantry, banners and city guard. But one young man, Adam Wayne, the Provost of Notting Hill, takes it all completely seriously, and when developers want to drive a road through his little street, he raises an army to defend it, and London is plunged into a war of the boroughs.
context: G. K. Chesterton published his first novel in 1904, a comic fantasy in praise of local patriotism and small, beloved places; it is sometimes said to have influenced Orwell's choice of the year 1984. Read [The Man Who Was Thursday](/book/1901?lang=en) and [Orthodoxy](/book/480?lang=en).

about: In two parts, G. K. Chesterton answers H. G. Wells's account of history as a story of gradual evolution. The first, 'The Creature Called Man', argues that human beings, from the cave painters onward, are radically different from other animals, and surveys the myths, religions and philosophies of the pagan world. The second, 'The Man Called Christ', argues that the story of Christ is unique among the world's religions, and that Christianity has repeatedly been declared dead and has always returned.
context: Published in 1925, the book had a great influence on C. S. Lewis, who said it helped bring him to faith. It is a lively, paradoxical defence of Christianity. Read Chesterton's [Orthodoxy](/book/480?lang=en).

about: These eight comic stories introduce the world of P. G. Wodehouse: the amiable, empty-headed young gentleman Bertie Wooster, always in trouble with his aunts, his friends' romances and his own engagements, and his valet Jeeves, a quiet genius who rescues him from every scrape, usually in return for the disappearance of some loud tie or hat he disapproves of. Half the stories feature Reggie Pepper, an earlier version of Bertie.
context: Wodehouse (1881–1975) published the collection in 1919, and the Jeeves and Wooster stories went on to become among the best-loved comedy in English. Read [The Inimitable Jeeves](/book/53824?lang=en) and [Leave It to Psmith](/book/54562?lang=en).

about: Psmith, a monocled, elegant and endlessly talkative young man, places an advertisement in the newspaper offering to do anything at all, 'crime not objected to'. Soon he is hired to steal a diamond necklace at Blandings Castle, home of the absent-minded Lord Emsworth, who cares only for his garden, and he goes there pretending to be a Canadian poet, while falling in love with the castle's new librarian, Eve Halliday, and dodging a pair of real crooks after the same jewels.
context: P. G. Wodehouse published the novel in 1923, bringing together two of his most famous creations, Psmith and Blandings Castle, and it is often counted among his best. Read [My Man Jeeves](/book/8077?lang=en) and [The Inimitable Jeeves](/book/53824?lang=en).

about: In these linked stories, Bertie Wooster's friend Bingo Little falls in love with a new girl in almost every chapter, from a waitress to a romantic novelist, and Bertie must help him win over his rich uncle; Bertie is pursued by his formidable Aunt Agatha's plans to marry him off; and at a country house the guests bet on everything, from the length of the local sermons to the village school races. Each time, Jeeves quietly arranges a solution.
context: P. G. Wodehouse published the book in 1923, and it is one of the funniest of the Jeeves and Wooster books. Read [My Man Jeeves](/book/8077?lang=en) and [Leave It to Psmith](/book/54562?lang=en).

about: In 1917 Richard Hannay is called back from the Western Front and sent undercover, disguised as a pacifist South African, into the world of conscientious objectors and radical intellectuals in a garden city in the Cotswolds and on Clydeside, to track down a German master spy who is passing British secrets to the enemy. The trail leads him to the Isle of Skye, a perilous escape in the Alps and back to the front for the great German offensive of 1918, while he falls in love with Mary Lamington, a young woman working for the intelligence service.
context: John Buchan published the third Hannay novel in 1919; its title and many of its themes come from Bunyan's [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en), which Hannay carries with him as a codebook. Read [The Thirty-Nine Steps](/book/857?lang=en) and [Greenmantle](/book/858?lang=en).

about: In Edwardian London, Katharine Hilbery, granddaughter of a great Victorian poet, helps her mother write his biography by day and secretly studies mathematics and astronomy at night. She becomes engaged, without love, to William Rodney, a pedantic poet, while Ralph Denham, a young lawyer from a poorer family, falls in love with her, and her friend Mary Datchet, who works for the women's suffrage movement, loves Ralph. The novel follows the four of them as they try to discover what love and marriage should mean.
context: Virginia Woolf published her second novel in 1919. It is more traditional than her later books, and Katharine was partly modelled on her sister, the painter Vanessa Bell. Read [The Voyage Out](/book/489?lang=en), [Jacob's Room](/book/5713?lang=en) and [Mrs Dalloway](/book/348?lang=en).

about: In the title story, Laura Sheridan, the daughter of a comfortable family in New Zealand, is helping her mother prepare a grand garden party when news comes that a young carter who lived in the poor cottages below has been killed in an accident. She wants to stop the party; her family will not, and afterwards she is sent down with a basket of leftovers to the dead man's house. The collection also includes 'The Daughters of the Late Colonel', 'Her First Ball', 'The Voyage' and 'Miss Brill'.
context: Katherine Mansfield (1888–1923), born in New Zealand, published the book in 1922, the year before she died of tuberculosis at thirty-four. Her delicate, impressionistic stories changed the modern short story. Compare Chekhov's [The Darling](/book/12036?lang=en); she admired him deeply.

about: Lilia Herriton, a lively young English widow, travels to Italy and, to the horror of her stuffy in-laws, marries Gino Carella, the handsome, penniless son of a dentist in a small Tuscan town. When she dies giving birth to a son, the Herritons send her young brother-in-law Philip and his rigid sister Harriet to bring the baby back to England, with the help of Caroline Abbott, who had been Lilia's companion, and the clash of English respectability and Italian life ends in disaster.
context: E. M. Forster published his first novel in 1905, at twenty-six; its title comes from Alexander Pope's line 'For fools rush in where angels fear to tread'. Read [A Room with a View](/book/2780?lang=en) and [Howards End](/book/3074?lang=en).

about: Claude Wheeler, the sensitive, restless son of a prosperous Nebraska farmer, feels out of place on the farm and in his loveless marriage to Enid, a cold, religious young woman. When America enters the First World War he enlists, survives an influenza epidemic on the troopship crossing the Atlantic, and in the army and on the battlefields of France finds, for the first time, a sense of purpose and comradeship.
context: Willa Cather based Claude on her cousin G. P. Cather, who was killed in France in 1918, and published the novel in 1922; it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923, though some critics, Hemingway among them, thought its war scenes unconvincing. Read [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en) and [A Lost Lady](/book/59836?lang=en).

about: Alice Adams, a pretty, clever and ambitious girl in a Midwestern city, longs to belong to the world of the rich young people she grew up with, but her family is poor: her father is a sick clerk at a wholesale drug company, and her mother nags him into starting a glue factory of his own. When the wealthy Arthur Russell begins to court her, Alice invents a grander life for herself and her family to impress him, and dreads the dinner at which he will see the truth.
context: Booth Tarkington published the novel in 1921, and it won him his second Pulitzer Prize, after [The Magnificent Ambersons](/book/8549?lang=en). The 1935 film starred Katharine Hepburn.

about: Three portraits of working women in 'Bridgepoint', a city modelled on Baltimore: the good Anna, a German servant who devotes her life to managing other people; Melanctha, a young Black woman searching restlessly for understanding and love in a long affair with a cautious doctor, Jeff Campbell; and the gentle Lena, a passive German immigrant girl married off to a man she hardly knows.
context: Gertrude Stein (1874–1946), the American writer whose Paris salon welcomed Picasso and Hemingway, published the book in 1909 at her own expense. Its repetitive, rhythmic style, shaped by Cézanne's painting and by the psychology of her teacher William James, was a landmark of modernist prose, though its racial language belongs to its time. Compare Sherwood Anderson's [Winesburg, Ohio](/book/718?lang=en).

about: Genji, 'the Shining Prince', is the beautiful, gifted son of a Japanese emperor and one of his lesser wives, removed from the line of succession and made a commoner. This first part of the tale follows his youth at the imperial court of Heian Kyoto: his secret love for his stepmother, the empress Fujitsubo, his many affairs, and his discovery of the young girl Murasaki, whom he raises to become his ideal wife, in a world of poetry, music, perfumes and refined feeling.
context: Written around the year 1000 by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese court, the Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel. This is the first volume of Arthur Waley's celebrated translation, published in 1925, containing nine chapters; the story continues in five further volumes. Compare Okakura's [The Book of Tea](/book/1051?lang=en).

about: A stranger staggers into Hercule Poirot's flat, covered in dust and close to death, and can only repeat the words 'the Big Four' and the number four before he dies. Poirot and his friend Hastings discover that the Big Four is an international criminal organisation, led by a Chinese mastermind and including an American millionaire, a French woman scientist and a deadly, unknown 'destroyer', which plans to seize control of the world. The chase leads through murders and traps from London to the Italian mountains.
context: Agatha Christie put the book together in 1927 from linked short stories, at a difficult time in her life, and it is an unusual Poirot adventure, closer to a spy thriller; its Chinese villain reflects the stereotypes of its time. Read [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: Ruth Kettering, the daughter of an American millionaire, is travelling to the Riviera on the luxurious Blue Train, carrying a famous ruby called the Heart of Fire, when she is found strangled in her compartment and the jewel is gone. Hercule Poirot, who happens to be on the train, investigates, together with Katherine Grey, a young woman who has just inherited a fortune and spoke with Ruth on the journey. The suspects include Ruth's charming, bankrupt husband and her lover.
context: Agatha Christie expanded the novel from an earlier short story and published it in 1928; she later said she disliked it, but it remains a lively Riviera mystery, and it entered the public domain in the United States in 2024. Read [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: At Chimneys, the great country house of The Secret of Chimneys, a group of young guests play a practical joke on Gerry Wade, a heavy sleeper, by placing eight alarm clocks in his room, but in the morning he is found dead of an overdose, with seven of the clocks lined up on the mantelpiece. The lively Lady Eileen 'Bundle' Brent investigates, uncovers a secret society that meets in masks at a nightclub in the Seven Dials district of London, and is helped by the quiet Superintendent Battle.
context: Agatha Christie published the novel in 1929 as a sequel to [The Secret of Chimneys](/book/59468?lang=en), and it entered the public domain in the United States in 2025. It is a light-hearted thriller full of 1920s high spirits.

about: Tommy and Tuppence Beresford, now married and a little bored, take over a detective agency, Blunt's International Detectives, as a cover for catching foreign spies, and solve a series of cases in the styles of famous fictional detectives, Sherlock Holmes, Father Brown, Dr Thorndyke and others, with Tommy and Tuppence imitating each one in turn. The stories are full of parody and jokes about the detective fiction of the 1920s.
context: Agatha Christie collected the stories in 1929, and the book entered the public domain in the United States in 2025. Read the first Tommy and Tuppence novel, [The Secret Adversary](/book/1394?lang=en), and Chesterton's [The Innocence of Father Brown](/book/523?lang=en).

about: Lord Peter Wimsey's elder brother, the Duke of Denver, is arrested for the murder of their sister's fiancé, Captain Denis Cathcart, found shot dead outside a shooting lodge in Yorkshire in the middle of the night. The Duke refuses to say where he was at the time and is put on trial for murder before the House of Lords. With his loyal manservant Bunter and his friend Inspector Parker, Lord Peter races to find the truth, from the moors to the other side of the Atlantic.
context: Dorothy L. Sayers (1893–1957), one of the great writers of the golden age of detective fiction, published the novel in 1926, the second Wimsey mystery after [Whose Body?](/book/53430?lang=en). The trial of a peer in the House of Lords was real legal history; the last one took place in 1935. Compare Agatha Christie's [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: Ten years after Little Men, Plumfield has grown into a college, and Jo, now a famous author pestered by admirers, watches the boys she raised grow into young men: Nat studies music in Germany, Dan goes west and falls into terrible trouble, Emil goes to sea and survives a shipwreck, and Tommy, Demi and the others choose their careers and their loves, while the girls, Nan and Josie, insist on becoming a doctor and an actress.
context: Louisa May Alcott published the book in 1886, two years before her death, ending the March family saga that began with [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en). Read [Little Men](/book/2922?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/alcott?lang=en).

about: Anne Shirley leaves Avonlea to study at Redmond College in the city of Kingsport, with her friends Priscilla and the beautiful, cheerful flirt Philippa, and they share a cosy house called Patty's Place. Over four years Anne writes stories, receives a series of comic proposals and falls for a dark, handsome stranger who seems her ideal, while refusing to see that she has long loved Gilbert Blythe, whose proposal she has turned down.
context: L. M. Montgomery published the third Anne book in 1915, drawing on her own year at Dalhousie College in Halifax. Read [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en) and [Anne of Avonlea](/book/422?lang=en).

about: Rilla Blythe, Anne's youngest daughter, is a pretty, rather vain fifteen-year-old who wants nothing but fun and parties when the First World War breaks out. As her brothers go off one after another to fight in France, Rilla grows up: she takes in a war baby whose mother has died, organises a Junior Red Cross, waits for letters and casualty lists and learns courage, while Susan, the family's devoted housekeeper, follows every battle on the map.
context: L. M. Montgomery published the novel in 1921, and it is one of the few novels of the First World War written from the home front by a Canadian woman who lived through it. Read [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en) and [Anne of the Island](/book/425?lang=en).

about: Dorothy Gale, sailing with her Uncle Henry to Australia, is washed overboard in a storm with a hen named Billina, who can talk, and lands in the magic Land of Ev, next to Oz. There she meets Tik-Tok, a clockwork copper man who must be wound up to think, speak and move, and Princess Langwidere, who changes her head every day. With Ozma, the ruler of Oz, she sets out to free the royal family of Ev from the cruel Nome King, who has turned them into ornaments in his underground palace.
