context: L. Frank Baum published the third Oz book in 1907, bringing Dorothy back for the first time since [The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](/book/314?lang=en). Read [The Marvelous Land of Oz](/book/427?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/baum?lang=en).

about: The five children of Five Children and It find a strange egg inside a second-hand carpet, and when it falls into the fire it hatches into a vain, talkative Phoenix. The carpet turns out to be magic and will carry them anywhere they wish, three wishes a day: to a tower in France, a tropical island, a bazaar in India and, disastrously, back home with a cargo of 199 Persian cats and a cow. Meanwhile the Phoenix insists on being worshipped at a London fire insurance office that bears its name.
context: E. Nesbit published the book in 1904, the second of her trilogy after [Five Children and It](/book/1060?lang=en). Read also [The Railway Children](/book/2073?lang=en).

about: A lonely, whimsical old bachelor living near Kensington Gardens in London befriends a small boy, David, and tells him stories as they walk in the park. The most famous of them explains how babies were once birds, and how one of them, Peter Pan, only a week old, flew out of his nursery window back to Kensington Gardens, where he lives on an island with the birds and the fairies, can never grow up and can never go home again.
context: J. M. Barrie published the book in 1902; it was the first appearance of Peter Pan, two years before the play, and its Peter Pan chapters were later published on their own as Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens. Read the later [Peter Pan](/book/397?lang=en).

about: The first of Andrew Lang's famous coloured fairy books gathers thirty-seven fairy tales from around the world: from Perrault and the Brothers Grimm come Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, the Sleeping Beauty, Rumpelstiltskin and Hansel and Grettel; from Norway, East of the Sun and West of the Moon; from the Arabian Nights, Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp; and from other lands Jack the Giant-Killer, Beauty and the Beast and many more.
context: Lang (1844–1912), a Scottish scholar and folklorist, published the book in 1889, and its success led to eleven more volumes, each named after a colour, which brought the world's fairy tales to generations of English-speaking children. Read Lang's [The Arabian Nights Entertainments](/book/479?lang=en).

about: In the fashionable spa town of Bath, the romantic young heiress Lydia Languish, who has read too many novels, wants to marry a poor soldier rather than a rich gentleman. So Captain Jack Absolute, who loves her, courts her disguised as the penniless Ensign Beverley, and finds himself his own rival when his father arranges for him to marry the same girl. Around them gather Lydia's aunt, Mrs Malaprop, who constantly confuses long words, a jealous lover, a cowardly country squire and a fire-eating Irish duellist.
context: Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote the comedy at twenty-three, and it was first performed in 1775. Mrs Malaprop's blunders, such as 'as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile', gave English the word 'malapropism'. Read Sheridan's [The School for Scandal](/book/2126?lang=en).

about: Mirabell, a witty young man of fashion, wants to marry the beautiful, independent Millamant, but half her fortune is controlled by her aunt, the vain, ageing Lady Wishfort, who hates Mirabell because he once pretended to court her. To win Millamant and her money, Mirabell sets up an elaborate trick in which his servant poses as a nobleman, while the scheming Fainall and his mistress plot against everyone. In the famous 'proviso scene', the two lovers set out the conditions on which they will agree to marry.
context: William Congreve (1670–1729) staged the comedy in 1700, and although it was not a success at first, it is now regarded as the finest of the Restoration comedies of manners. Compare Sheridan's [The School for Scandal](/book/2126?lang=en).

about: Gregers Werle, the idealistic son of a rich merchant, returns home after years away and visits his old school friend Hjalmar Ekdal, a photographer, who lives happily with his wife Gina, their fourteen-year-old daughter Hedvig and his old father, who keeps a wounded wild duck and other animals in the attic as a make-believe forest. Gregers, convinced that their happiness rests on lies, decides to tell Hjalmar the truth about his marriage, with devastating consequences for the child.
context: Henrik Ibsen wrote the play in 1884, a turning point in his work: a tragicomedy that asks whether people can live without their 'life-lies'. This translation is by Eleanor Marx, the daughter of Karl Marx. Read Ibsen's [A Doll's House](/book/338?lang=en) and [An Enemy of the People](/book/2596?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/ibsen?lang=en).

about: Harpagon, a wealthy widower of Paris, loves money more than anything in the world, including his own children. He keeps a box of ten thousand crowns buried in his garden, suspects everyone of stealing, starves his servants and his horses, and plans to marry his son to a rich widow and his daughter to an old man who will take her without a dowry, while he himself courts Mariane, the young woman his son loves. When the money box is stolen, he goes mad with grief.
context: Molière first staged the comedy in 1668, basing it on a play by the Roman writer Plautus, and Harpagon's name became a French word for a miser. This translation is by Charles Heron Wall. Read Molière's [Tartuffe](/book/2217?lang=en).

about: In the Greek city of Troezen, Phaedra, the wife of the hero Theseus, is consumed by a guilty, hopeless passion for her stepson Hippolytus, who loves the princess Aricia. When false news comes that Theseus is dead, Phaedra confesses her love to Hippolytus, who recoils in horror. Then Theseus returns alive, and Phaedra's nurse, to protect her mistress, accuses Hippolytus of attempting to seduce his stepmother, and Theseus calls down the curse of Neptune on his son.
context: Jean Racine (1639–1699), the greatest tragic poet of French classicism, staged the play in 1677, drawing on Euripides and Seneca, and it is considered his masterpiece. This translation is by Robert Bruce Boswell. Compare the [Medea](/book/31777?lang=en) of Euripides.

about: Young Ellie Dunn arrives for a weekend at the strange, ship-shaped country house of the eccentric old Captain Shotover, an inventor of explosives who is half mad and wholly wise. Among the guests, all of whom seem to be lying to themselves and to each other, are Ellie's father, her fiancé, the rich businessman Boss Mangan, and the captain's two dazzling daughters. As their illusions fall away one by one, bombers appear in the night sky.
context: Bernard Shaw wrote the play during the First World War and published it in 1919, calling it 'a fantasia in the Russian manner on English themes', after Chekhov, as a portrait of the cultured, idle Europe that drifted into the war. Read [Pygmalion](/book/3914?lang=en) and [Arms and the Man](/book/3712?lang=en).

about: On an island off the west coast of Ireland, old Maurya has lost her husband, his father and four of her sons to the sea. Now her daughters wait for news of the fifth son, Michael, missing at sea, while her last son, Bartley, insists on taking horses across to the fair on the mainland though a storm is coming. In one act of spare, rhythmic prose, the play moves towards its quiet, devastating end.
context: John Millington Synge based the play, first performed in 1904, on what he saw on the Aran Islands, and it is often called the finest one-act tragedy in English; Ralph Vaughan Williams set it as an opera. Read Synge's [The Playboy of the Western World](/book/1474?lang=en).

about: The Titan Prometheus, who stole fire from heaven and gave it to humanity along with the arts of civilisation, is chained to a rock at the edge of the world by order of Zeus. Visited by the daughters of Ocean, by Oceanus himself and by the wandering Io, a girl tormented by Zeus's desire and turned into a heifer, he refuses to bow, for he alone knows a secret that could one day overthrow the king of the gods. The volume also contains Aeschylus's Seven Against Thebes.
context: Attributed to Aeschylus, though some scholars doubt it, the play has made Prometheus a symbol of rebellion against tyranny for Shelley, Goethe, Marx and many others. This prose translation is by Theodore Buckley. Read Aeschylus's [The House of Atreus](/book/8355?lang=en).

about: Athens has lost its great tragic poets, so Dionysus, god of the theatre, travels down to the underworld, disguised as Heracles and followed by his grumbling slave Xanthias, to bring back Euripides. After crossing the lake of the dead, where a chorus of frogs croaks 'Brekekekex koax koax', he finds himself judging a contest between Euripides and the older Aeschylus, who even weigh their verses on a giant scale, and Dionysus finally chooses the poet who can best save the city.
context: Aristophanes staged the comedy in 405 BC, soon after the deaths of Euripides and Sophocles and shortly before Athens lost its war with Sparta, and it won first prize. It is the earliest work of literary criticism in the form of a comedy. Read his [Lysistrata](/book/7685?lang=en) and the [Medea](/book/31777?lang=en) of Euripides.

about: In the village of Grand-Pré in Acadia, today's Nova Scotia, Evangeline Bellefontaine is betrothed to Gabriel Lajeunesse when, in 1755, the British expel the French-speaking Acadians from their homeland, burn their villages and scatter them along the coast of America. Separated on the shore, the lovers are carried to different places, and Evangeline spends her life searching for Gabriel across the continent, from the bayous of Louisiana to the prairies, until she becomes a nurse among the poor of Philadelphia.
context: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published the poem in 1847, in unrhymed hexameters beginning 'This is the forest primeval', and it made the expulsion of the Acadians known around the world. Read Longfellow's [The Song of Hiawatha](/book/400?lang=en).

about: In 1833 Alfred Tennyson's closest friend, the brilliant young Arthur Henry Hallam, engaged to Tennyson's sister, died suddenly in Vienna at twenty-two. Over the next seventeen years Tennyson wrote these 131 short poems of mourning, moving from shock and despair, through doubt, as the new science of geology seemed to show a nature 'red in tooth and claw', to a hard-won faith and hope: ''Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.'
context: Published anonymously in 1850, the poem became Queen Victoria's great comfort after the death of Prince Albert, and Tennyson was made Poet Laureate the same year. This is the first edition, published by Edward Moxon. Read Tennyson's [Idylls of the King](/book/907?lang=en).

about: In 1643 the English Parliament ordered that every book must be approved by an official censor before it was printed. John Milton replied with this speech, written as if addressed to Parliament, arguing that censorship insults readers, cannot work and stifles the search for truth: 'Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties.' Truth, he says, has nothing to fear from a free and open encounter with falsehood.
context: Milton published the pamphlet in 1644, without a licence, naming it after the Areopagus, the hill of Athens where a council met, in memory of a speech by the Greek orator Isocrates. It became one of the founding texts of the freedom of the press. Compare [Mill's On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en), and see [Milton's life](/author/milton?lang=en).

about: Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu), the great Taoist philosopher of the fourth century BC, teaches through stories, jokes and paradoxes rather than arguments. He dreams that he is a butterfly, and on waking cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he is a man; a cook carves an ox so skilfully, following its natural lines, that his knife never grows dull; and a giant tree survives because it is useless for timber. Behind them lies a call to give up fixed ideas and live in harmony with the Tao.
context: This translation, published in 1889 by the British diplomat and sinologist Herbert Allen Giles, with a note by Aubrey Moore, was one of the first complete English versions, and Oscar Wilde praised it in a famous review. Read the [Tao Teh King](/book/531?lang=en) and [The Analects](/book/258?lang=en).

about: At twenty-two, Friedrich Engels, the son of a German textile manufacturer, was sent to work in his father's firm in Manchester, then the industrial capital of the world. Walking its streets with the Irish working woman Mary Burns, he recorded what he saw: the airless courts and cellars where workers' families lived, the filth and disease, child labour, the long hours and accidents in the mills, and the gulf between the comfortable middle-class districts and the slums hidden behind the main streets.
context: Engels published the book in German in 1845, at twenty-four, and it became a founding work of the socialist movement and an influence on his friend Karl Marx. This English translation of 1887 is by the American reformer Florence Kelley. Read [The Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en) and Elizabeth Gaskell's [Mary Barton](/book/2338?lang=en), set in the same city.

about: Starting from the fantasies and poems of a young American woman known as Miss Miller, Carl Gustav Jung follows the images of the unconscious mind through the myths and religions of the world: the hero's journey, the sun god, sacrifice, the mother and rebirth. He argues that libido is not only sexual energy, as Freud held, but a general psychic energy, and that myths express patterns shared by all humanity.
context: Published in German in 1912 as Transformations and Symbols of the Libido, the book brought about Jung's break with Freud, his former mentor. This English translation of 1916 is by Beatrice M. Hinkle. Read Freud's [The Interpretation of Dreams](/book/159?lang=en) and [Dream Psychology](/book/13801?lang=en).

about: What is education for in a democratic society? John Dewey argues that it should not be the passive filling of children's minds with facts, but a process of growth through experience, in which children learn by doing, by solving real problems and by working together. A school, he says, should be a small democratic community, and education is not merely a preparation for life but part of living itself, the means by which a society renews itself.
context: Dewey (1859–1952), the American philosopher and reformer who founded an experimental school in Chicago, published the book in 1916, and it remains one of the most influential works on education ever written. Compare William James's [Pragmatism](/book/5179?lang=en).

about: Three years after The Prisoner of Zenda, Rudolf Rassendyll's old enemy, the charming, unscrupulous Rupert of Hentzau, gets hold of a farewell letter that Queen Flavia has written to Rassendyll, the Englishman she still loves, and plans to show it to the jealous, sickly King Rudolf to ruin her. Fritz von Tarlenheim, the queen's loyal friend, who tells the story, and Rassendyll himself must stop him, and once again the Englishman's likeness to the king leads to a dangerous masquerade.
context: Anthony Hope published the sequel in 1898, and it is darker and more tragic than the first book; Rupert is one of the most charming villains in adventure fiction. Read [The Prisoner of Zenda](/book/459?lang=en).

about: In twenty books, Flavius Josephus tells the history of the Jewish people for Greek and Roman readers, from the creation of the world through the stories of the Hebrew Bible, the Persian and Greek periods, the revolt of the Maccabees and the reign of Herod the Great, up to the eve of the great revolt against Rome in AD 66. He adds much that is not in the Bible, and his short passages about John the Baptist and Jesus have been debated for centuries.
context: Josephus finished the work in Rome around AD 93, after his [Wars of the Jews](/book/2982?lang=en), and it is an essential source for the history of Judea under Herod and the Romans. This is the classic translation of 1737 by William Whiston.

about: Writing in a monastery in the north of England, Bede tells the history of Britain from the Roman invasion to his own day, and above all the story of how the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms became Christian: the mission of Augustine, sent by Pope Gregory in 597, the Irish monks of Iona and Lindisfarne, kings and saints, councils and miracles. It includes the famous image of human life as a sparrow flying through a lighted hall in winter, out of darkness and back into darkness.
context: Bede (about 673–735), the most learned scholar of his age, finished the book in 731, and he did much to spread the custom of dating events from the birth of Christ. It is the foundation of English history. This translation is by A. M. Sellar. Compare [The Confessions of St. Augustine](/book/3417?lang=en).

about: This famous medieval book presents itself as the account of an English knight, Sir John Mandeville, who left England in 1322 and travelled for thirty-four years through the Holy Land, Egypt, Persia, India and China, serving, he says, the Sultan of Egypt and the Great Khan. He describes the holy places of Jerusalem and the pilgrim routes, includes a surprisingly respectful chapter on the beliefs of Muslims, and tells of marvels: the land of Prester John, people with their faces in their chests, the fountain of youth and a lamb that grows on a tree.
context: Written in French around 1357 and soon translated into many languages, the book was one of the most popular of the Middle Ages, and Columbus is said to have read it. Its author was probably not a traveller at all but a skilful compiler of other travellers' accounts. This edition was published by Macmillan in 1900. Compare [The Travels of Marco Polo](/book/254?lang=en).

about: From the first day of 1660 to May 1669, Samuel Pepys, a young official in the English Navy Office, kept a secret diary in shorthand. He records the great events of his time, the return of King Charles II, the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London in 1666, which he watched from a boat on the Thames, alongside every detail of his private life: his quarrels with his wife, his flirtations, his dinners, his music, his new clothes, and his worries about money and his failing eyes.
context: Pepys (1633–1703) rose to become one of the most important naval administrators in English history. His diary was deciphered and first published in 1825; this text, edited by Lord Braybrooke, is an early edition that leaves out its franker passages. It is one of the most vivid personal records ever written. Compare Defoe's [A Journal of the Plague Year](/book/679?lang=en).
